The cipher Simple substitution of invented signs for Spanish letters, with a dotted sign for que and a dotted H for Xebres (Chièvres). How it was read Tomokiyo’s key, rebuilt from Ayala’s letter of 12 July (R10024), fits unchanged. After three transcription passes all but seven words were read. What it says The first cipher line reads cerca delos oficios que estan vacos en estos reynos . Still open Doubtful words marked [?]. The letter had been deciphered in 1849 and printed in 1875, found only after this reading; that print settles the seven words. Credit Tomokiyo for the key.

AGS 0001 (DECODE image 1) is Ayala’s clear opening page. The cipher runs over AGS 0002–0006, which DECODE shows in the order 8, 2, 3, 6, 4. AGS 0008 is the address leaf, endorsed 1516 and Cardenal de España . The cipher is a simple substitution of invented signs for Spanish letters. It has a few variants ( a written 9 or 6, o with or without a stroke above), a dotted sign for que and a dotted H for Xebres (Chièvres). Words are separated by small spaces or dots. The key is Tomokiyo’s, transcribed in targets/ayala1516/KEY.md . Three signs are not in it: an arch-shaped sign (perhaps cl ), a tall I (an s variant) and Φ (= m on AGS 0004). Offices (AGS 0002) cerca de los oficios que estan vacos en estos reynos y los inconvinientes que ay de proverse a personas que los venden a don Xebres … dizen que V. S. los provee todos … por tanto que haga V. S. tan bien alla lo que aconseja, cierto que verian que alla no se proveyese en ninguno, y asi lo escrive Su Alteza. Los oficios que Su Alteza a dado y prometido … al marques de Villena un regimiento de Toledo que era de Baeza, a Rodrigo Niño otro de Plasencia … el regimiento de Cuenca diz que tiene Su Alteza para Vasco de Acuña, hermano de Pedro de Acuña … crea V. S. que quanto esta vaco esta pedido y prometido para alla o hecha la provision. The King has many servants here who have served him; Cisneros should give them offices, since it is said here that he fills most of them with his own men. The Genoese are referred to him over the Cartagena galleys: provea V. S. alla como vere conviene a servicio del rey; no se altere por carta ni cedula que alla vea, que aca muchas cosas se proveen por ymportunidades. Castile and Queen Germaine (AGS 0003–0004) The King was glad of the pacification of the kingdoms and that the Constable and the Infantado stood with Cisneros. Ayala warned His Highness that Queen Germaine trae tratos con franceses , and a marriage with the house of the Duke of Alba is in hand. On AGS 0004: don García de Padilla, the cedula for the Orders, and que obedezcan primero y se castigue , for if disobedience goes unpunished it will spread through the kingdom; the people of Arévalo, and mil males del reyno . The peace and the voyage (AGS 0005) la paz se concluyo entre el rey nuestro señor y el rey de Francia, como por los capitulos della vera V. S., que aqui le enbio; manda Su Alteza que luego la haga V. S. pregonar … De la yda hago saber a V. S. que el rey … sabado treynta de agosto, y en el se acordo de partir sin falta … y se partira para Gelanda … todo estara a punto, y dandole Dios [tiempo] enbarcara, y para esto no tiene estorvo ninguno sino el tiempo. The peace is Noyon (13 August 1516). The secretary Barroso arrived six days earlier; Ayala spoke to the King before him and gave him his credence, and Cisneros’s protests have done much good. Orders and Toledo (AGS 0006) pienso que esta llevara lo de las ordenes, y no es posible; yo pido una cedula para que V. S. pueda poner presidentes cuales le pareciere que conviniente … en lo del corregidor de Toledo … V. S. provea de corregidor, que al rey le plazera. The rest of AGS 0003 and 0004 (second pass) AGS 0003 goes on to a man at court who writes mil mentiras : …ho credito a sus avisos, y yo no se por que a ese le quiso dar V. S. tanta autoridad, aviendo sido avisado de cuan mal todos estavan con el en lo de las ordenes de Calatrava y Santiago y Alcantara; por eso se enbio a V. S. el poder para que lo remedie . On AGS 0004 the Comendador mayor of Calatrava protested against Cisneros’s power; Malaga nos a puesto en mucha confusion with a commission bearing two hundred signatures; teniamos lo por acabado . The marriage is con el duque d’Alva , and some there write que V. S. dize mal de Xebres . The end of the letter (AGS 0005–0006) The King junto consejo on the Saturday; by 15 September he will be at Antwerp. Ayala gave the King his credence y requerile que por negocio ninguno cesase su partida . On AGS 0006: y respondeme a esto que pues el rey va que alla se hara, y si la yda cesare que la daran ; he has named for the posts don Alonso Tellez and a don Pedro; he gave Cisneros’s credence a solas , and was told that el y el chanciller son una persona (Chièvres and Chancellor Le Sauvage). The letter closes on the friendship to be made entre V. S. y el que la desea , y con esta amistad se hara mucho servicio a Dios y al rey . There is no signature in cipher. Third pass New on the third pass: Malága’s courier came con cinco mil y tantas firmas ; Ayala always insisted que obedezcan primero y se castigue su inobedencia, porque si no se castiga sera dar enxenplo de inobediencia a cuantos lugares ay en el reyno . From Cisneros’s own household it is written que v. s. dize mal de Xebres y que se arma contra el, y que ay en casa de v. s. se dize que el rey es inabil, y que yo e escrito mil males del reyno . At Antwerp the King will take leave of the Estates y hara la orden de la Tusion (the Golden Fleece) before Zeeland. The two nominees are don Alonso Tellez y don Pedro su sobrino ; the corregidor of Toledo is to be named at once y como sea hecho quitar se a de ynportunidades .

The address leaf carries, upside down, the note Copiado lo descifrado para D. … García. Simancas 14 de Ag[osto] de 1849 and a second Copiado lo descifrado p[ar]a los Sres. … . The copy went into Pascual de Gayangos and Vicente de la Fuente, Cartas de los secretarios del cardenal D. Fr. Francisco Jiménez de Cisneros durante su regencia (Madrid 1875). The edition splits the letter in two. Carta XLIX (pp. 213–219) has the clear opening and the cipher on offices, Málaga and Arévalo, and is cited as Estado 496 fol. 318. Carta LIV (pp. 238–241) runs from the peace to the end, is cited as fol. 22, and is misdated 1517. The decipherment here was finished before the edition was found. Checked against it: The seven open words: sábese ; the code sign after gente del is emperador ; condestable, infantadgo, Benavente ; era engañado ; diziendo en quanta perdición están ; yo ; and the dotted sign is Xebres: Mos de Xebrés oyó la creencia . Corrections to the decipherment here: el de Lanuça (deciphered here as nu[n]ca ), solo por tocar a v. s. , después de oyda , con fe que me dio , con juramento lo comunicásemos . Everything else agrees, apart from the editors’ spelling.

Before the edition was found, a third pass enlarged every doubtful word four times and settled it against the transcribed signs and the Spanish. Seven stayed open, and the print has since settled all of them (above): AGS 0002 l.12 a word rabese (perhaps sabese ); l.15 a dotted code sign after gente del , value unknown. AGS 0003 l.5 venavente after condestable e ynfantado ; l.19 empeñado or engañado . AGS 0004 l.13 the sense of diziendo en cuanta ; AGS 0005 l.18 the form of yo ; AGS 0006 l.17 a dotted person sign (Mos[iur] de …), not in the key. Also short gaps on AGS 0004 (the Arévalo sentence) and at the end of three paragraphs. Key corrections to Tomokiyo’s table: Φ = m and the hook = j/x; the tall I and a looped sign are s; X· is que and q inside words; H· is Xebres; a dotted sign is Francia; a curled t variant.

The transcription and the decryption of every document on this page, so that the reading can be used and checked. Short files are shown here; all are in the repository. Brussels, 30 Aug 1516 (AGS 0002-0006) Diego López de Ayala, Cisneros's agent at Charles's court in Brussels, reports that offices in Castile are sold at court to unworthy men and granted from Flanders over the regent's head, on the Arévalo and Málaga affairs and the power over the military Orders, and that peace (probably with France) is concluded and the king resolved to embark from Zeeland. reading.txt is the project's reading; the two print files are the 1849 Simancas decipherment as printed by Gayangos and de la Fuente (1875), split into Cartas XLIX and LIV. Page labels kept. --> # Diego López de Ayala (Brussels) to Cardinal Cisneros, 30 August 1516 (AGS Estado leg. 496 fol. 22, DECODE R9954): English translation of the ciphered part AGS 0002 As to the offices that are vacant in these kingdoms, and the drawbacks of their being filled from here with persons who sell them to base men, His Highness says that this will be looked to closely from now on. People say that Your Lordship fills all of them, and His Highness hardly any; so let Your Lordship do there as well what you advise here; certainly they would see that none was filled there, and so His Highness writes. The offices that His Highness has given and promised, as far as I know, are these: to the Marquis of Villena a regidorship of Toledo that was Baeza's; to Rodrigo Niño another of Plasencia; and this one ⟨is known? — ciphertext "rabese"⟩ here that Your Lordship gave to a nephew of Carvajal; that His Highness, they say, holds the regidorship of Cuenca for Vasco de Acuña, brother of Pedro de Acuña of Toledo, who is colonel of certain troops of the ⟨a nomenclator word, value unknown⟩. Your Lordship may believe that whatever is vacant has been asked for and either promised for there or the appointment made. And on this, too, Your Lordship should consider that the King has many here who have served him, and that he should do them favour, and that Your Lordship should obtain offices for them when they are capable of them; for here it is said that you give most offices to your own servants; remember those of the King. The Genoese refer to Your Lordship the matter of Cartagena and the galleys; the provision carries some favour; let Your Lordship provide there as you see fit for the King's service; do not be moved by any letter or warrant that you AGS 0003 may see there, for here many things are granted out of importunity and not from any wish that they be carried out. His Highness is very glad of the pacification of these kingdoms and of the peace there is in them, and to know that these lords, the Constable [and] the Infantado, ⟨unread word⟩ are in agreement with Your Lordship for his service. I say again that it should be greatly valued. I also informed His Highness that Queen Germaine is having dealings with the French, etc. Your Lordship is much to blame for what is done with her, because of what was asked at the beginning. They are informed; likewise of how she is guided by Alba in this business of Arévalo, she has won; for it is written from here that she is negotiating a marriage with the Duke of Alba. These people are still for giving her those places, and I always advise them to put it off; and everything I said about her, I said with the protest that it should be secret. I also told His Highness who the ambassador was, and how ⟨pledged? deceived?⟩ to write a thousand lies; they are quite sure that it is so, or else no great credit is given to his reports; and I do not know why Your Lordship chose to give that man so much authority, having been warned how badly everyone stood with him in the matter of the orders of Calatrava, Santiago and Alcántara. That is why the power was sent to Your Lordship to remedy it, and nothing more is needed for it AGS 0004 ... the forces of them, which Your Lordship has, to remove and appoint whom you see fit. Don García de Padilla, as Your Lordship will already have learned, cannot go, for he is so busy now. I send the provision or warrant for the matter of the orders as Your Lordship asks for it. The Comendador Mayor of Calatrava sent a courier about Your Lordship's power; here they have laughed a great deal at his coarse conscience, and the one of the nu[n]cio would not properly involve himself in it, although the courier came to him, only through another letter to Your Lordship. In this step there has been good, and that is why I write it, and I would wish it to continue. Málaga has put us in great confusion with a courier they sent with five thousand and some signatures, saying how much[?] everything is lost; and from the letters Your Lordship had written we held it as settled. There have been many opinions on it: whether to send someone to deal with it, or to revoke the first provision. I have always insisted that they should obey first and their disobedience be punished, because if it is not punished it will be to give an example of disobedience to every town in the kingdom; it is being put back to Your Lordship. As you will see, let Your Lordship deal with them as His Highness wishes. Those of Arévalo protest ... the Queen has won in this tenure[?] ... that from there they have written here that she is negotiating a marriage with the Duke of Alba[?], very wickedly. Those of that league write from there; now they have written that Your Lordship speaks ill of Chièvres and is arming against him, and that in Your Lordship's house there it is said that the King is incapable, and that I have written a thousand evils of the kingdom and of them; by God, let Your Lordship take ... AGS 0005 Peace has been concluded between the King our lord and the King of France, as Your Lordship will see from its articles, which I send you herewith. His Highness orders Your Lordship to have it proclaimed at once. I have never been able to get them to let this courier go sooner. What kind of peace this is, there is no need for me to say, since they show it. Of the journey I inform Your Lordship that the King held a full council on Saturday the thirtieth of August, and in it it was agreed to leave without fail, for on the fifteenth of September he will be at Antwerp; he will take leave of the estates and hold the chapter of the Golden Fleece, and before that he will leave for Zeeland, where without fail everything will be ready, and he will wait for the weather, and with it, God granting, he will embark; and for this he has no hindrance but the weather. What I suspect is that, once His Highness has arrived there and done this ceremony, some hindrance will not be lacking, although, as I say, everyone desires the journey, and the King much ... Secretary Barroso arrived here six days ago, and I[?] spoke to the King before he did, and gave him my credence, and urged him not to give up his departure for anything, with the protests that Your Lordship writes; and without doubt it has done much good for everyone to answer His Highness, who will soon [write] by another post; and from now on let Your Lordship not allow any to be despatched without Your Lordship's knowing of it. AGS 0006 I think this letter will carry the matter of the orders, and it is not possible; I am asking for a warrant so that Your Lordship may appoint presidents as you think fitting, and they answer me on this that since the King is going, it will be done there; and if the journey were called off, they will give it. It seems to me that Your Lordship should write about this[?] and [?] name the persons who seem good to you for it; and here I have named Don Alonso Téllez and Don Pedro his nephew; they are satisfied with the two. In the matter of the corregidor of Toledo, it seems to me that Your Lordship should at once appoint a corregidor there, which will please the King, and once it is done it will put an end to importunities; and I say: pay no heed to any letter they write to you about him, because they order me to write this, so that if I make no mention of it in my own letter, Your Lordship should overlook it. Monsieur de ⟨6·⟩ [?] I [gave him] Your Lordship's credence, which I gave him alone, and [?] what means of keeping what I told him; and after my going he told me that since he and the Chancellor are one person, ... we three should communicate in everything, to make a good friendship between Your Lordship and him, which he desires; and as to providing for the rest I have no answer yet; I expect a good one, and with this friendship much service will be done to God and to the King. The named Battier key in NA 1.10.29 inv. 1209 reads Dutch reports from Madrid. Three letters validate the key, including 19 December 1686: four passages, 186 tokens, compared with the contemporary decipherment on 32R. Two letters pass the strict sense screen without a known contemporary decipherment: 24 April 1687, conservatively 230/235 (97.9%), and 8 April 1688, 313/323 (96.9%), conservatively 312/323 (96.6%). The volume remains partial; the earlier estimate was roughly 55%, with no revised denominator for the 235-token addition. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 7 October 2026 · updated 23 October 2026 Method: read with known key · Extent: partial (78% of the cipher) · On the map Contributed by WAINUT (solution) and Feyseel Nur (new cipher with solution) · Also credited · Contemporary key or decipherment (key or decipherment used) known key At a glance Known key applied · partial (78% of the cipher) The letters Pieter Battier, Dutch envoy extraordinary in Madrid, to Grand Pensionary Gaspar Fagel, 1686–1688. Where Nationaal Archief 3.01.18, inv. 401, 109 scans. The key is in 1.10.29, inv. 1209, 86 scans; DECODE R2794 gives an obsolete or erroneous inventory number, 5345. The cipher A homophonic letter table and an alphabetical Dutch codebook: the same numbers repeat in fifteen blocks distinguished by overhead marks and struck digits. How it was deciphered The key headed “Voor den Heer Extraord. Envoye Battier” was applied to the transcribed figures. Separate contemporary decipherments validate three letters, including the four numbered passages on 32R for 19 December 1686, strengthening the identification of inv. 1209 as Battier’s key. Result Two letters pass strict sense without a known contemporary decipherment: 24 April 1687, 230/235 = 97.9% conservatively ; 8 April 1688, 313/323 = 96.9%, conservatively 312/323 = 96.6%. The 19 December 1686 reading is validation against 32R: four passages, 186 tokens. 4 December 1687 and 12 February 1688, below 95% in that review, were deciphered again as whole letters on 22 October 2026 after their cipher blocks were re-read on the scans; eight more passages located in the volume were deciphered on 23 October. What it says Gastanaga may be removed or employed in Peru or Catalonia; the Emperor’s ambassador seeks the Queen’s favour through a nun, the confessor, ministers and friendship with the Countess of Soissons. Madrid delays funding the Netherlands and appointments prompt factional manoeuvres: “brouwen wat met malkander”. Still open Six passages decoded, not read (67L, 73R, 80R, 94R after line 5, 99L, 102L); WAINUT’s eight 1687 passages wait on an eye check of 158 machine-read key rows; names, mark choices and several constructions remain uncertain. The volume estimate is about 78%. Credit Decipherment by Feyseel Nur (with Claude and Codex). Manuscript images: Nationaal Archief, CC0. The cipher after “voor den Opperstal Meester te vinden syn” describes a sworn party: the Constable, Osuna(?) and Monterey “brouwen wat met malkander”. Osuna remains speculative. Manuscript image: CC0.

Battier's correspondence survives in inv. 401 of archive 3.01.18. The key in the Fagel papers, archive 1.10.29, inv. 1209, names him explicitly. DECODE R2794 holds the key but cites “inv. nr. 5345”; that number is absent from the current 1.10.29 inventory. This contribution applies the known key, rather than recovering an unknown system. The prior-art search covered De Leeuw (2000), DECODE, Tomokiyo, editions and the Nationaal Archief digitised series. No edition was found. De Leeuw's 2000 study discusses Fagel codebooks but does not discuss Battier. The letters are not in DECODE. Contemporary decipherments do exist for 5 December 1686 (28R), 19 December 1686 (32R), 30 January 1687 (42R–43R), and interlinearly on 101R (26 February 1688). The parallel States General set, 1.01.02 inv. 12588.120–125, is not digitised. This is a bounded prior-art finding, not proof that no unpublished reading exists.

Scans 31R and 32L contain 186 cipher tokens. All 186 are key-attested and pass the review's strict sense screen. Scan 32R carries a numbered list 1–4 in a contemporary clerk's hand giving the plaintext of the four cipher passages. The key reading reproduces that list apart from spelling and “niet gedaan” versus “niet afgedaen”. This is a third validation letter, not a new reading, and strengthens the identification of inv. 1209 as Battier's key. The following are the ciphered stretches, with editorial spacing; the surrounding clear text discusses candidates for the Netherlands governorship and the money needed for it. van de Graaf van Mansfeld, maar sedert het dese laatste eens gemanqueert heeft, is syn persoon weynigh geaestimeert, en syn credit hier aan 't hof seer geringh, en daarom ook voor hem weynigh apparentie. maar daarom werden de publicqe affairen niet gedaan en blyft alles traineren. maar soo men die helft vinden kost, soude haastelyk een ander gouverneur de reys na Vlaanderen aannemen. soo veel impressie, dat men dan soo voorts op geen defensie gedenckt; en wat noch meer is, men mach se ook soecken te desabuseren soo veel men kan, soo syn se soo seer gepersuadeert dat Engelandt en de Staat de Spaansche Nederlanden par raison d'interessen sullen moeten defenderen, dat se weynigh op andere middel gedenken. The contemporary list confirms 15:325 = wat (32L, token 65) and 12:409 = syn (32L, token 93). The latter retains its legacy C grade for a contextual mark choice, but now has contemporary-plaintext confirmation. On 31R, line L05, tokens 57–59 are 8:721 = niet , 4:294 = gedaan , 4:696 = en ; 32L continues “blyft alles traineren”. There is no separate af prefix token in the recorded sequence. The clerk’s “afgedaen” expands the recorded key reading; a token omitted from the transcription cannot be excluded without checking that cipher line against the image. Mansfeld has little standing at court. Public business drags on. Madrid is so convinced that England and the States must defend the Spanish Netherlands out of self-interest that it gives little thought to other means. Full clear context and token readings are preserved in the repository.

Scans 58R–59L contain 235 cipher tokens (73 and 162). The conservative Codex sense screen is 230/235 = 97.9% . Legacy grades H 212, C 21, M 1, I 1 give H+C 233/235 (99.1%); that total does not establish coherent Dutch sense. No token is 81. The decipherment-sheet check covered 58L–60R : no interlinear plaintext, numbered list or marginal passage numbers were found. 58L endorses the 10 April letter, 59R is blank, 60L endorses this letter, and 60R begins the next letter. This is the second passing letter without a known contemporary decipherment; the local check does not establish publication novelty. Gastanaga may be removed before the end of his three years or employed in Peru or Catalonia. His exact condition of departure remains uncertain. The Emperor’s ambassador seeks the advantages enjoyed by his predecessor and beweeght hemel en aarde om weder in de Koninginne goede gra[tie] te komen He works through a nun, the confessor and ministers. Renewed friendship with the Countess of Soissons is intended to obtain her good offices; the exact participants in the plural sy remain uncertain. Battier concludes that it appears Hare Majt. het quaat van den Amb. van den Keyser haar aangedaan noyt niet vergeten sal. The final sal is encoded at 59L:160–162. The five exclusions are a surplus bare 8 = e (possible encipherment slip), 5:623 gra[tie] (key scan 29R, column 1, partly covered by a pasted slip), and the unresolved meanings of gehelyk , sedert dat and soo als hy . The conservative screen is an editorial assessment, not a confidence probability. The verbatim review qualifies the fluent summaries in the reading files; Mansfeld’s identification is not established by these cipher tokens.

Scans 107R, 108L, 108R and 109L contain 323 tokens: 322 are key-attested, but only 313/323 = 96.9% pass the strict sense screen; the conservative count is 312/323 = 96.6% . This is one of two focus letters that pass without a known contemporary decipherment. Visual inspection of scans 107–109 found no decipherment list. Inv. 401 has 109 scans; the letter ends on 109 with the signature “Mad. den 8 April 1688”. The reviewed reconstruction below retains repairs and gaps. It is not a diplomatic transcription. Ellipses separate excerpts; brackets mark uncertainty or editorial repair. Den Grand Maestre aan syn agent geordonneert de oude Koninginne te verseekeren … Oropeza … Melgar sollicitee[r]t noch. Alleen om Altamira tot vice Roy van [12:6?0 unread] te kunn[e]n maken … De Spaanse mesnagie blyct nu hier uyt klaarlyke … Soo lange als Castanaga gouverneren blyft. Holsteyn … Oropeza overgegeven … Ondertusschen soo formeert sich een gesworen partye tegen den selven: Connestable van Castille, Os[t]una en Mon[i→t]ere [Monterey?] brouwen wat met malkander. By Oropeza te willen gaan klagen, waarover Mont[i→e][u→r]ey soo quaat is geworden dat hy met moeyte uyt syn huys heeft kunnen raken. Mont[i→e]rey soude nu ook lichtvaardelyk President d'Italien willen wesen, of gelyk de Flandersche presi[s→d]ence profitabeler is. Want hy merckt wel, dat als den G[t→r]and Maeist[u→r]e offe een creatuer van Oropesa na Vlaanderen komt, de Nederlandse toestemminge, gelyk in tyt van Grana is geschiedt, door syn handen niet veel sullen passeren. The agent's instruction, the condition on Gastañaga's tenure, and the formation of a faction are solid within the transcription. The Holsteyn project and Monterey's interest in the Italian or Flemish presidency are plausible. Troop and money figures in the project, and the promise of Imperial letters within fourteen days, are in the clear text . Osuna remains speculative : the spelling needs deletion of a real t. Holsteyn's identity, the pronouns in the complaint episode, and the exact meaning of toestemminge are unsettled. Translating the latter simply as “Netherlands business” hides the problem. The final clause reads “Grana is geschiedt” , not “Grana's geschiedt”. The review does not independently establish the Grand Master's modern identification.

On 4 December the government of the Netherlands is to be deliberated, Melgar and Leganés nearest to it; Novelli sounds out a post for the Palatine son; in Vienna the Grand Master is to be made president of the war council; Gastañaga complains he is left to perish while bills of exchange go out. On 12 February the Count Palatine’s letter to Novelli asks on what conditions the King would give Flanders to his son, and Rougemont, who opened it by mistake, lets the Countess of Soissons know its contents. No decipherment sheet, slip or gloss for either letter is on scans 90–94 or 98–102. On 23 October 2026 every letter of the volume listed as unread was checked on the full-size scans. Eight build sentences: 2 January 1687 (35R/36L, aligned with its interlinear decipherment of the time: 30 codes agree), 13 March 1687 (54R and 55R), July 1687 (69L), 11 September 1687 (78R, the second run), 18 December 1687 (93R/94L), 1 January 1688 (95R) and 11 March 1688 (103R: Oropesa to speak for Cogolludo, Melgar and Balbases; Holstein desists). Six are decoded, not read: June 1687 (67L), August 1687 (73R), 25 September 1687 (80R), 18 December 1687 after line 5 of 94R, 99L and 26 February 1688 (102L). The texts are in readings/r2n/ . With them the share of the volume’s cipher in letters that build sentences is estimated at about 78%.

The letter table covers 2–98, with eight homophones per vowel and three per consonant, on key scans 3–6. The one-part codebook repeats 99–999 in fifteen blocks: none, ~, backslash, ^, slash, e, l, r, bar, two dots, first/second/third digit struck, c/, reversed c/. Block 13 begins at 100. Spanish councils and grandees occur on scan 59; places on scans 78–82. The transcriptions record block and number separately. The transcriptions were made by LLMs from the Nationaal Archief scans and checked against the key images. The merged key contains 1,417 distinct dictionary codes: 1,393 earlier codes and 24 additions in the 27 rows of key/dict/nw.tsv . Three codes already occur in the repository (15:165, 2:825 and 11:431); the preserved review identifies only the first two duplicates. Software reapplied these values to the transcribed tokens. Contemporary decipherments for 5 December 1686 (369 tokens) and 30 January 1687 (781) give 1113/1132 = 98.3% agreement where comparable, with 94.7% key-alone agreement. Eighteen positions were not comparable. This validation is not a blind holdout claim. The third validation, 19 December 1686, adds four passages, 186 tokens compared with the numbered decipherment on 32R , with spelling differences and the “gedaan”/“afgedaen” distinction above. The earlier percentages describe the first two letters only; they are not an aggregate score for all three. The shuffle control, run with scripts/control.py in the target folder, finds 72% of spelled runs segment into Dutch words or names, compared with a mean of 1.2% and maximum of 4.1% across 300 permuted letter tables. That supports the structure of the decoding, not every proper name or interpretation. The fixed lexicon and names list influence this result; the original OpenTaal word list is required to reproduce it and is not bundled.

The volume estimate is about 78% of the cipher in inv. 401 in letters that build sentences (estimated, not measured token by token). The October review counted about 55%; the reading audit of 22 October 2026 took out 4 December 1687 and 12 February 1688 (about 49%); their re-reading the same day and the thirteen passages read on 23 October (section 05) brought it to about 78%. The volume is not a complete decipherment. 24 April 1687: surplus 8=e, partly covered 5:623 gra[tie], and the meaning of gehelyk, sedert dat and soo als hy remain open, including Gastanaga’s exact departure condition. 81 is i in the key. Of 17 occurrences, 14 are interpreted contextually as e and three retain i. None of the three validation letters contains 81; those decipherments do not confirm an 81=e habit. The 365 alphabetical reversals in the dictionary, 96 touching focus tokens, are not proven misreads. Historical spelling, inflection and thematic lists complicate the check. 12:908, first transcribed as getwist where Turck(en) was inferred, is Turcken on the key scan (22 October 2026). 12:6?0 on 108L is unread. Osuna, precise pronoun referents and the administrative sense of toestemminge remain speculative. 4 December 1687 and 12 February 1688: groups without sense after the re-reading (92L 889 and the letters before “soon”; 91R 11:466 and the end of the Novelli sentence; 99R 431 374 137 512 and 604; 100L four groups; 100R the struck groups after Madrid and after gesoubconneert ). Scans 90–94 and 98–102 hold no decipherment sheet for either letter. Six passages located on 23 October 2026 are decoded, not read: 67L, 73R, 80R, 94R after line 5, 99L and 102L. In 11 September 1687 the first run of nine groups gives no sense with the marks as read; the letter builds coherent sentences elsewhere but reads at 86.3%, under the 95% bar. The letter of 2 January 1687 (35R, 36L) was listed as having no contemporary decipherment. It has heavy interlinear decipherment over the cipher, so it was deciphered at the time (WAINUT, 21 October 2026). Its groups were transcribed from the scan on 23 October and agree with the interlinear text (30 codes; 10:703 rabat against the clerk’s “een”); a few words rest on the interlinear only. The letter builds coherent sentences but reads at 89.6%, under the 95% bar. The independent review is software re-decoding, not independent paleography . Digit and mark choices, dictionary variants and shifted annotations still need image checks. Contributed, 21 October 2026. WAINUT , a Dutch AI company, applied this key to the 1687 letters listed as not read ( pull requests #65 and #67 ): 16 January, 13 and 27 February, 13 March (55L), 10 June (67R), 20 November and 18 December (94R, lines 1–5), 1,389 groups in all, every group checked by eye on the scans and 39 left uncertain. Montalto refused the government of the Spanish Netherlands only for lack of money; Gastañaga is told he will not be removed before his three years are out, while complaints come in that he does nothing but spend and “soigneuslyke borse te maken”; the Countess of Soissons recommends her son for the same post. These readings are not counted in the figures above: 158 of their code values come from a machine read of the key not yet checked row by row, and the language-model control is not in the repository. The texts are in targets/battier1686/wainut/ . They also correct one key row: 11:718 is soetjens and 11:719 soetelaars . The reading TSV grades are legacy labels: H secure key/sense, C contextual mark choice, M conjecture, I unread. They are preserved verbatim and are not repository-grade counts. Under repository terminology, primary-key support is H, contemporary-plaintext support C, uncertainty M and inference I. The conservative semantic screen, rather than a sum of legacy H+C labels, supplies the headline results.

[Ick blyve ...] English gist: Oropesa will not yet be made first minister (his confessor dissuades him, the King is not keen); public business stalls because everyone looks after his own interest; he could become Caballerizo mayor but would then have to give up the presidency of Castile, and he would not like Cardinal Salazar to become president. For the Netherlands nothing has yet been resolved, nor can it be until a good sum of money is found ... Nor is it known whether one of the said three will obtain the governorship. The Count of Melgar had good hopes, but since then the Admiral has written to Don Manuel de Lira in such terms about his son's disgrace that the King is very ill pleased with it. Now there is also talk of the Marquis of Leganés, and some speak⟩ of the Count of Mansfeld; but since this last once failed, his person is little esteemed and his credit here at court very slight, and therefore there is little likelihood for him either. ⟨The Count of Oropesa remains in great credit; the King's confessor, who was not his friend, has asked for and obtained his dismissal, and another has already been named;⟩ but for all that public business is not done, and everything goes on dragging. ⟨Mr Cantelmo, envoy of the Marquis of Gastañaga, obtains little; he demands 800 thousand patacoons,⟩ but if half of it could be found, another governor would soon undertake the journey to Flanders. ⟨Of Vander Haghen's project there is no more talk. The Marquis of Gastañaga also proposes to make a new alliance with Brandenburg, Brunswick-Lüneburg and Hesse-Kassel, but without money it cannot be done; and besides, the professed goodwill (as they put it here) of the King of France, the removal again of the posts near Namur, together with the hope of the amicable settlement at Dinant⟩ make so much impression that people think no further of defence; and what is more, however much one may try to disabuse them, they are so persuaded that England and the State will have to defend the Spanish Netherlands for reasons of their own interest that they think little of any other means. ⟨The Duc d'Arré intends to leave here in a few days ...⟩ 30 Jan 1687 (scans 41R, 42L, 44R) Battier to Fagel; the contemporary decipherment on scans 42R-43R (file misdated 16 Jan) deciphers this one letter and is transcribed beside the key reading. Since the last post I have consulted with Cantelmo how best to work for Castañaga, and we have thought it good to do it underhand, for otherwise it could be harmful to Castañaga, because [?they] are so touchy here and do not want their neighbours to meddle in their domestic affairs. The Emperor's ambassador has already spoken of it openly everywhere, and the Master of the Horse of Aureis came to tell me that he had heard, on a visit of consequence, that His Highness had written in Castañaga's favour, and that it was taken ill. I merely answered that I knew nothing of it, for I noticed that he had come to sound me out in order to report back to the Emperor's ambassador. I have nevertheless done my duty wherever I thought it necessary. Monterrey assures me that, to his knowledge, nothing has yet been resolved, and perhaps will not be resolved so soon either. The King is distrustful and becomes obstinate when he thinks he notices that people want to give away offices against his will; and the Duke of Medinaceli lost the King's favour chiefly by wanting to make Don Pedro of Aragon President of Castile by force; and therefore Castañaga's friends do nothing but keep His Majesty in his distrust. It had been said that he would be sent from Brussels to Peru as viceroy, which would [?indeed] be better for him. [?Meanwhile], now and by the next post I shall do further duty. Otherwise there is still talk of Melgar, Montalto and the Marquis of Leganés, but without the least certainty, and above all because there is no money at hand. It also seems that the Emperor's ambassador is still flattering himself; but if the Queen, who hates him greatly on account of the Cantons affair, which he fomented so strongly, has once already been able to [make] him perplexed, she will now too surely be able to dispose the King, to please her, not to visit him. The reason why the Emperor's ambassador had the French courier waylaid is thought to be that he [?himself] had been to his commissary several times and could not learn on what matter; he suspected that it was about consenting to turn the Twenty Years' Truce into a peace, and that it was to be done behind the Emperor's back. He lately [?asked] me whether I did not know what Their High Mightinesses thought of it; I said I did not, but that I could easily imagine that Their High Mightinesses had no other interest than the general peace and the satisfaction of their [?allies], and that if His Imperial Majesty made peace with the Turks, France would then apparently undertake nothing. He is perplexed and imagines that even the Emperor's friends begrudge him his victories and would gladly see him forced by whatever [?] it may be to put an end to the Turkish war. And when an express courier came from Brussels last Saturday, he was at once alarmed; but on Sunday it was learned that it concerns only the settlement of [?Philippeville]. ⟨Right Honourable Sir, Your Honour's humble and obedient servant Battier. Same holes; modern spelling. --> # Battier to Fagel, Madrid, 4 December 1687 ## Translation ### 91R It is now absolutely intended that the government of the Netherlands shall be deliberated upon; that the Count of Melgar and the Marquis of Leganés would be the nearest to it, and that, if Leganés prevails, the Marquis of Gastañaga would then receive the viceroyalty of Catalonia; but all without the least certainty. On the contrary, Monsieur Novelli [is] sounding out [the post of] Hofmeister for the son of the Palatinate, and [?expects] further work [from the] Elector Palatine [...] [?armed]. The Spaniards have so far not wished to show their hand much, so as not to be obliged to improve the conditions, and the Palatinate for its part will form no claim, for fear that no advantage would then be obtained; and meanwhile there comes the news that in Vienna they are working to make the Grand Master president of the council of war and to send the Margrave of Baden to Regensburg, or, if that does not come off, to appoint the Grand Master as principal Imperial commissioner. Here they will not press [11:466] much, not only because there is still time enough, but also because they want to give the Palatinate time ### 92L to think it over well. Meanwhile no remittances are sent to the Netherlands, and the Marquis of Gastañaga complains greatly that he is being left to perish; and yet His Excellency sent last post 50,000 and by this post another 80,000 guilders, the proceeds of offices sold, in bills of exchange on a Netherlands merchant. The Spanish gentlemen also still have the old speculations about the Netherlands, without one being able to make out whether they are in earnest or not: namely, when peace with the Turks is concluded, and consequently the Emperor and the Elector of Bavaria no longer need their troops in Hungary, then to hand over the army in the Spanish Netherlands to the Elector of Bavaria, or to enter into some arrangement with the Emperor and the Roman Empire. But because I know for certain that [889] the [?...] son of the Palatinate [...] suspected [...] to govern, that the old "Sex" (the key's word; perhaps the Queen Mother) pushes the Palatine intercession, that everything is kept [?certainly] [?secret] so that the French notice it the less, and that the Count of Oropesa does not oppose it, it is probable that they will not hurry. There is also talk of two other marriages in the Palatine house, with Tuscany and Parma. The factions in Vienna also fear the Count Palatine and the Grand Master, since His Electoral Highness would cede and give up the electorate to the Electoral Prince, not to govern as viceroy in Hungary, but to stay in Vienna and direct affairs there, especially if the Grand Master should obtain the presidency of the council of war. Catalonia is still full of disorder; the towns complain that ### 92R Leganés wants service and lodging money for 14,000 men, whereas by their account there are not 4,000 men actually in service. The Prince of Parma has arrived with a train of 140 persons; and although His Excellency is well paid 1,000 pistoles a month by the reigning Duke his brother, and also has 40,000 pieces of eight assigned on the Cruzada to receive from his office of prince de la mer, it is not believed that this train, winter though it is, will stay unmelted. His Majesty has given the husband of his mistress María de la O a post in Granada and charged him to take his wife with him, so that she had already left before the Prince arrived. Señor Valenzuela now enjoys more freedom and better treatment, so some think His Excellency will come back into His Majesty's favour. They work continually at setting the monarchy to rights, without making much progress, partly because it is very hard to heal an old wound all at once, and partly because it is better fishing in troubled water than in clear, and there are more fishermen than healers at this court. I remain, Right Honourable Sir, your most humble and obedient servant, Battier. Madrid, 4 December 1687. 29 Jan 1688 (scan 97R) Battier to Fagel from Madrid; no contemporary decipherment recorded. Since my most humble last letter I have read the letter that the Count Palatine wrote to Monsieur Novelli on behalf of the Grand Master, to this effect: His Electoral Highness orders him to sound out on what footing and conditions His Majesty would hand over the government of Flanders to his son, and His Electoral Highness hoped that the last [431] [374] [137] [512] would have brought his son into [604] reputation and credit, so that His Majesty would also take it into account. But because His Highness in this letter also offers Novelli the post of Resident at this court, which for many years has been, and still is, held by Monsieur de Rougemont, and the said Rougemont opened Novelli's letter by mistake and now seeks friends everywhere to forestall this move (although, as a sick man who cannot otherwise subsist, he is much protected by the Old Queen), he has also made no difficulty about letting the Countess of Soissons, who through one ### 100L of her servants had offered him her credit, know the contents of the said letter. And since this business has so far [...] the Queen [...], it is easy to infer that these two will throw something in the way. As soon as I learn more of it I shall not fail to advise Your Honour in detail. The other gentleman is still having work done under hand, and I hope in a fortnight to be able to tell Your Honour something more about it. In the matter of Monsieur Robiano nothing further has happened. The French ambassador presented a memorial about a fortnight ago and, in his King's name, reclaimed the French refugees who had been held prisoner in Bilbao, so that they could be brought to the Catholic religion. His Excellency was then shown the attestation the Corregidor sent, that they had been delivered onto an English ship, and, as His Excellency presses for it, this answer will also be given in writing. A rumour has run that the said French ambassador had presented a memorial, or at least put forward orally, that his King wished to have the succession of this monarchy secured to the Duke of Burgundy, and to that end a royal declaration, and for its execution Pamplona and Barcelona, as well as the title ### 100R of Prince of Asturias and a certain allowance as presumptive heir; but without the least foundation; on the contrary, it seems that Mansfeld had all this put about in order to have the Imperial prince come to Madrid [11:719], [which] [?...] nevertheless cannot be done. I must also tell Your Honour that the Grand Master, by the last letters, found himself [suspected] [11:759], [and is] to consult his lord father how best [?...] this matter could be put forward by the Emperor to the Council of the Netherlands; so it seems that it is now in earnest, and that the Imperial letters are expected with the first post. I remain with respect, Right Honourable Sir, Your Honour's most humble and obedient servant, Battier. A seven-word telegram in the commercial “Unicode” phrase code that Bell copied into a letter to his wife from a steamer on the Thames, telling her she might have some fun deciphering it. All six code words are in the 1896 Unicode phrase book and give: telegram received, glad to hear from you, wrote to you by this morning’s post, quite well and writing by post, weather very fine and sea quite smooth. One word, Promulgo , is a betting phrase the letter does not explain. Bell struck out Sigma and wrote Signinus , so the Library of Congress transcription’s signature “Signinas” is a word of the message. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 31 October 2026 Method: read with known key · Extent: complete · On the map Credits · Contemporary key or decipherment (key or decipherment used) known key At a glance Known key applied · complete The letter Alexander Graham Bell to his wife Mabel, 27 August 1900, on board the SS Ulunda on the Thames, bound for Halifax by way of St John’s, Newfoundland. He says he has sent her a “Unicode” message “which you may have some fun in deciphering” and copies its words into the letter. Where Library of Congress, Manuscript Division, Alexander Graham Bell Family Papers, magbell.04100117 , image 1 of the letter. Catalogue entry 763. The cipher A commercial phrase code: “Unicode”, The Universal Telegraphic Phrase-Book, gives a Latin word for each of thousands of stock phrases. The key is the printed book. How it was read Each word was looked up in the 1896 edition on archive.org and checked on the page image; the 1889 edition was read in its text layer only. The sentence it makes fits the letter. What it says “Telegram received. Glad to hear from you. Wrote to you by this morning’s post. Am quite well, and writing by post. Weather very fine, sea quite smooth.” One word, Promulgo , is a betting phrase that the letter does not explain. Still open Why Bell used Promulgo (“Put me £1,000 to win on —”); what Bert stands for. No portraits yet (Wikimedia was not reachable).

The message as Bell wrote it into the letter. Sigma is struck out and Signinus written under it. Image: Library of Congress, Alexander Graham Bell Family Papers, magbell.04100117, image 1 (master JPEG). The letter is dated “SS. Ulunda — on the Thames, August 27 1900” and addressed to Mrs A. G. Bell at 9 rue Boccador, Paris. It opens “Received your telegram on reaching steamer and have sent you the following ‘Unicode’ message which you may have some fun in deciphering”, and gives the words: Roboro, Diallage, Siquando, Adalligo, Signinus, Promulgo, Bert . The rest of the letter is about a night bell for Mabel’s room, the slowness of the steamer (“looks like a tramp — and slow”), his plan to call at St John’s, and keeping the voyage secret. The Library of Congress transcription lists five words and a signature, “Signinas”. The image shows something else: Signinus is a correction in the middle of the message. Bell wrote Sigma after Adalligo , struck it out, and wrote Signinus below the line. Bert is plain text.

word phrase in the book page, 1896 ed. Roboro Telegram received 88 Diallage Glad to hear from you 35 Siquando Wrote to you by this morning’s post 96 Adalligo Am quite well, and writing by post 5 Signinus Weather very fine, sea quite smooth ( Sigma , struck out: Weather very fine) 95 Promulgo Put me £1,000 to win on — 78 Bert not a code word — Telegram received. Glad to hear from you. Wrote to you by this morning’s post. Am quite well, and writing by post. Weather very fine, sea quite smooth. [ Promulgo : Put me £1,000 to win on —] Bert. Bell’s change from Sigma to Signinus shows he was picking phrases: “Weather very fine” sits two lines above “Weather very fine, sea quite smooth” on page 95, and he chose the longer one. The four messages about the post, his health and the weather are the kind of thing a husband on a ship would send. Promulgo is the one that does not fit. Page 78 of the book has it beside “Put me £1,000 to win on —”, one of the racing-bet phrases, and the letter gives no reason for it. It may be a joke for Mabel to puzzle over, but that is a guess, so it is read as printed and marked as odd.

The catalogue entry named the book: “Unicode” Universal Telegraphic Phrase-Book, in print from 1886. Two scans are on archive.org: an 1896 edition ( UnicodeUniversalTelegraphicPhraseBook ) and an 1889 one ( unicodeuniversa00unkngoog ). The text layer prints the phrases and the code words in separate columns, so each word was first paired to its phrase by counting entries on its page (on the Promulgo page 36 phrases and 36 words match). Then the page images were opened and each word read beside its phrase: pages 5, 35, 78, 88, 95 and 96 of the 1896 edition. All six pairings were right. The 1889 scan was checked in its text layer only, not on its page images: it has all six words ( Roboro and Signinus garbled by the OCR), and prints Roboro and Diallage on the same line as their phrases. The 1898 edition, named in the catalogue, was not found online, so Promulgo is confirmed in the 1896 edition only. No part of the key was recovered from the ciphertext: the book is the key, so this is a known-key reading, and the work is the transcription and the lookup. No earlier decipherment was found (Library of Congress record and transcription; project notes, checked 28 and 29 October 2026).

Promulgo , “Put me £1,000 to win on —”: the book’s value is certain (page 78); why Bell sent it is not known. The 1898 edition was not checked for a different entry. Bert : left as plain text. It may be a name or a sign-off; it is not checked against other letters. The writer’s spellings were read on the master image at display size: Siquando , Adalligo , Promulgo agree with the book letter for letter.

Two short ciphered passages in the regent’s letters of 15 September and 10 November 1610 (BnF fr. 3789 ff. 17r, 19r). Brice Dudout deciphered them with Henri IV’s 1610 key for Brèves, which is on BnF fr. 3462 view 112 (R2077’s note mistypes it as 3642). Checked here sign by sign: 96 of 98 glyphs supported, two signs conflict with the table. George Lasry contributed his CTTS key, with a repeat sign, and a second document in the same key (PR #61). 7̄2 4 7̄9 b J r c J y · 4̄1 3 ð J r x f a, y, que le pape re[c]ognoi… · leurs arogance et 4 = le pape · a, = ce · y, = et · x, = en Paris → Rome · homophonic cipher with a nomenclator · 15 September and 10 November 1610 · external key matched Marie de Médicis to Savary de Brèves, Rome, 1610 from Marie de Médicis Go to the full text ↓ Two short ciphered passages in the regent’s letters to her ambassador in Rome, deciphered by Brice Dudout with Henri IV’s key for Brèves and checked here sign by sign against that key. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 20 October 2026 · updated 23 October 2026 Method: read after matching with key from external sources · Extent: partial (99% of the cipher) · On the map Contributed by Brice Dudout (solution) and George Lasry (key or decipherment used, solution) and Satoshi Tomokiyo (verification) and Norbert Biermann (key or decipherment used) key matched At a glance External key matched · partial (99% of the cipher) The letters Marie de Médicis, regent after Henri IV’s death, to François Savary de Brèves, ambassador in Rome, 15 September and 10 November 1610, countersigned Brulart. Clear French with a few lines in cipher. Where BnF Français 3789, stamped ff. 17r and 19r (Gallica btv1b9059628m views 32 and 36). DECODE R2075 and R2076, listed as not deciphered. The cipher A homophonic alphabet of two to five signs a letter, letters with a comma for short words ( a, = ce, y, = et), and plain and overbarred numbers for names and words. How it was deciphered Brice Dudout found that Henri IV’s 1610 key for Brèves, on BnF fr. 3462 view 112, fits the regent’s passages. Here every glyph was compared with the cell of the key it matches. What it says That the pope, “recognoissant leurs arogance et sentant sa timidite”, will not be pressed to the point of a humiliating refus; and, in September, that further difficulty would show “their malice and ambition”. Still open Two signs conflict with the key as it stands on the page, and four barred numbers (six occurrences) are on a part of the key that is not in hand; their values come from Satoshi Tomokiyo and agree with George Lasry’s key. Credit Decipherment by Brice Dudout, with Claude and Codex (October 2026). Satoshi Tomokiyo identified the key’s shelfmark and corroborated four number values. The key was first broken by George Lasry with Norbert Biermann and Tomokiyo (2021) on Henri IV’s letter, DECODE R2077; Lasry contributed his CTTS key, a second document in the key and his decryption of the November passage (pull request #61, 21 October 2026).

Henri IV was killed on 14 May 1610, and Marie de Médicis governed for the child Louis XIII. Her letters to Brèves in Rome are in BnF Français 3789, a volume of royal and ministerial letters to the ambassador. The BnF notice’s folio numbers run two ahead of the stamped foliation: its no. 11 (“fol. 19”) is stamped f. 17, Gallica view 32, and its no. 12 (“fol. 21 et 23”) is stamped f. 19, view 36. The subject of both is Savoy: in September the journey of the duke’s son to Spain, in November the disarmament after Spain’s refusal. The digits visible on f. 19v are show-through from the recto. 10 November 1610, f. 19r: the cipher begins after Aussi vois-je bien with the barred 72 ( que ), 4 ( le pape ) and barred 79 ( re ), and ends before ne sera pressé . Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3789 f. 19r (Gallica btv1b9059628m view 36). 15 September 1610, f. 17r: the first passage runs from de la difficulté to the barred 72 ( que ), the second from devoir estre to the barred 86 ( se ) before selon la constitution . Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3789 f. 17r (Gallica btv1b9059628m view 32). This project transcribed both passages on 21 September 2026 and closed them unread. DECODE’s record of Henri IV’s letter to Brèves of 5 January 1610 (R2077, BnF fr. 3541) said that the key was in “BNF Français 3642”, which is not on Gallica, and that R2075 and R2076 “may be in the same cipher”. The only image of the key here was an 833-pixel photo on that record, and trying its candidate letters for each sign, scored against seventeenth-century French, gave nothing that read.

Brice Dudout looked in BnF Français 3462 instead, a volume of cipher keys, and found the table on Gallica view 112. Satoshi Tomokiyo has since confirmed to him that “3642” on R2077 was a mistyping of 3462 and that this is the Henri IV–Brèves key image he knew. The same volume holds the office’s table for Brèves’s earlier Constantinople cipher (f. 103; see the 1603 letters , a different cipher, with its own page). The key: plaintext letters across the top with their homophones in columns below, the t–z box on the right, and the number codes for persons (4 le pape , 14 le roy d’Espagne , 34 le duc de Savoye ) down the left. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3462 view 112 (Gallica btv1b9058227h). The table gives each letter two to five signs, many of them Latin letters used as signs: under m stand a , b , c and a delta; under n stand c , a hooked f , g and h . A letter followed by a comma is a word: a, ce, x, en, y, et. Plain numbers 4–99 are persons and words from a to c (72 is “le S r Conchine”, 86 “armee”); overbarred numbers run from 1̄ to 4̄6 across words from f to m (3̄9 le , 4̄1 leurs ). The barred numbers above 46 that the regent’s letters use, 7̄2, 7̄9, 8̄6 and 9̄0, belong to a continuation for later letters of the alphabet that is not on view 112. Tomokiyo gave Brice their values: que , re , se , tion .

Two passages on f. 17r, lines 22–24, in Brice Dudout’s reading. The clear text of the letter is in roman, the deciphered words in italics; brackets are his, the notes after them are from the check below. … si avec cela ilz y apportent encores de la difficulté, ce sera trop manifester leurs malice et ambition que j’estime, s’il en falloit venir a l’effet, devoir estre acompagne[z?] d’imprudence et [de?] foiblesse selon la constitution presente de leurs affaires. “… if on top of that they still raise difficulty, it will show their malice and ambition too plainly; and that ambition, I think, if it came to action, would be accompanied by imprudence and weakness, given the present state of their affairs.” am[b?]ition , foi[b?]lesse : both signs are the first b of the key, a b with a flag. The key settles Brice’s brackets. acompagne[z?] : the sign is like a ß with a descender. On view 112 it is either the third e (drawn as ß) or the second z (a 3 joined to a long s). With e the word is acompagnee , agreeing with ambition , which is the better grammar. The images do not settle it. [de?] : the sign is J, , which on view 112 stands against an entry that reads De (the first word of its column, before Du and Don ). Probable. se (twice), tion and que are barred 86, 90 and 72, which are not on view 112.

Two lines on f. 19r, lines 5–7, the passage of catalogue item 25: Aussi vois-je bien que le pape re[c?]ognoi[s?][s?]ant leurs arogance et [s?]entant sa timidite ne sera pressé jusques a l’extremité du desarmement pour recevoir enfin la honte d’un refus absolu … “So I see well that the pope, recognising their arrogance and feeling his own timidity, will not be pressed to the extreme of disarmament only to receive in the end the shame of an outright refusal …” Brèves’s reply of 9 December 1610, in his Rome letter-book (BnF Cinq cents de Colbert 351, pp. 724–730), answers the letter on the pope and the Spanish disarmament, in paraphrase. The passage builds coherent sentences but reads at 93.8%, under the 95% bar. [s?]entant : the first sign is the looped crossed t that the key gives for s . Settled. re[c?]ognoissant : the sign is the flagged b , the same as in ambition ; none of the four c signs of view 112 ( u , a hook, a 5-shape, a ʒ) looks like it. The word needs c . recognoi[s?][s?]ant : the first s is the looped t of s ; the second is a small loop with a diagonal stroke that has no cell under s . George Lasry’s key explains it: it is the cipher’s repeat sign, which doubles the letter before it (section 06). Settled. leurs : barred 41, whose entry on view 112 reads Leurs to me, with an uncertain ending; Tomokiyo gives leur . It is one code either way, and leur arogance is the more usual grammar.

On 20 October Gallica refused image requests from here, so the check used the copies in Brice’s repository: the key at 1800 × 1580 pixels and his line crops of the two folios, both BnF images. Each of the 98 glyphs was set against the cell of view 112 that it matches, one line per glyph in alignment.tsv . Glyphs 15 Sept 10 Nov All In a cell of view 112 that gives Brice’s value 52 34 86 Fit an entry whose word is not certain (4̄1, J, ) 2 1 3 Barred numbers not on view 112, values from Tomokiyo 4 2 6 Conflict with the key as it stands 1 2 3 Total 59 39 98 So 89 of 98 glyphs (90.8%) are supported by the page itself and 95 (96.9%) with Tomokiyo’s values; with Lasry’s repeat sign (section 06), 96 (98.0%). The words manifester , malice , d’imprudence , arogance and sentant sa timidite come out of the table letter for letter, which is hard to get by chance from a homophonic key over this many signs. The three conflicting signs fall inside words that the context fixes. They are what Brice calls variants of a “very close” key: either the clerk slipped, or the regent’s table differed from Henri IV’s in a few cells. The check also showed why the 21 September attempt failed. Our transcription missed the bars over 72 and 79 (plain 72 is “le S r Conchine”, which sent the first guess wrong), wrote two signs of 10 November as one (3 and a raised crossed delta) and one glyph of 15 September as two ( tu , a single sign for u , as Brice found), and gave one letter to shapes that the key keeps apart: our d was the p , m or r of the key, our z its a , p or t . With the 833-pixel photo those shapes could not be told apart.

Contributed, 21 October 2026. George Lasry sent the CTTS project of his 2022 decipherment in this key, improved with Opus 5.5 in October 2026 ( pull request #61 ; files in targets/breves1610/lasry2022/ ). It has three parts. A full key. His key gives every sign of the cipher a value, including a repeat sign that doubles the letter or word before it. That sign is the “second s ” of recognoissant above, which no s cell explained: his longer document uses it ten times ( l’alarme , intelligence , aage , necessaire , brouillons ). His key also gives the four barred numbers Tomokiyo supplied the same values (72̄ que, 79̄ re, 86̄ se, 90̄ tion). His CTTS sign names are labels, not the table’s letters: on view 112 the m column holds signs shaped like a , b , c , d , while his labels b , c , d name other signs. A second document in the key , two images with 766 cipher signs, three of them unresolved: marriage negotiations carried on under cover names (La Hale, Le Cormier, La Cheville, Pindare, Saint Paul), the alarm they raised, and the need for calm at home and friendship with neighbours, “au grand desplaisir de Sa Sainteté”. Its shelfmark and date are not given; it reads like Henri IV writing to his ambassador in Rome, but it is not identified with R2077 without a matching archival image. The second document, first image, with Lasry’s decryption in red. Image: Manuscript crop supplied by George Lasry (pull request #61; shelfmark not stated), with his CTTS decryption overlay. His decryption of the November passage , which agrees with Brice Dudout’s reading word for word.

re[c?]ognoissant , one sign: the key gives b . Lasry’s key gives it c , but from this word alone; his longer document does not use the sign. Needs the regent’s own table. acompagne[z?] or acompagnee , one sign: the two candidate cells differ by a stroke that the image does not settle. Barred 72, 79, 86 and 90, six occurrences: the part of the key with barred numbers above 46 is not in hand; the values are Tomokiyo’s, and each fits its context. Brice asked whether this project has Lasry’s R2077 decipherment. Lasry has since sent his CTTS work (section 06), including a longer document in the key; whether that document is Henri IV’s letter R2077 is not established.

Two ciphered despatches of the Milanese ambassador to Matthias Corvinus with no contemporary decipherment. Somogyi published the key in 2016 only as numbers; matching her numbering to the symbols of a letter with a clear copy turned it back into a usable key, which was applied. Somogyi (key or decipherment used) · Contemporary key or decipherment (key or decipherment used) known key At a glance Known key applied · partial (56% of the cipher) The documents Despatches of Maffeo da Treviglio, Ludovico Sforza’s man at Buda from summer 1489. Two had no decipherment: Buda, 22 November 1489 (four pages) and Buda, 12 January 1490. Where Milan state archive, Carteggio Sforzesco, Ungheria 642 and 650; Vestigia 2831 (1489) and DECODE R1098 (“Partially decrypted”, 1490). The cipher A monoalphabetic sign cipher with nomenclator signs, reconstructed by Judit W. Somogyi (2016), who printed the key only as two-digit numbers with no sign shapes. How it was read Her numbers follow first appearance in the letter of 2 April 1490, which survives with its clear copy (Vestigia 267/268). Matching the two restores the signs; about twenty more came from the decipherment itself. What it says In January 1490 the king has left for Vienna and the ambassadors follow on the 15th. The November 1489 letter covers the peace with the Emperor, the Diet, the Corvinus marriage and a warning that intercepted cipher letters have been deciphered. Still open Four signs are unvalued; page 3 of the 1489 letter is read only in patches (about a third of its words); lines 5, 6 and 9 of the 1490 letter and three nomenclator shapes are unconfirmed. Credit The key reconstruction is Judit W. Somogyi’s ( Verbum 17, 2016). The 1489 letter is the oldest cipher text this project has deciphered; the previous oldest was of 1497.

Five letters of Maffeo survive with both a ciphered original and a contemporary clear copy; Somogyi used them to build her key. Two others have no decipherment beside them; those are the ones deciphered here. One of them, R1098, turned out to have its contemporary extract printed in 1878.
