R1146 and R1158 are in two other ciphers. The crib. Above, the opening of the ciphered letter of 2 April 1490 (Vestigia 267, after the clear word “Lo”); below, the contemporary clear copy filed beside it (Vestigia 268), headed “Extractus litterarum in ziffra Maphei Trivilensis Ill.mo D. Lud.co, 2 Aprilis 1490, Vienne”. Because Somogyi numbered the signs in order of their first appearance in this letter, the copy assigns a shape to each of her numbers. Image: Archivio di Stato di Milano, Carteggio Sforzesco, Potenze Estere, Ungheria 642, via Vestigia (images 267 and 268).

Somogyi's appendix prints the key as a table of numbers: a = 11, 29, 39; m = 12; b = 13; and so on through five nulls, three word signs ( et , in , che ), five doubled-letter signs, thirty-two syllable signs and six nomenclator entries (“il vescovo varadino”, “S. V.”, “ser.mo Re de Hungaria”, “madonna Bianca”, “zo. Corvino”, “la sua Maestà”). She also prints the first two lines of the 1489 letter twice, once as numbers and once deciphered. She prints no image of a sign, and her numbers are her own labels for the fifteenth-century signs. The order of her numbers gives the link. Her numbers 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16 stand for a, m, b, sa, to, re , which is “ambasatore”, the first word of the letter of 2 April 1490. 17, 18, 19 are d, e, l (“del”), 20 to 23 t, u, r, co (“turco”). The numbering simply follows that letter word by word, so the ciphered original supplies the shapes in the same order. From there the clear copy carries the alignment to the end of the letter and fixes about forty signs. The rest came from the two letters without a decipherment, each fixed by a word that could be nothing else: the long 7 -shaped stroke is f (“Fedrico”, “fosse”, “satisfare”); an n with a crossed 4 is ss (“essere”, “potesse”); x with a tick is do (“quando”, “havendo”); a with a colon is gli (“meglio”); a looped b joined to o is st (“stato”, “questo”); d with a colon is fi (“figliolo”, “iustificare”); an n with a long crossbar is tt (“littere”); and a capital with a mark stands for the correspondent’s title (the original key gives a# = “Vostra Dominatio”; it had been taken for “Ex.tia Vostra”). Numerals are written as figures, not enciphered: “ali 8 del presente”, “ali 15”, “in 20 o 25 di”. Latin words sometimes stand in the clear inside the cipher (“etiam apud”, “Sed hoc non fallet divinam sapientiam”). The original key. On 23 October 2026 the key itself was found among the Sforza chancery’s keys: Sforzesco cart. 1597 no. 111, DECODE R5411, undated and unattributed there, headed “Cum Mapheo Triviliensi”. It has the alphabet (torn at the upper right, from T to &), doubles, nulls, syllables and a nomenclator of 22 entries (transcribed in key_R5411.md ). It confirms Somogyi’s reconstruction where both exist and names the word signs: M+ is Regina (read “la sua Maestà” before), a# Vostra Dominatio , o+ Imperatore , M̄ Zuan Corvino , Q. Duca de Milano , Ra madonna Bianca , + Vescovo Varadino ; x̄ is ma and ƀ fa . Words of the September reading that the signs do not carry were withdrawn. A second sheet headed “Cum Mafeo Triviliensi” (R5407) is a different alphabet.

The ten ciphered lines of the letter of 12 January 1490, below the clear text that breaks off at “…in mane sue”. Image: Archivio di Stato di Milano, Sforzesco 642/1, 4, via DECODE R1098. The letter's clear first page is about church appointments; the cipher begins where the news turns delicate. Questo Ser.mo Re partite de qua ali 8 del presente per andare ad Vienna, non ta[nto] per che la speranza de la dieta lo tiri, quanto per proprio desiderio de andarli; et che sia el vero, questi prelati mi hano dicto che in questo camino divertira ad tutti li lochi ove ha facto [...] edificare, che sono molti, et non si condura ad Vienna piu [...] presto che in 20 o 25 di. Lo legato et li altri oratori hano, et io con loro havemo, deliberato partire ali 15 de questo, et siamo rimasti dreto, perche Sua Maiesta mi fece dire che andassimo recta via ad Vienna, perche lei voleva andare spassando. Non sono piu [...]. “This Most Serene King left here on the 8th of this month to go to Vienna, not so much because the hope of the Diet draws him as from his own wish to go there; and in proof, these prelates have told me that on this journey he will turn aside to all the places where he has had building done, which are many, and will not reach Vienna sooner than in 20 or 25 days. The legate and the other ambassadors have, and I with them have, decided to leave on the 15th of this month, and we have stayed behind because His Majesty had me told that we should go straight to Vienna, since he wished to travel at leisure.” Lines 5–10 were re-read on 23 October 2026 from native crops of the DECODE image with the original key, and the result was set against the contemporary decipherment printed by Nagy and Nyáry in 1878 (MDE IV no. 91, pp. 161–162, “Extractus Ziffri Maphei Triviliensis. 12. Januarii 1490”): the re-read signs agree with it at each place (“tutti li lochi ove ha facto edificare”, “siamo”, “andassimo”, “spassando”); “mi” and “perche” in the last lines are taken from the print. The September reading’s guess “Tulln” was wrong. The letter also confirms the decipherment from inside: its own second page says in clear words that “lo legato et li altri oratori et io siamo insieme deliberato partire alli 15 de questo … andare per la via ad Vienna”. The cipher says the same thing in the same order, and the word “Vienna” is spelled with the same signs in lines 2, 6 and 10.

Four pages. Somogyi printed the first two lines as a specimen; no contemporary decipherment, copy or edition of the rest was found. Matthias Corvinus had six months to live, his war with Frederick III was in suspense, and two marriages were in play for his illegitimate son John Corvinus: Bianca Maria Sforza, Ludovico's niece, and a daughter of don Federico of Aragon, Naples's candidate. Queen Beatrice of Aragon opposed the succession of her stepson. Every cipher line of page 1, page 2 lines 1–17 and page 4 was re-read sign by sign from per-row crops of the Vestigia plates and decoded with the original key (23 October 2026); page 2 has 31 lines, and its first line had never been transcribed. The unread groups were then put through the shared Italian model over every alternative symbol value, and five more words were adopted where every letter is carried. Spelling is as decoded; […] marks unread groups, [?word] a word only partly carried by the signs. The opening of page 1: La Ex.tia vra intende ad quali termine la pratica de pace, et per consequente questa dieta. Questo Ser.mo Re de Hungaria e tenero del honore suo, como ho scripto altre volte; non e dubio che […] desidera la pace, ma non tanto pero ch'el voglia recevere una […] […] de la […] sua. Non […] ne […] e[x]presamente de andare ad la dieta, ben che ancora in Imperatore non veda [?fondamente] de pace, perche non se gli potesse imputare che per lui fosse rotta la pratica. Gli pare anche duro andarli per non fare niente et riceverne scorno; et pero desiderana havere littere da Imperatore che lo […] andare affirmando li essere ben disposto a la pace, et con questo si [?contenta] andarli, anchora che fosse certo che niuna conclusione ne ne dovesse riuscire, perche gli pare […] potersi sempre ben iustificare et satisfare al honore suo. “Your Excellency understands at what point the peace negotiation stands, and consequently this Diet. This Most Serene King of Hungary is jealous of his honour, as I have written at other times; there is no doubt that […] desires peace, but not so much that he will accept a […] of his […]. … It also seems hard to him to go there to obtain nothing and receive scorn; and so he wants letters from the Emperor … affirming that he is well disposed to peace, and with this he is [?content] to go, even if he were sure that no conclusion would come of it.” The page goes on to the new Neapolitan ambassador, who has again proposed the daughter of don Federico, and to the Queen, who says freely that the Milan match was made in spite of her. Page 2 opens with the rumour that Zuan Corvino would marry don Federico’s daughter: et respondendoli colui parerli imposibile, essendo cocto quello de Milano, solenemente replico essere vero, dicendo ch'el parentato de Milano era gia […]. Sono ancora stati de cortesani li quali, havendo inteso de la deliberatione che era facta, che [?messere] Francisco andisse ad Napoli, gli hano dicto: voi andarete ad disfare quello che haveti cocto. “…and when that man answered that it seemed impossible to him, the Milan match being cooked, he solemnly replied that it was true, saying that the Milan marriage was already […]. There have also been courtiers who, having heard of the decision that had been made, that [?messer] Francesco should go to Naples, told him: ‘You will go and undo what you have cooked.’” Maffeo warns that the Queen will try everything to turn the King from his purpose, “et in questo non cedera a la isacia[b]ile ira de Iunone”. The two cipher lines of page 4 end: “Sed hoc non fallet divinam sapientiam de la Vostra Dominatio.” Page 2 lines 18–31 and page 3: decoded, not read. They were re-read sign by sign from the plates with the original key (b25, 23 October 2026), re-cropped at full resolution for page 3 and segmented with the shared Italian model; the partial text ( v2831_p2p3_r2l_reading.md ) touches on intercepted cipher letters, Francesco’s mission to Naples, the Turk and the Bishop of Várad. An independent second reader then transcribed eight lines blind from the plates: 93.3% of the signs agree, but 9 of 92 words of the reading (9.8%) are not carried by the signs after each disputed sign was re-checked. At that rate across the unsampled lines these pages fall below the bar, so they are shown for checking and not counted. The next step is to bracket those words and check every word of the two pages against the signs the same way.

Page 4: the cipher stops after two lines and Maffeo goes on in the clear, about money. Image: Archivio di Stato di Milano, Sforzesco 650, via Vestigia. Nothing on this page is secret, and it was never enciphered. It is also the only part of the letter that is about Maffeo himself. Credo che la Ex.tia V.ra havera facto dar quelli ducento ad m. Fran.co; che, se cosi e, la ringratio infinite volte de la clementia et bonta sua infinita. Et perche quelli denari non mi portavano fin al fine de decembre, et partendosi lui non saperia da chi imprum[ut]are uno quatrino se non dal Thexaurero Regio, che seria con graveza de la persona vostra propria … Se de questa spesa non gli ne faria honor, sonno contento che non me ne proveda; io gli posso affirmar etiam cum iuramento che, doppoi che sonno qua, ultra quello ho havuto et tolto in nome del Ill.mo S. V.ro, ho speso di mei piu de centocinquanta ducati tra mi, veste et cavalli … che la provisione che me e ordinata non mi basta, dovendo tener questo loco secundo la dignita sua. Et perche in questa novita facta de Cancelleri forse poteria esser dome[n]ticato, La supplico ordini ad chi li par che provedi sia compreso in el numero de li altri Can[cellieri] et in lassignatione facta ad la Cancellaria. A V.ra Ex. de continuo me recomando. Bude xxij Novembris 1489. E[iusdem] Ill.me D[ominationis] V[ostre] servus, Magister Trivilien[sis] . “Since I have been here, beyond what I have had in Your Lordship's name, I have spent more than a hundred and fifty ducats of my own on myself, clothes and horses … the allowance assigned me is not enough to keep this post according to its dignity. And because in this recent reshuffle of the chancery clerks I might be forgotten, I beg you to order whoever you think fit to see that I am counted among the other chancellors.” The phrase “et in lassignatione facta ad la Cancellaria” is the explicit by which the archive catalogues the letter.

The images are the Vestigia plates (3240×4320, no login needed: the record page at vestigia.hu/documents/<id> carries the whole record as JSON, and the originals are served from /media/<file id>/<file name> ) and, for R1098, the DECODE scans of the same negatives. The working loop was: connected-component segmentation of each page into glyph boxes, line assignment by the peaks of the horizontal ink projection, merging of the two-stroke signs and of superscripts with the letter below them; then numbered strips, one line at a time, transcribed into values by hand against a sheet of sign exemplars cut from the letters themselves; then the values segmented into Italian, and any place where the Italian failed sent back to the image. The 2 April pair was aligned by dynamic programming against its clear copy to seed the key. Several rounds were needed: the first pass on the 1489 letter produced letter strings, the second, working from contrast-stretched crops of whole lines rather than from boxes, produced sentences. Two practical notes for anyone continuing. The automatic line segmentation misassigns glyphs in the lower half of pages 2 and 3 of the 1489 letter, where the lines converge; transcribe those from the plate with per-row crops. And the stacked line crops drift from line 18 onward on page 3, which cost one pass its accuracy.

Letter groups of the 1489 letter that decode letter for letter but give no word, between secure words: page 1 lines 3, 4, 8, 11, 12, 17, 19–22, 25–29; page 2 lines 15, 16, 19–21, 25, 28–31; page 3 lines 2, 3, 5–8, 15, 18, 21, 22, 27, 29, 31; page 4 line 2. Four passes and a model segmentation over every alternative symbol value left them; they need the values in the torn columns of R5411. Signs in the torn columns of R5411 (x, y, z, &, part of t), the r-ring on page 3 line 15, and the o-form, read t in most words but b by the key. Page 3 line 15: one or two signs under an ink blot; page 1 lines 21–29: the last words of each line under a stain at the right edge (re-checked at three times on 23 October 2026; the Vestigia plate is the only image). Page 2 lines 18–31 and page 3: decoded, not read (section 04). The letter of 12 January 1490: the two signs after “ove ha facto” (the key’s o+ is Imperatore) have no word in the printed decipherment and stay open, and the cipher’s last words, “non sono piu lon[…]”, are not in the printed extract.

Vestigia 2831, Buda 22 Nov 1489: p. 1, p. 2 ll. 1-17 and the two cipher lines of p. 4 (p. 2 has 31 lines) read in part Maffeo da Treviglio to Ludovico Sforza: King Matthias will not go to the Diet without letters from the Emperor that let him come away justified; the new Neapolitan ambassador is to reconcile the Queen with the King and has raised again the match of John Corvinus with don Federico's daughter, which the King takes as made in spite of the Milanese marriage; courtiers tell messer Francesco he goes to Naples 'to undo what you have cooked'; Maffeo advises that the Queen will spare no effort to turn the King and will not yield 'to the insatiable wrath of Juno'. Builds coherent sentences, but under the read bar of 95% of words read as sense (90% here); the holes are marked in the reading. Translation v2831_r2e_en.md # Vestigia 2831, Buda 22 Nov 1489: p. 1, p. 2 ll. 1-17, p. 4 cipher lines — English (r2e, 23 Oct 2026) Translation of `v2831_r2e_reading.md`, same holes: `[…]` unread, `[?word]` partly carried, `[word]` supplied. ## Translation *Page 1.* Your Excellency understands at what point the peace negotiation stands, and consequently this Diet. This Most Serene King of Hungary is jealous of his honour, as I have written at other times; there is no doubt that […] desires peace, but not so much that he will accept a […] […] of his […]. He will not […] nor […] expressly to go to the Diet, since even in the Emperor he does not see a [?foundation] for peace, so that it could not be imputed to him that the negotiation was broken off by him. It also seems hard to him to go there to obtain nothing and receive scorn; and so he wants letters from the Emperor which […] him to go, affirming that he is well disposed to peace, and with this he is [?content] to go, even if he were sure that no conclusion would come of it, because it seems to him […] he can always justify himself and satisfy his honour. […] that this new ambassador of Naples, in negotiating the reconciliation of the Queen with the Most Serene King, to dispose her to the will, as he says, of the […], for the benefit of the son. He has once again tried and [?made] mention of the daughter of don Federico, and I have these conjectures of it: first the words he said to the Most Serene King, that […] the son should have regard to the honour of the Queen. It seems to me it matters to nothing but this, because she saying freely that this [?match] was made in spite of him, it does not seem to me he sees anything better by which […] he should hold himself [?satisfied] in his honour, this [?match] standing, unless they wanted […]. […] that it is impossible […] not […] from Your Lordship the […]. The Most Serene King having had [?messer] Francesco told that he wants him [?to go] to Na[ples], these prelates who love the Queen little have entered […] […] and have suspected that the Most Serene King had […] purpose, and that […] the Queen, making a show of sending him to make the treaty of […] the daughter of don Federico, which displeased him [?to death], when it had been […] with a Neapolitan gentleman who is with the said ambassador. He has […] to say to a person who […] has […] *Page 2, ll. 1-17.* reported, that this Zuan Corvino […], and that the marriage would be made with the [?daughter] of don Federico, and that the ambassador was to send him to Naples for this; and when that man answered that it seemed impossible to him, the Milan match being cooked, he solemnly replied that it was true, saying that the Milan marriage was already […]. There have also been courtiers who, having heard of the decision that had been made, that [?messer] Francesco should go to Naples, told him: "You will go and undo what you have cooked." […] also that the aforenamed ambassador has complained in the name of his king of Your Lordship, because when the Most Serene King told [?messer] Francesco about going to Naples, [he] added that he wants […] to reconcile King Ferdinand with Your Lordship. I tell Your Lordship freely what I feel, and my wit offers it, so that Your Lordship, who is most wise, may with […] judgement take the part that will [?seem] good to him, provided he holds this as certain: that the Queen wants it sweet and […], so that one can want it […] capital, […] and that she will not hold back from making every attempt to turn the Most Serene King from the purpose, even if he [?saw] the […] […] that […]; and in this she will not yield to the insatiable wrath of Juno, […] and […], even among these, nor the father, and to fail to serve his appetite … *Page 4, the cipher lines.* … what he knows and can do. But this will not deceive the divine wisdom of Your Lordship. It is said also that the […] one […] […] to the Sultan. The cipher A two-part numeric code of about 2,450 groups for syllables, words and names; homophonic, with short alphabetical runs. Groups written with a fifth figure are nulls. How it was read Three 1823 Paris letters (R9569, R9571, R9589) in the same code were deciphered between the lines, as were ten lines of despatch 3874 (R9566). Aligning these glosses group by group gave the key; an earlier pass on 21 September had found no key. What it says Despatch 3874 (Paris, 1 December 1816) reports a conversation between the French interior minister and the Spanish minister Onis about the cession of the Floridas. Still open The key values 45% of the groups in the target letters; about a third of its values are inferences, and no letter is yet decrypted in full. R9566 p. 3, despatch 3874 (Paris, 1 December 1816), with its contemporary interlinear decipherment: “questo Minro dell' Interno Cte di Cazes che gode sempre del piu gr. favore presso del Re di Fra ha avuto una confer.za col Minro di S.M. Cattolica Sigr Onis al suo passaggio per qui, nella quale parlandogli della cessione delle Floride, e di quella di cui si è parlato…” Image: Archivio di Stato di Napoli, Ministero degli affari esteri, busta 2337, p. 3, via DECODE R9566.

All the documents are in busta 2337 of the Esteri series, photographed for DECODE (records R9553–R9589, access by login). The headings give the dates and places: London, 1816: 1 April (R9553, no. 2314, headed “Cifra della Segreteria di Stato”), 30 August, 6 September, 26 September, 4 October (R9556, R9557, R9579, R9558). Paris, 1816: 3 June (R9555), 17, 19 and 23 October (R9559, R9560, R9587), 30 November (R9561, seven pages), 1 December (R9566, despatch 3874, with a second fragment in another hand), 3 December (R9562). Undated, to Circello: R9554 (no. 2589), R9563 (2814), R9564 (3388 or 3588), R9565 (3721), R9567 (4086). The fragments R9582–R9585 date from 1817–1819. Paris, 1823, to the Cavaliere de’ Medici: 4, 8 and 11(?) September, 9 October (R9569, R9571, R9570, R9589). The papal conclave that followed Pius VII’s death is the theme. Another code: R9586 and R9588 (values 100–1100, faint pencil glosses), two undated letters signed by Castelcicala, are a different cipher, with their own page . R9590 (Paris, 12 March 1830) is also in another code. The images are not in reading order. R9579 runs P2, P3, P1, P4; R9569 P2, P1; R9561 begins at P2.

The groups run from 1 to about 2,450, with dots between them. The same frequent groups appear in 1816 and 1823 (2201, 2211, 332, 1909, 2450, 2232, 1864, 1843), so one book served for seven years. Its units are syllables, common words and names, and a word is spelled from as many as it needs: groups reading 1708 2027 1994 · 1708 1531 1994 ele·va·zione · ele·(null)·zione 1609 2448 2221 1951 2450 · 1609 2380 2221 2076 pon·ti·fi·ca·to · pon·te·fi·ce 2009 2211 1725 2295 · 2012 2448 1535 2169 Car·di·na·le Cas·ti·gli·one 2367 2290 1404 1535 · 2367 2232 2450 par·lan·do·gli · par·la·to 2357 1758 2318 · 1919 2318 · 1739 1714 2318 li·ber·tà · No·ta · un·i·ta It is homophonic : di is 1112 and 2211, pa is 1201 and 2363, ere is 1836 and 2381. It is a two-part code with local alphabetical runs : 2201 che, 2205 ci, 2211 di, 2221 fi, 2230 l, 2231 l’, 2232 la; 2082 del, 2083 dell’, 2084 della; 2045 quella, 2049 questo; 2161 is, 2162 Isola; 1919 no, 1920 non; 2445 ter, 2448 ti, 2450 to. Between runs the order is scattered. A group written with a fifth figure (21900, 18900, 16480; about a hundred cases) always falls where the decipherer wrote nothing, so these are nulls.

1 December 1816 (R9566, first ten lines). Decazes, the Minister of the Interior, “who still enjoys the greatest favour with the King of France”, has met the Spanish minister Onís on his way through Paris. Speaking of the cession of the Floridas, and of the cession of Cuba to England that had been talked of, he “skilfully insinuated”… The gloss stops there. 8 September 1823 (R9571). “La Francia desidera il Cardinale [?Vo...] Castiglione per Papa, ma si biasima di avere il Duca di Lavalle troppo fatto ciò vedere, e si teme che ciò nuoccia al suddetto porporato per la sua elevazione al Pontefica[te]. Non esiste alcuno accordo tra la Francia. L'Austria per la elezione del Pontefice.” (France wants Cardinal Castiglioni as Pope. The Duc de Laval is blamed for making this too plain, which may harm the cardinal’s chances. France and Austria have no agreement on the election.) Castiglioni was elected as Pius VIII only in 1829; Leo XII was chosen on 28 September 1823. 9 October 1823 (R9589). Now that the King of Spain has his liberty and the orders given in Medici’s despatch no. 688 of 28 September, there can be no question of Castelcicala passing the note to the Conference. Postscript: the Duc d’Angoulême will not be back for two months. 4 September 1823 (R9569) has only a fragmentary gloss, and the letter is decoded, not read. It concerns the election to the papacy and whether France would use its veto; one sentence of the gloss now holds: “... ed io ho motivo di credere di no, e che [...] la suddetta elezione la Francia gli darebbe l'esclusiva”.

The 27 records were fetched from DECODE and transcribed from full-resolution crops by two transcription agents: 9,428 groups in the 25 letters in the main code, 1,315 distinct. The glosses were aligned group by group, and the key was extended by hand from repeated contexts. Its 162 values are graded in key.tsv : 90 taken directly from a contemporary gloss (G), 18 glossed and confirmed in a second context (X), and 54 inferred here and unconfirmed (I). With them, 45% of the groups in the target letters get a value (4,340 of 9,286 counted without the five-figure nulls, 46.7%). Scoring candidate syllables for each unknown group with an Italian 5-gram model did not separate the candidates. The known neighbours are too sparse, and the segmentation into syllables or words is unknown. So no letter is decrypted in full . The partial decode ( reading_partial.txt ) is a working file, not an edition of the text. Some I values are surely wrong: “il Sr troppo l d’An ta” in R9579 must be a name. The next step is to decrypt the 1816 letters one at a time, around the Floridas–Cuba–Decazes themes the gloss supplies, using the alphabetical runs to bracket unknown groups. The code book itself, if it survives in the Esteri or the Segreteria di Stato papers of the ASNa, would settle it at once. The consular keys of Borbone 1666 on DECODE (R9532–R9541) are from 1859–60 and do not apply.

Archivio di Stato di Napoli, Ministero degli affari esteri, busta 2337, items 4–41, photographed for DECODE ( R9554 , R9566 , R9571 , R9589 and neighbours). The images are not in the public domain; only a crop is shown. Busta 2317 (DECODE R9549): a 1797–98 Vienna despatch with its decipherment, in a different code. It is not the plaintext of these letters, whatever DECODE’s note suggests. Fabrizio Ruffo, principe di Castelcicala: Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani . No edition of his ciphered despatches was found. Transcriptions, key, scripts, notes and profile: targets/castelcicala1816/ in the repository.

Two cipher passages in a clear letter from the king’s lieutenant at Langres, in a homophonic substitution whose small crosses and strokes make new signs. An outside contributor, Alex Zarco, rebuilt the key from the interlinear decipherment of the sibling letter on f. 128, completing a partial key published by NoAutopilot; 514 of 522 cipher tokens read, checked here on the images and against the 1882 print of f. 128. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 21 September 2026 · updated 26 October 2026 Method: key recovered based on adjacent plaintext · Extent: partial (98% of the cipher) Contributed by alejandrozarco (solution) · Also credited · NoAutopilot (earlier solution) · Contemporary key or decipherment (key or decipherment used) adjacent text At a glance Key from adjacent plaintext · partial (98% of the cipher) The letter Dinteville, royalist lieutenant in Champagne, to the Duke of Nevers, dated at Langres on 4 July 1592 (the date was corrected from 3 July): clear French with two cipher passages and an autograph postscript in clear. Where BnF Français 3621, no. 116, f. 130 (DECODE R9451; Gallica btv1b52524472n, view 269). DECODE calls it a “letter, with cipher and decryption”, but the image shows no decipherment. The cipher A mixed set of digits, letters and marks, roughly 400 to 450 symbols, many barred, crossed or dotted. How it was read Alex Zarco (pull request #24, 6 October 2026) rebuilt the key from the interlinear decipherment of the sibling letter f. 128, the crib found here on 21 September, and read f. 130, building on NoAutopilot’s partial key. This project verified it. Credit Solution by Alex Zarco; prior partial key by NoAutopilot. Still open 8 of 522 cipher tokens. The sections below describe the 21–24 September attempt, made before this solution, and have not yet been rewritten.

f. 130r, the head of the letter: clear French with the first cipher passage (lines 4–8) set inline. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3621 f. 130r, via Gallica (btv1b52524472n, view 269). f. 130 (no. 116) is a clear French letter signed by Dinteville, dated de Langres le iiij e Juillet 1592 . Its subject in clear is the enemy’s threat to return to Châteauvillain and the town’s request to the King and Nevers for two hundred horse and two hundred foot. The cipher breaks into it twice: about four lines near the top (ll. 4–8) and six full lines in the middle (ll. 11–16), 522 cipher symbols in all. After the date comes an autograph postscript in clear, cramped and partly struck out, on the Lorraine army; the verso carries only the address. Nothing on the leaf glosses the cipher, although DECODE describes R9451 as a letter “with cipher and decryption”. The day is iiij e , as the 1882 summary in the Revue de Champagne et de Brie also gives it; the “3 July” of DECODE and of the first version of this page was a misreading. f. 128 (no. 114) , two leaves earlier, is Dinteville’s letter of 1 July 1592 to the same recipient, in the same symbols. Its three and a half lines of cipher (180 symbols) carry a contemporary decipherment written above each line, and the whole letter is printed in the Revue de Champagne et de Brie t. XII (1882), p. 340.

f. 128r, 1 July 1592: the cipher lines, with the contemporary decipherment written above each (“auoir veu dassender a gennes” over the second line). Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3621 f. 128r, via Gallica (btv1b52524472n, view 265). The key was recovered by Alex Zarco (GitHub alejandrozarco), who sent it as pull request #24 on 6 October 2026, working with an LLM. Two things opened the crib that the first attempt here had failed on (section 05): The marks belong to the symbols. The small crosses and strokes on some symbols, earlier taken for the decipherer’s marks, make separate cipher symbols: ∇ is a and ∇ with a rising stroke t ; Δ with a tail below is a and plain Δ f ; the o-shaped symbol with a cross above is s and with a plain ascender p ; ψ is o and ψ with a cross below a null. The gloss says Gennes. The interlinear reads a gennes (Genoa), not Geneve , and the cipher spells dessendre . With both, Zarco made a new transcription of f. 128 and f. 130 that keeps every diacritic, and the alignment of f. 128’s second line against its gloss admits exactly one key, with only the leading double bar as a null. He then valued the symbols that occur only on f. 130 from context. The system is a homophonic substitution of 46 symbols: one to three symbols for each letter, four nulls (ψ with a cross, # with a long stroke, the double bar and a joined a-loop), and two symbols that the writer used for two letters each, # for c or d and 1 for e or i , so that context decides, as it did for the decipherer of 1592. No code words for names were seen. The full table is key.tsv in the repository. NoAutopilot had published a partial key from the same gloss in their cipher-lab repository from 3 October 2026, with word fragments of f. 130, leaving the rows for h , Δ and a stemmed zero open. Zarco reports that he found their folder only after his decipherment and his blind test; every fragment they give agrees with his text, and his key settles their three open rows. The checks made here on 7 October 2026: The cipher under the f. 128 gloss and three lines of f. 130 (ll. 5, 6 and 14 at their openings) were compared with the transcription on the Gallica images, symbol for symbol. On f. 128, four tailed deltas had been written as plain Δ, so the final key gave f for a in auoir , Besançon , quarante and n’ayans ; corrected, f. 128 decodes cleanly. The decipherment of f. 128 agrees word for word with the 1882 print, including Gennes , doiuent partir where the gloss abbreviates, and d’escorte under the blot. Scored on f. 130 with a French word model, the key gives −2.00 log-probability per letter; the best of 200 shuffled keys gives −4.29 (median −5.37). The key fixed on f. 128 alone, before any value was taken from f. 130, already gives 71% of f. 130 in words. A second transcription of f. 130, made blind from crops and a shape legend, agrees with the first on 95.6% of symbols and decodes to 97.3% of the same text. The statistical validation of 11 October ( docs/_validate.py ) passes: z = 7.6 against random keys and 25.2 against keys fitted to the shuffled ciphertext.

f. 130r, the second cipher passage (ll. 11–16): from si les forces n’y sont placees to l’honneur , then clear comme luy . Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3621 f. 130r, via Gallica (btv1b52524472n, view 269). The two cipher passages in their clear context, in the writer’s spelling. Clear text is in ⟨ ⟩; […] marks the four open symbols of line 4, [?] an uncertain word, [?word] a doubtful one, and square brackets round letters mark letters supplied. ⟨…ce que J’ay eu auiourdhuy aduis de plusieurs endroitz que l’ennemy [?] faict estat dy retourner et⟩ l’emporter, […] il n’y estoit pourveu, qui me faict les y renvoier avec de la pouldre. ⟨Vous Iugerez aussi s’il vous plaist, Monseigneur, que⟩ je demeure seul ici avec les habitans et ⟨que la[rmée] … Lorrains [?] se fortiffie de ce qui estoit du coste de Strasbourg⟩ et, retournant a moi, il me seroit malaisé d’y conserver ceste place en l’obeissance qu’[?elle] y est. ⟨Messieurs de la Ville supplient tres humblement le Roy et vous d’y placer deux cens chevaulx et deux cens hommes de pied…⟩ ⟨…Il y a plus de cinq cens chevaulx de garnison ennemye et le pais est […] soubz contributions sur ce qu[i …]⟩ si les forces n’y sont placées, oultre le hasart que court la ville, il ne se leuera un denier de tailles. D’aultre costé, l’en y voi[t] le dedans si bien basti qu’il ne soit plus a craindre que le dehors; les forces serviront tant a les contenir a leur devoir que a la deffence de la ville. Le Roi et vous m’excuserez si je [?pass] de mot, que [?] s’il ne plaist a Sa Maiesté d’y pourvoir, de m’en retirer, d’aultant qu’il y a a perdre la vie et l’honneur ⟨comme [?] luy. Je la doibs a sa Ma(jes)te…⟩ In English: the enemy means to come back and carry Châteauvillain unless it is provided for, which is why Dinteville is sending the men back there with powder; he is left alone in Langres with the townspeople, and if the Lorraine army turns on him he can hardly keep the town in its obedience. Without troops, besides the danger to the town, not a penny of taille will be raised; the troops would serve as much to keep the inhabitants to their duty as to defend the walls. If it does not please the King to provide, he asks leave to withdraw, since life and honour are at stake. The full translation is under Full texts below. Each cipher run continues the grammar of the clear text on either side ( retourner et | l’emporter , que | je demeure , l’honneur | comme luy ), and the cipher gives the reasons behind the request the letter makes in clear. Of the 522 cipher symbols, 514 give sense (98.5%), none emended; counted by words of the reading, 95.5% read as sense. The Revue de Champagne of 1882 summarises this letter from its clear text only and marks the rest “En chiffres”; apart from NoAutopilot’s fragments, no earlier decipherment of these passages was found.

The cipher passage of the letter of 1 July, with the clear lead-in in ⟨ ⟩ as the print summarises it: ⟨…[un gentilhomme de M. de Gondy venant de Florence]⟩ m’a dit auoir veu dessendre a Gennes deus millions d’or d’Espaigne. Il y a laissé a Besançon quarante cinq mulets chargés qui doiuent partir dans trois jours et prendre le chemin de Vesou[l], n’ayans que cent chevaux d’escort[e] [blot] A gentleman of M. de Gondi, coming from Florence, saw two million in Spanish gold unloaded at Genoa; forty-five laden mules left at Besançon are to set out in three days by the road to Vesoul, with only a hundred horse as escort. This is Spanish money on its way up through Franche-Comté. The text builds coherent sentences, but by words 93.2% read as sense, under the 95% that the project counts as complete: the opening words are the print’s summary of the clear lead-in, which has not been transcribed here, and the last letters of Vesoul and escorte lie under an ink blot.

The first session here, on 21 September 2026, found the volume on Gallica, established that f. 130 carries no decipherment, and found the f. 128 crib two leaves earlier. It then transcribed 50 symbols of f. 128’s second cipher line by eye and searched ( align.py ) for a key of one symbol per letter, homophones allowed, with up to three null types, against the gloss read as avoir veu d’ascendre a Geneve deux millions d’or d’Espaigne . No key fit: auoir sat cleanly over the first symbols, but α then had to stand for both o and d . The session concluded that the cipher probably held code symbols for words and closed the target as not deciphered. Both inputs were wrong. The crosses and strokes had been merged into their base symbols, which made pairs such as ψ and ψ+ look like one symbol with two values, and the gloss had been taken as Geneve and d’ascendre . Zarco’s bourdeau_test.py re-runs the same search: with the marks merged or the old gloss it finds no key; with the marks kept and the gloss read dessendre … gennes it finds exactly one. The search itself was sound; the transcription was not.

f. 130, line 4: the four symbols after l’emporter (the key gives ? i u s , perhaps ou s’il or puis ). Blocker: the first symbol is unclear on the image. f. 130, line 7: two symbols in qu’[?elle] y est . Blocker: the symbols are unclear on the image. f. 130, line 14: the last symbol of pass[?] and the symbol after que . Blocker: the shapes are doubtful and no key value fits. f. 128: the endings of Vesou[l] and escort[e] , under an ink blot (the print supplies both), and the clear lead-in, given here from the print’s summary. The clear text of f. 130 has uncertain words throughout, and the autograph postscript is legible only in fragments. These are clear-text questions; a better image or the original would settle them. Checked for more material: ff. 127–131 of the volume; Tomokiyo’s catalogue of the Nevers ciphers, which has no Dinteville key; the 1882 print. The DECODE record is due a correction: R9451 has no decipherment on the leaf, the date is 4 July, and the key source is f. 128.

Catalogue item 4, letters of the French ambassador in London to Montmorency (BnF fr. 3077, fr. 3078) listed with no decipherment; the four of 1529, in Bayonne’s cipher of that year, are printed in clear by Le Grand (1688) once their years are known (the fifth, of 1528, is another cipher with its own page). The two passages that edition left blank, a block of 16 June 1529 and the opening of 22 October 1529, are printed in clear in Rémy Scheurer’s edition (1969). The 16 June block was transcribed here (194 signs) and lines 0–6 deciphered with a key re-derived from the 22 June interlinear before Scheurer was found; his text agrees word for word. ʊ o~ Y ε 8 —e ꝡ ♀ □ 3 ξ ✝ j̈ = B ◇+ si vous trovez bon ⊑ = que · ℒ = vous · R = faict · 4 = madame · ꝛe = roy London → the Court · homophonic symbol cipher with word signs · 1529 · existing decipherment Jean du Bellay to Montmorency, London 1529 from Jean du Bellay → to Anne de Montmorency Go to the full text ↓ Every passage of du Bellay’s London letters of 1529 in his cipher of that year is already in print in clear, including the two that older editions left blank, which Rémy Scheurer printed in 1969. The item’s fifth letter, of 28 October 1528, is in another cipher. Where Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3077 and fr. 3078 (catalogue item 4). The 16 June letter is fr. 3078 p. 21, DECODE R3688, catalogued there as not decrypted. The BnF notice gives day and month but no year. The cipher “Bayonne’s cipher” of 1529: an alphabet of drawn symbols with two to five signs for each letter, a few nulls, and single signs for words such as roy , madame , vous , faict . How it was done The letters were matched to their printed texts once their years were known. The key was re-derived from a sibling letter of 22 June 1529 that has the decipherer’s reading written over every sign. With it, lines 0–6 of the 16 June block were deciphered from the leaf before any printed text was found. Scheurer’s edition then supplied three word signs and the last line, and agrees word for word. What it says On the Cambrai peace talks of summer 1529: du Bellay advises that the powers for the treaty be dated de ce temps là et du lieu ou sera le Roy . Still open Three isolated signs in the last cipher line. Whether the boxed cross is one word sign or two ( madame Marguerite here, le Cardinal on 17 October). The 22 October opening: Scheurer’s text is seen only in Google Books snippets, and the reading made here from the leaf (fr. 3005 ff. 165r–166r, 23 October 2026) leaves stretches of f. 165v and f. 166r unread, so it counts as decoded, not read. Credit Rémy Scheurer, Correspondance du cardinal Jean du Bellay t. I (1969), prints both passages in clear: no. 12 p. 41 (16 June) and pp. 111–112 (22 October). The other letters are in Joachim Le Grand (1688). Satoshi Tomokiyo’s table of the cipher (Cryptiana) was the starting point for the key.

Jean du Bellay was ambassador of François I in England from 1527 to 1529, in the years of Henry VIII’s divorce suit and Wolsey’s fall. His despatches to Montmorency are bound in BnF fr. 3077 and fr. 3078 by day and month, across several years. Omont’s inventory, followed by the BnF notice, gives only the day and month and calls the letters lettre chiffrée or avec chiffre . The catalogue took this to mean that no decipherment was known. Once each letter was dated from its content and matched to Le Grand’s Histoire du divorce (1688), Brewer’s Letters and Papers IV and Bourrilly’s edition of the first embassy (1905), all five turned out to be printed in clear. Four are of 1529, in the cipher of this page: Notice Date Leaf Printed in clear DECODE fr. 3078 no. 5 15 June 1529 pp. 31–33 Le Grand III 323–326; L&P IV 5679 R3690 fr. 3077 no. 18 18 Sept 1529 f. 113 Le Grand III 354–359; L&P IV 5945 R4252 fr. 3077 no. 20 4 Oct 1529 f. 125 Le Grand III 359–363; L&P IV 5983 R4253 fr. 3078 no. 17 17 Oct 1529 pp. 113–117 Le Grand III 369–375 (from the deciphered copy, Clair. 330 f. 71); L&P IV 6011 R3691 fr. 3078 no. 19 27 Oct 1529 pp. 133–134 Le Grand III 379–381; L&P IV 6030 R3692 The fifth, fr. 3077 no. 23 of 28 October 1528 (pp. 145–147, DECODE R4254), is in du Bellay’s first cipher, which Bourrilly and de Vaissière broke in 1905 and George Lasry solved again in 2022: a different cipher, with its own page . The 1529 letters use a second cipher, described below. Two more passages came up in the sweep of the volumes. The first is fr. 3078 no. 3, 16 June 1529 (p. 21), a clear letter with eight lines of cipher in the middle. It is not in Le Grand, Brewer or Bourrilly, and DECODE lists it as not decrypted. The second is the opening of 22 October 1529 , which is not in these volumes (the signed original is fr. 3005 ff. 165r–166r). Le Grand prints the rest of that letter with the note le commencement de cette lettre est en chiffre non déchiffré . Brewer (L&P IV 6019) and Tomokiyo say the same. A DECODE search for the same correspondence found one more letter, fr. 3040 f. 68 (R4229), of 30 June 1529. It is also printed in clear by Le Grand (III 333 ff.) and calendared in L&P IV 5742. Both of the passages left blank in 1688 are printed in clear in Rémy Scheurer’s Correspondance du cardinal Jean du Bellay , t. I (1969): the 16 June block as letter no. 12, p. 41, and the 22 October opening on pp. 111–112. So nothing in the item is without a printed decipherment. Scheurer’s volume was seen only in Google Books snippets.

Tomokiyo reconstructs the cipher from two deciphered letters of June 1530 (Clair. 333 ff. 24, 27). It is a homophonic alphabet of drawn signs, with two to four signs for most letters, a few nulls, and word signs for roy and madame . There is no k or w, and u and v are one letter. Paul Friedmann’s nineteenth-century reconstruction is BnF NAF 4206 no. 5 (DECODE R9467), but no image is attached to that record. The key used here was re-derived from fr. 3078 itself. The letter of 22 June 1529 (pp. 23–27, DECODE R3689) has the Court decipherer’s reading written above every cipher sign, and Le Grand prints its clear text, so sign and letter can be lined up one by one. This added signs that are not in Tomokiyo’s table: B and ∩ for o and a, and the word signs V = bien , R = fault and —ʔ = paix . Some examples: Letter Signs Letter Signs a c ∪ ⊔ ∩ ɔ o 3 ε B e ω ✝ ✗ p Λ λ H i —o o— ⊽ r ⊡ □ l △ ⧋ ẍ s ʊ —e ᒐ m, n, t a diamond with a stem (m), with a side cross (n), on a cross (t) u/v 8 ℓ y ξ The same key reads the catalogue’s 17 October letter (pp. 113–117) directly from the leaf. That letter is four pages of cipher with no interlinear decipherment, and the first lines of p. 113 give j’ay est[é] veoir [le Cardinal] en ses e[nnuis], ou que l’y ay trouvé le plus grant exemple , as in Le Grand III 370. This was a check of the key, not a new text.

The letter is in clear except for eight lines. In the clear part du Bellay writes about a bishopric he hopes for and la menée qu’on me veult faire against him, and asks Montmorency to send his decision with the next despatch. The cipher begins after Monsr , where some clear words have been struck out, and the clear text resumes with Toutesfoiz, Monsr, vous ne luy en ferez semblant . fr. 3078 p. 21, the letter of 16 June 1529: clear text above, the eight cipher lines below, and the clear text resuming on the last line with toutesfois . Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3078 p. 21, via DECODE R3688. The block was transcribed sign by sign from the high-resolution crop on DECODE: 194 signs in eight lines ( p21_signs.txt ; an earlier count of 167 had skipped line 6). Before any printed text was known, lines 0–6 had been deciphered with the key above and Tomokiyo’s table: si vous [?] trouvez bon l’advis que piecza vous ay envoé de faire semblant que madame ne fust allée pour conclure, et qu’estant là [boxed cross] luy ayt par importunité [R] envoyé querir pouoir, il ne [ℒ] faudroyt oublyer a le faire dater de ce temps là et du lieu … This pass also fixed several signs. ẍ (x over x) is l, as in allée . ⊑ is q and stands for que . ⊽ is i, as in piecza and importunité . The diamond signs split into m, n and t by their stroke. One “=” stands for b in bon , where it is f everywhere else, which is either a slip or a homophone. Scheurer’s edition then turned up. His letter no. 12 prints the whole block in clear, and it agrees with the reading from the leaf word for word. It also gave what the leaf reading lacked: ℒ = vous ; R = faict here (the 22 June gloss has fault , so R is the word sign for fault / faict ); the boxed cross with a loop at its centre = madame Marguerite ; and line 7 = ou sera le Roy , ending in ꝛe, Tomokiyo’s word sign for roy . The sign ꝡ, which comes after vous in line 0 and after roy in line 7, has nothing matching it in the print either time, so it is a null. The deciphered block, signs to letters, as transcribed here (word signs in small capitals in the reveal): Monsr, si vous trouvez bon l’advis que piecza vous ay envoé de faire semblant que Madame ne fust allée pour conclure, et qu’estant là madame Marguerite luy ayt par importunité faict envoyé querir pouoir, il ne vous faudroyt oublyer a le faire dater de ce temps là et du lieu ou ser[a le] Roy. My lord, if you approve the advice I sent you some time ago, to give out that Madame had not gone [to Cambrai] in order to conclude, and that, Madame Marguerite being there, she pressed her into sending for powers, you must not forget to have them dated from that time and from the place where the King will be. Madame is Louise of Savoy and Madame Marguerite is Margaret of Austria, who were about to negotiate the Peace of Cambrai (signed 3 August 1529). Du Bellay’s advice seems to be about presentation in England: the French powers should look as if they had been asked for at Cambrai, not prepared in advance. There are two small differences from the snippet of Scheurer’s text. The signs give et qu’estant là madame Marguerite (⊑ ✗ -ʊ- t a n t l a), where the snippet shows et que ostant madame Marguerite , which is probably a misprint or an OCR slip. And envoyé in line 1 is enciphered envoe , with no y. Of the 194 signs, 191 have a value (a letter, a word sign or a null), 98.5%. Every word of Scheurer’s text is accounted for by the signs. Line 3 of the block: -clure et qu’estant là [madame Marguerite] luy ayt par- . The boxed cross in the middle is the word sign that Scheurer’s text gives as madame Marguerite . Le Grand (III 377–379) and Brewer (L&P IV 6019) print this letter from Escripvant ceste lectre, ay sceu que monsr le Legat vient d’estre mys hors de sa maison onward and say that the opening is in cipher with no decipherment. Tomokiyo lists the copy, fr. 3005 f. 165, as unread. Scheurer (pp. 111–112) prints the letter from its first words, Monseigneur, la ou je vouldroye, si ne me sçauroye-je guarder d’accorder au cardinal d’York sa requeste , about a request Wolsey sent through an Italian servant who was still loyal to him (Agostino, his physician, according to Scheurer’s note). The snippets do not show whether Scheurer deciphered the passage himself or found a deciphered copy. On 23 October 2026 the leaf was reached through the BnF’s IIIF service (fr. 3005, Gallica btv1b90599952, canvases 259–261): the signed original, 34, 35 and 5 lines of cipher on ff. 165r, 165v and 166r, with no decipherment on or near it. It was deciphered sign by sign with the 1529 key ( texts/22oct1529_reading.md , with English). The first five lines agree with Scheurer’s snippets word for word, and the reading found new values (the cup = a , the barred cup = s , ƕ = f ; R = faict , V = bien , 4 = madame confirmed). The first half builds sentences: Mardi luy fut osté le seau, faict inventaire de tous ses biens jusques a ung escu, comandement faict a tous ceulx qui ont [?eu] manié quelque chose de luy depuys vingt ans de rendre compte de tout, dont ilz sont bien empeschez, car ne se trouant la sixiesme partie de [?ce] qu'on esperoit, ilz sont bien aseurez d'avoir maint tour de corde. “On Tuesday the seal was taken from him; an inventory was made of all his goods down to a crown; an order was given to all who [?have] handled anything of his these twenty years to render account of everything, which troubles them greatly, for since not a sixth part of [?what] was hoped for is found, they are sure to get many a turn of the rope.” Wolsey chose to answer before the King rather than Parliament; the charges include the plunderings, lese-majesty, the legation, and bringing Ferrara into the league at Amiens without the King’s knowledge. The rest (f. 165v lines 21–35 and f. 166r lines 1–5) keeps unread stretches, and two word signs read as the two Kings rest on sense only, so the opening counts as decoded, not read; Scheurer’s complete text, seen only in snippets, would settle it.

The years of the five catalogue letters were found from their content and matched to Le Grand, Brewer and Bourrilly. That closed the item as already deciphered. The key was re-derived from the 22 June interlinear decipherment and Tomokiyo’s table, and checked on the 17 October letter against Le Grand. The 16 June block was transcribed and its lines 0–6 deciphered from the leaf before Scheurer was found. These lines hold 181 of the 194 signs, and only four of them were left without a value: ꝡ, ℒ, R and the boxed cross. That part of the reading is independent of the print. The values of those four (ꝡ a null, ℒ vous , R faict , the boxed cross madame Marguerite ) and the reading of line 7 came from Scheurer. Scheurer’s text for the 22 October opening was checked against the cipher only for its first five lines, the part the snippets show; they agree.

Three signs in line 7 of 16 June. Between lieu and ou are three signs with no counterpart in the print: ρ with a triangle foot, ȸ, and a small x. ȸ is probably Tomokiyo’s ƒ-shaped null; the other two are unexplained. A smudged sign stands where the print has a le before Roy . These are probably nulls or a slip, and they are too few to settle. The boxed cross: one sign or two? On p. 21 Scheurer’s text gives the boxed cross as madame Marguerite . On p. 113 (17 October) a boxed cross lines up with le Cardinal in Le Grand’s text. The p. 21 sign has a loop at the centre of the cross, so the two may be different word signs. If they are the same sign, one of the two identifications is wrong. The p. 113 sign has not been re-examined to tell them apart, and this question is left open. Scheurer’s text was seen only as Google Books snippets. A full copy would confirm estant against ostant and show which copy he used for 22 October. 22 October 1529. Read sign by sign from fr. 3005 ff. 165r–166r on 23 October 2026: f. 165v lines 21–35 and f. 166r lines 1–5 keep unread stretches, and the word signs ꝑ and ℋ (the two Kings, by sense only), ꝏ and # are open.

Monseigneur, ce qu'il leur a donné le plus chault alarme, c'est que le Duc de Suffock a escript au Roy son Maistre, comme j'ay sa Lettre mesmes, que le Roy luy avoyt dict que, venans les Dames à ce Parlement, ce seroit tout faict et conclud en deux jours; la dessus ils jugent que les choses sont accordées de ceste heure, qu'il n'y fault plus que ung petit de cerimonie, disans qu'en cela vous estes allez trop faintement avec eulx, leur monstrant tousiours, disant et escripvant que ne voyez aucun fondement en la matiere. Je vous asseure, Monseigneur, que sans fiction Monsieur le Legat est en terrible paine, car encores jusques à ceste heure il avoit tousiours asseuré son Maistre et tout le monde, et en privé et public, que ce ne seroyt riens, et que ne ferez chose quelle qu'elle feust sans eulx. Il se doute fort à present du contraire, et je vous laisse penser s'il parle bien à moy, et s'il dit bien que je l'ay abusé, et ay esté cause qu'il a abusé son Maistre, consequemment que je l'ay mis en ung tres-mauvais chemin; je m'ayde à cela et deffends du bec et des ongles, encores à la fin me viendra-t'il rechercher, et desia, comme voyez, il a voulu que soye allé veoir le Roy, et que le servisse des meilleurs propos du monde, ne le mectant entr'aultres choses totalement hors d'espoir que la venue de Monsieur Feuguillaume ne feust pour mectre quelque retardement en ceste Assemblée; ce que je sens bien qu'il me fault faire, partie à bonne fin et pour entretenir ces choses en bon train, partie pour se desmesler, afin qu'ayant ma part de la charge envers sondict Maistre, la sienne en soyt d'autant moindre. Il fauldra bien, Monseigneur, que celluy qui viendra apporter les nouvelles de paix soyt bien embouché de honnestes propos. Aussi, Monseigneur, j'ay entendu de bon lieu que Madame Marguerite vous presse fort de venir à bonne conclusion (vous sçavez s'il est vray), alleguant la peine qu'elle a eu d'avoir sa commission de l'Empereur, encores que tous les Ambassadeurs de ses parens et alliez, les plus grans Seigneurs d'Espaigne, luy en tombassent à genoulx, qu'il veist Monseigneur d'Orleans en desespoir de vie, ses affaires le plus mal du monde en Italie, en Espaigne chacun mal content et en voulonté de se mutiner, la Germanie si troublée, et l'appareil du Turc si grand qu'il n'est possible de plus; et que à ceste heure, pour estre aulcunes desdites causes cessées, et les aultres povoir avec le temps cesser, qu'elle craignoit merveilleusement qu'il revoquast ladicte commission, et que desia elle en avoyt quelque bon divertissement. Je n'en ay rien ouy; mais c'est ce me semble estre bon à dire, et mesme au Duc de Suffock. Il est vray, Monseigneur, qu'ayant les enfans c'est le principal, mais qui peut contenter tout c'est bien faict. Je croy que Feuguillaume a porté commandement à Monsieur de Soufforck de s'en retourner; j'entends qu'ils ont Lectres du Roy du xvj, où tout cruement il mectoyt qu'il partoyt de Paris pour tirer vers Cambray, comme s'il se y debvoit trouver, dont je vous asseure que le Cardinal d'Yort ne seroit content. Monseigneur, le Legat vouldroyt bien que, m'escripvant le Roy de sa bonne affection et voulenté d'ayder au Roy son frere en son affaire, il feist expresse mention que d'autant plus il se y [?venit] employer qu'il en est et a continuellement esté requis et pressé de mondict sieur le Legat; et me semble, Monseigneur, que ce sera bien faict d'ainsi le faire. Il pourroyt estre que trouverez mauvais que si souvent je vous envoye des couriers expres; mais, Monseigneur, il fauldroyt que je n'escripvisse point, car premierement les pacquets ne seroient point portez, et d'aultre part demourans sur la table, comme je suys seur qu'ils seroyent; il y a par toutes les postes gens du Duc de Sufforc qui ne me fauldroyent en si beau pays. Le Cardinal d'Yort m'en a adverty assés prés, et je trouve que un pacquet s'est perdu depuys que suys icy, dont suys en paine. Vous verrez par les Lectres du Roy en quel estat ils sont de leur divorce; tout ce qu'ils vous demandent d'ayde envers le Pape, c'est qu'il ne revoque sa commission. Quant à vos affaires, ils sont icy assez bien, ils ont quasi passé la moitié de leur deul, et tiennent la paix pour faicte; voyant qu'ils en estoyent si avant, j'ay faict avec le Cardinal d'Yorc ung Sermon qui a servy à la matiere; je faits mon compte que, puysqu'ils ont ung bon [?Juillet] preparatif, on leur fera d'autant plus aisement avaller ung de ces jours la medecine. Qui a fort fasché Monsieur le Legat a esté un advis qu'il avoyt eu, comme je croy de Rome, que piecza les choses sont accoustrées et accordées par le moyen de Monsieur de Savoye, ce que je luy ay bien monstré n'estre vray. Le Roy a esté fort ayse de ses artichots, pour venir du lieu qu'ils viennent, et en faict grant feste parmy ses amys; ce a esté une petite demonstration faicte à propos. Mondit sieur le Legat m'a demandé si Monsieur le Chancelier se trouveroyt à ceste veuë; j'ay respondu que pensoye que non, si n'estoyt qu'on veist trop grande apparence à la conclusion des choses. Il a dict veoir evidemment que Madame Marguerite, pour vouloir ladite veuë estre dés le xviij, ne manque à s'avancer pour deux causes: l'une, pour dresser le passage de l'Empereur; l'autre, pour garder que luy ne se y trouve, pensant bien que sa presence n'amanderoyt les affaires dudict Empereur, pour le cognoistre assez clairvoyant; parquoy conseille que Madame ne faille de mener mondict sieur le Chancelier, car si quelque chose se faict, il pourra myeulx qu'ung aultre prendre garde que ne perdiez à la marchandise; qui sera la fin de la presente, aprés que me seray recommandé humblement en vostre bonne grace, et qu'auray requis nostre Seigneur vous donner, Monseigneur, bonne vie et longue. De Londres le xxij Juing. Ainsi signé, vostre humble serviteur J. du Bellay, Evesque de Bayonne. Il n'y peult avoir dangier de faire tenir à Salviati le pacquet de Campege; je vous supplye, Monseigneur, le vouloir commender. Sur le dos de la Lectre est escript: A Monseigneur, Monseigneur le Grant Maistre et Mareschal de France. Monseigneur, what has given them the hottest alarm is that the Duke of Suffolk has written to the King his master — I have seen his very letter — that the King had told him that, when the Ladies came to this parley, everything would be done and concluded in two days; on that they judge that matters are already agreed, that nothing is needed but a little ceremony, saying that in this you have dealt too falsely with them, always showing them, saying and writing that you saw no foundation in the matter. I assure you, Monseigneur, that without pretence the Lord Legate is in terrible distress, for until this very hour he had always assured his master and everyone, in private and in public, that it would come to nothing, and that you would do nothing whatever without them. He now strongly suspects the contrary; and I leave you to imagine whether he speaks to me, and whether he says that I deceived him and was the cause of his deceiving his master, and consequently that I put him on a very bad road. I help myself at this and defend myself tooth and nail; yet in the end he will come to seek me out again, and already, as you see, he has wanted me to go and see the King, and to serve him the best talk in the world, without among other things putting him entirely out of hope that Monsieur Feuguillaume's coming was not to put some delay into this Assembly; which I well feel I must do, partly to a good end and to keep these things on a good course, partly so that he may extricate himself, so that, my having my share of the burden towards his said master, his own may be so much the less. It will be very necessary, Monseigneur, that whoever comes to bring the news of peace be well primed with fair words. Also, Monseigneur, I have heard from a good source that Madame Marguerite is pressing you hard to come to a good conclusion (you know whether it is true), alleging the trouble she had in getting her commission from the Emperor, although all the ambassadors of his relatives and allies, the greatest lords of Spain, fell on their knees to him for it, [saying] that he saw Monseigneur d'Orléans despairing of his life, his affairs in the worst state in the world in Italy, everyone discontented in Spain and minded to mutiny, Germany so troubled, and the Turk's preparations as great as could be; and that now, some of those causes having ceased and the others being able to cease in time, she feared greatly that he would revoke the said commission, and that she already had some good diversion from it. I have heard nothing of it; but it seems to me a good thing to say, and even to the Duke of Suffolk. It is true, Monseigneur, that having the children is the main thing; but whoever can satisfy everything does well. I believe Feuguillaume brought Monsieur de Suffolk orders to return; I understand they have letters from the King of the 16th, in which he put quite crudely that he was leaving Paris to go towards Cambrai, as if he were to be there himself, with which I assure you the Cardinal of York would not be pleased. Monseigneur, the Legate would much like that, when the King writes to me of his good affection and will to help the King his brother in his affair, he should expressly mention that he [?comes] to employ himself in it all the more because he is and has continually been asked and pressed to do so by my said Lord Legate; and it seems to me, Monseigneur, that it would be well to do so. You may perhaps take it ill that I send you express couriers so often; but, Monseigneur, I would have to not write at all, for in the first place the packets would not be carried, and besides, they would stay lying on the table, as I am sure they would; at every post there are men of the Duke of Suffolk who would not miss me in so fair a field. The Cardinal of York has warned me of it closely enough, and I find that a packet has been lost since I have been here, about which I am troubled. You will see from the King's letters in what state they are in their divorce; all the help they ask of you with the Pope is that he should not revoke his commission. As for your affairs, they are going well enough here; they have almost got over half their grief, and hold the peace as made. Seeing they had gone so far, I preached with the Cardinal of York a sermon that served the matter; I reckon that, since they have had a good [?July] preparation, it will be all the easier to make them swallow the medicine one of these days. What greatly vexed the Lord Legate was a report he had had, from Rome as I believe, that things were long since arranged and agreed through the Duke of Savoy, which I have shown him well is not true. The King was very pleased with his artichokes, coming from where they come from, and makes much of them among his friends; it was a small gesture well timed. My said Lord Legate asked me whether the Chancellor would be at this meeting; I answered that I thought not, unless there were too great a likelihood of matters being concluded. He said he saw clearly that Madame Marguerite, in wanting the said meeting to be from the 18th, is pressing on for two reasons: one, to prepare the Emperor's passage; the other, to keep him [the Chancellor] from being there, thinking well that his presence would not improve the said Emperor's affairs, knowing him to be quite clear-sighted. Therefore he advises that Madame should not fail to bring my said Lord Chancellor, for if anything is done, he will be able better than another to see that you do not lose in the bargain. Which will be the end of this letter, after I have commended myself humbly to your good grace and asked our Lord to give you, Monseigneur, a good and long life. From London, the 22nd of June. Thus signed, your humble servant J. du Bellay, Bishop of Bayonne. There can be no danger in having Campeggio's packet delivered to Salviati; I beg you, Monseigneur, to be pleased to order it. Monseigneur, depuis les Lettres que je pensoye sur l'heure envoyer, cette depesche a esté retardée jusques à present, parce qu'il a fallu faire et refaire les Lettres que je vous envoye tout plain de fois, et pour ce aller et venir souvent, tant les Ducs mesmes qu'aultres de ce Conseil, à Vvindesore, dont toute à cette heure ils les m'ont envoyées en la forme que verrez par le double d'iceulx. Ils me prient le plus fort du monde de faire qu'on ne trouve mauvais si en ces expeditions, et mesmement en ce que touche le principal de la depesche, je ne suis du tout satisfait comme je vouldroye, et aussi eulx-mesmes, s'excusans que leur maniere de negocier envers leur Maistre n'est encores bien dressée; mais pour l'advenir doibvent faire merveilles, et en baillent de si grands asseurances et si bien jurées, que je ne me puis guarder de les croire. Je n'ay point refreschy mes Lettres au Roy, car je ne voy point qu'il y en ayt matiere. Au demourent, j'ay esté voir le Cardinal en ses ennuis, où que j'y ay trouvé le plus grand exemple de fortune que on ne sçauroit voir. Il m'a remonstré son cas en la plus mauvaise rethorique que je viz jamais, car cueur et parolle luy failloient entierement; il a bien plouré et prié que le Roy et Madame voulsissent avoir pitié de luy, s'ils avoyent trouvé qu'il leur eust guardé promesse de leur estre bon serviteur autant que son honneur et povoir se y est peu estendre; mais il me a à la fin laissé sans me povoir dire autre chose qui vallist mieux que son visaige, qui est bien descheu de la moitié de juste pris. Et vous promets, Monseigneur, que sa fortune est telle que ses ennemis, encores qu'ils soyent Angloys, ne se sçauroyent guarder d'en avoir pitié; ce nonobstant ne laisseront de le poursuivre jusques au bout, et ne voyt de moyen de son salut, aussi ne fais-je, sinon qu'il plaise au Roy et à Madame de l'ayder. De legation, de seau, d'auctorité, de credit il n'en demande point; il est prest de laisser tout jusques à la chemise, et que on le laisse vivre en ung hermitaige, ne le tenant ce Roy en sa malle grace. Je l'ay reconforté au mieulx que j'ay peu, mais je n'y ay sceu faire grant chose. Depuys, par un en qui il se fie, il m'a mandé ce qu'il vouldroit qu'on feist pour luy de la plus grant partie, luy voïant qu'il ne touchoit au bien des affaires du Roy qu'on luy accordast la plus raisonnable chose qu'il demande: c'est que le Roy escripvist à ce Roy qu'il est ung grand bruict de par delà qu'il l'ait recullé d'autour de luy, et fort eslongné de la bonne grace, en sorte qu'on dict qu'il doibve estre destruict, ce que ne pense totalement estre comme on le dict; toutesfois, pour la bonne fraternité qu'ils ont ensemble, et si grant communication de tous leurs plus grans affaires, l'a bien voulu prier de y avoir esgard, affin qu'il n'en entre souldainement quelque mauvaise fantasie envers ceulx qui ont veu qu'en si grant solemnité et auctorité il ait servy d'instrument en cette perpetuelle amitié tant renommée par toute la Chrestienté; et que si d'adventure il estoit entré en quelque mal contentement de luy, il veüille ung peu moderer son affection, comme il est bien seur que luy vouldront conseiller ceulx qui sont autour de sa personne et au maniement de ses plus grandes affaires. Voila, Monseigneur, la plus raisonnable de toutes ses demandes, en laquelle ne me veulx ingerer de dire mon advis; si diray-je bien qu'il n'y a personne icy qui deust prendre à mal telle Lettre, et mesmement là où ils considereront, comme de faict ils font, qu'il sont forcés de prendre et tenir plus que jamais vostre party. Et davantage asseureray bien que la plus grant prinse qu'ils ayent peu avoir sur luy du commencement, et qui plus leur a servi à le broüller envers ce Roy, a esté qu'il declara à ma venuë deça trop ouvertement de vouloir aller à Cambray, car les aultres persuaderent au Maistre ce que c'estoit seulement pour éviter d'estre à l'expedition du mariage; et outre cela vous promets que sans luy les aultres mectoyent ce Roy en ung terrible train de rompre la practique de paix, dont vous escripvis quelque mot en ce temps-là; mais j'en laissay dix fois plus en la plume, voyant que tout estoit rabillé; je vous les diray estant là, et je suis seur que le trouverez fort estrange. Il me semble, Monsieur, que à tout cela, et plusieurs aultres choses que bien entendez de vous-mesmes, on doibt avoir quelque esguard. Vous donnerez, s'il vous plaist, advis au Roy et à Madame de tout cecy, affin qu'ils advisent ce qu'il leur plaira en faire; s'ils pensent n'empirer par cela leurs affaires, je croy que voulentiers, outre ce que sera quelque charité, ils voudront qu'on cognoisse qu'ils ayent retiré ung leur affectionné serviteur, et tenu pour tel par chascun, des portes d'enfer. Mais sur tout, Monseigneur, il desire que ce Roy ne cognoisse qu'ils en ayent esté requis, et que il les en ayt fait requerir en façons du monde; cela l'acheveroit d'affoller. Car pour vous dire le vray, et horsmis toute affection, je vous asseure que la plus grant prinse que ses ennemis ayent euë sur luy, outre celle du mariage, ce a esté de persuader ce Roy que il avoit tousiours eu, en temps de paix et de guerre, intelligence secrette à Madame, de laquelle, ladicte guerre durant, il avoit eu de grans presens, qui furent cause que, Suffolc estant à Montdidier, il ne le secourut d'argent comme il debvoit, dont advint que il ne print Paris; mais ils parlent en l'oreille de ce propos, afin que je n'en sois adverty. Quant ausdits presens, il espere que Madame ne luy nuira où il en sera parlé; de toutes aultres choses il s'en recommande en sa bonne grace. La fantaisie de ces Seigneurs est que, luy mort ou ruiné, ils defferent incontinent icy l'estat de l'Eglise, et prendront tous leurs biens, qu'il seroit ja besoing que je misse en chiffre, car ils le crient en plaine table. Je croy qu'ils feront de beaux miracles. Si m'a dict vostre grant Prophete au visaige bronzé que ce Roy ne vivra gueres plus que […], auquel, comme vous sçavez, à ce que je voy par ses escriptures, il n'a baillé terme que de la monstre de May. Je ne veulx oublier à vous dire que si le Roy et Madame veullent faire quelque chose pour le Legat, il fauldroit se haster; encores ne seront jamais icy les Lettres que il n'ait perdu le Seau; toutesfois il ne pense plus à cela; elles serviront pour le demourant. Aussi, venant icy mon Successeur, comme chacun s'attend qu'il viendra dans peu de jours, il luy donnassent charge d'en parler. Le pis de son mal est que Mademoiselle de Boulen a faict promettre à son Amy que il ne l'escoutera jamais parler; car elle pense bien qu'il ne le pourroit garder d'en avoir pitié. Monseigneur, tout ce qui sera de bon en tout ce discours, vous le sçaurez prendre comme tel; s'il y aura riens qui semble party de trop d'affection, je vous supplie m'ayder à en excuser, et qu'il soit pris de bonne part; car là où la matiere seroit mauvaise, si vous asseureray-je bien que l'intention n'est telle; et là-dessus est bien temps pour vous et pour moy que je face fin à la presente, me recommande humblement en vostre bonne grace, et pryant nostre Seigneur qu'il vous doint bonne vie et longue. De Londres le xvij d'Octobre. Signé, Vostre humble serviteur J. du Bellay, Ev. de Bayonne. Et sur le dos de la Lettre est escript: A Monseigneur, Monseigneur le grant Maistre et Mareschal de France.
