Monseigneur, since the letters I thought to send at once, this despatch has been delayed until now, because the letters I am sending you had to be made and remade a great many times, and for that reason there was much going and coming to Windsor, both of the Dukes themselves and of others of this Council; and only now have they sent them to me in the form you will see from the copy of them. They beg me as hard as they can to see that no one takes it ill if in these despatches, and especially in what touches the main point of the despatch, I am not altogether satisfied as I would wish, nor they themselves, excusing themselves that their way of negotiating with their master is not yet well settled; but for the future they are to do wonders, and they give such great assurances of it, and so well sworn, that I cannot keep from believing them. I have not renewed my letters to the King, for I do not see that there is matter for it. For the rest, I went to see the Cardinal in his troubles, where I found the greatest example of fortune one could ever see. He set out his case to me in the worst rhetoric I ever saw, for heart and speech failed him entirely; he wept much and begged that the King and Madame would be pleased to have pity on him, if they had found that he had kept his promise to be a good servant to them as far as his honour and power could extend; but in the end he left me without being able to say anything better than his face, which has indeed fallen by half its just value. And I promise you, Monseigneur, that his fortune is such that his enemies, although they are English, could not keep from pitying him; nevertheless they will not fail to pursue him to the end, and he sees no means of his safety, nor do I, unless it please the King and Madame to help him. Of legation, of the seal, of authority, of credit he asks nothing; he is ready to give up everything down to his shirt, and to be left to live in a hermitage, provided this King does not hold him in his displeasure. I comforted him as best I could, but I could not do much. Since then, through someone he trusts, he has sent me word of what he would like to be done for him for the greater part, and, seeing that it did not touch the good of the King's affairs, that the most reasonable thing he asks should be granted him: namely, that the King should write to this King that there is a great rumour over there that he has put him away from about him and far from his good grace, so that it is said he is to be destroyed, which he does not think is altogether as it is said; nevertheless, for the good brotherhood they have together, and the great communication of all their greatest affairs, he has wished to beg him to have regard to it, so that no bad fancy should suddenly arise towards those who have seen that, with such great solemnity and authority, he served as instrument in this perpetual friendship so renowned throughout Christendom; and that if by chance he had become discontented with him, he would be pleased to moderate his feeling a little, as he is quite sure those who are about his person and in the handling of his greatest affairs will advise him. That, Monseigneur, is the most reasonable of all his requests, in which I do not wish to intrude by giving my opinion; but I will say that there is no one here who ought to take such a letter ill, and especially when they consider, as indeed they do, that they are forced to take and hold your side more than ever. And moreover I will assure you that the greatest hold they could have on him at the beginning, and what most served them to set him at odds with this King, was that on my coming here he declared too openly that he wished to go to Cambrai; for the others persuaded the master that this was only to avoid being present at the dispatch of the marriage. And besides that, I promise you that without him the others were putting this King on a terrible course of breaking off the peace negotiations, of which I wrote you a word at that time; but I left ten times more of it in my pen, seeing that everything had been patched up; I shall tell you of it when I am there, and I am sure you will find it very strange. It seems to me, Monsieur, that all this, and several other things that you well understand yourself, deserve some regard. You will, if you please, inform the King and Madame of all this, so that they may consider what they will be pleased to do about it; if they think they will not worsen their affairs by it, I believe they will gladly — besides its being a work of charity — wish it to be known that they have drawn back from the gates of hell one of their devoted servants, held as such by everyone. But above all, Monseigneur, he wishes that this King should not know that they have been asked to do it, and that he had them asked in any way in the world; that would finish driving him mad. For to tell you the truth, and setting aside all affection, I assure you that the greatest hold his enemies have had on him, besides that of the marriage, has been to persuade this King that he always had, in time of peace and war, a secret understanding with Madame, from whom, during the said war, he had received great presents, which were the reason that, when Suffolk was at Montdidier, he did not help him with money as he should have, whence it came about that he did not take Paris; but they speak of this in whispers, so that I may not be informed of it. As to the said presents, he hopes that Madame will not harm him where it is spoken of; for all other things he commends himself to her good grace. The fancy of these lords is that, once he is dead or ruined, they will at once overthrow the state of the Church here and take all their goods, which I would hardly need to put in cipher, for they shout it at a full table. I believe they will work fine miracles. Yet your great Prophet with the bronzed face told me that this King will not live much longer than […], to whom, as you know, so far as I see from his writings, he gave no term beyond the muster of May. I do not want to forget to tell you that if the King and Madame wish to do something for the Legate, they would have to hurry; even so the letters will never be here before he has lost the Seal; however he no longer thinks of that; they will serve for the rest. Also, when my successor comes here, as everyone expects him to within a few days, they should give him charge to speak of it. The worst of his trouble is that Mademoiselle Boleyn has made her lover promise that he will never hear him speak; for she well thinks that he could not keep from pitying him. Monseigneur, whatever is good in all this discourse you will know how to take as such; if there is anything that seems to come from too much affection, I beg you to help me excuse it and that it be taken in good part; for even where the matter might be bad, I can still assure you that the intention is not; and thereupon it is high time, for you and for me, that I make an end of this letter, commending myself humbly to your good grace and praying our Lord to give you a good and long life. From London, the 17th of October. Signed, your humble servant J. du Bellay, Bishop of Bayonne. And on the back of the letter is written: To Monseigneur, Monseigneur the Grand Maître and Marshal of France. 30 June 1529, fr. 3040 f. 68 (R4229; Le Grand III pp. 333 ff.) Je laisseray ces propos; ils ne serviroient de riens pour ceste heure. Bien vous puis dire que, quand il ne fera rien de ce que vouldrez, il ne tiendra au Cardinal, qui est plus saige que luy, ny serviteur qu'il ayt. Advisez un peu comme il vous maine ses gens: c'estoit de la menée de […] et […] que le Duc de Suffolch estoit allé vers vous, pensant ung [*] à Amiens quant j'arrivay icy […]. Le Cardinal voulut rompre leur voyage, et aller incontinent à Cambray; il veist que ce Roy le trouvoit mauvais, il plia, mais il rendit leur commission digne de Maistre Bryan, puis par bon moyen les a revoqués pour n'estre à ceste Assemblée; et ne pensez pas qu'il soit le plus marry du monde si tout sera conclu avant l'arrivée de ceux qui y vont, quelque mine qu'il fasse, pourveu qu'il ne se fasse riens au prejudice de ce Roy pour retourner au mariage. Je vous avois écrit qu'il y auroit grant longueur, mais je voy que depuis la venuë de Stephen et Briant, aportant, comme je pense certainement, de la fausseté du brief, le Campege est demy vaincu d'abreger, pour plusieurs raisons longues à deduire, si n'est que le Pape se hastast de revoquer la commission; et ne pense pas que ce ne soit fait dans ung mois, si autre chose ne survient, et plustost par advanture; et si riens en empesche le Cardinal Campeige, sera à mon avis la crainte qu'il aura, sans occasion toutesfois, que le Roy et l'Empereur s'accordent et fassent amis, laissant celui-cy un peu derriere, et par consequent luy aussi. Je fais en cela bon office, toutesfois sans m'y mectre trop avant: j'ay prié de la part du Roy d'y entendre et accelerer avec force bonnes paroles, disant avoir Lectre, et cela leur a déja servi. A ce propos, Monsieur le Cardinal suplie le Roy tres humblement et tres affectionnement qu'il écrive un mot de sa main audict Campege, le priant de l'expedition de cette affaire, et l'asseurant bien que là où il feroit quelque chose en son bien, il le tiendra comme fait à luy-même, et luy en souviendra en tems et lieu, avec autres telles paroles ou semblables. Pour vous dire verité, Monseigneur, je ne voy pour cette heure chose quelle quelle soit plus pour servir à leur matiere, laquelle venant à fin ne vous peut estre que merveilleusement à propos; car outre l'amitié que le Roy porte au Roy son bon frere, sera un moyen pour l'advenir de vous faire tomber ce Roy à genoux. Par adventure ne seroit-il besoing que le Roy écrivist si apertement: Lectre demoure, et si n'y faudroit date, mais remettre le demourant sur ce que luy en auray dit dernierement, suivant ce qu'en avois dechargé par mes Lectres. Vos Ambassadeurs partiront Vendredy, et iront à grandes journées: j'espere que ce sera le retour de matines. Je n'ay voulu vous envoyer Courrier exprés, afin que, vous arrivant le pacquet, les dix jours soient expirez. Envoyant au Docteur Benet les Lettres de Monsieur le Legat, faites faire excuse de la longueur, que mon Courrier s'est rompu ung pied en chemin et a baillé le paquet à ung autre; il les croiront, car j'ay pourveu à cela; autrement ils verroient que j'aurois tout exprés mis cette longueur. Monseigneur, je me recommanderay à tant humblement en vôtre bonne grace, et prieray notre Seigneur vous donner bonne vie et longue. De Londres le dernier de Juing. A la Haye je n'écris à Madame, esperant que les Lettres du Roy et vostres luy serviront; je ne luy remetrois que redites. Nevertheless I forgive him, in my opinion, for he is somewhat timorous, and not only fears but is dying of fear that, if the Emperor comes into Italy, the Pope will revoke his commission; whoever said I had done the work, when I am with him, would be very much inclined to lie. I shall leave this talk; it would serve for nothing at present. I can indeed tell you that when he does nothing of what you would wish, it will not be the fault of the Cardinal, who is wiser than he, nor of any servant he has. Consider a little how he leads his people for you: it was by the contrivance of […] and […] that the Duke of Suffolk had gone to you, thinking a [*] at Amiens when I arrived here […]. The Cardinal wanted to break off their journey and go at once to Cambrai; he saw that this King took it ill, he gave way, but he made their commission worthy of Master Bryan, then by good means had them recalled so as not to be at this Assembly; and do not think that he would be the sorriest man in the world if everything were concluded before the arrival of those who are going there, whatever face he may put on it, provided nothing is done to the prejudice of this King in returning to the marriage. I had written to you that there would be great delay, but I see that since the coming of Stephen and Bryan, bringing, as I certainly think, [evidence] of the falsity of the brief, Campeggio is half won over to cut it short, for several reasons too long to explain, unless the Pope should hurry to revoke the commission; and I do not think it will not be done within a month, unless something else intervenes, and perhaps sooner; and if anything hinders Cardinal Campeggio in it, it will in my opinion be the fear he will have — without cause, however — that the King and the Emperor may come to terms and become friends, leaving this one a little behind, and consequently him too. I do good service in this, but without going too far into it: I have begged on the King's behalf that they attend to it and hasten it, with many good words, saying I had a letter, and this has already served them. On this subject, the Lord Cardinal most humbly and most affectionately begs the King to write a word in his own hand to the said Campeggio, asking him to expedite this affair, and assuring him that wherever he does something for its good he will hold it as done to himself and will remember it in time and place, with other such or similar words. To tell you the truth, Monseigneur, I see for the present nothing whatever that would serve their matter better; and its coming to an end can only be marvellously convenient for you, for besides the friendship the King bears the King his good brother, it will be a means in future of bringing this King to his knees before you. Perhaps the King need not write so openly: the letter remains, and there would be no need for a date, but to refer the rest to what I shall lately have told him about it, in accordance with what I had discharged by my letters. Your ambassadors will leave on Friday and travel by long stages: I hope it will be the return from matins. I did not want to send you an express courier, so that, when the packet reaches you, the ten days will have expired. When you send Doctor Benet the Lord Legate's letters, have an excuse made for the delay, that my courier broke a foot on the way and gave the packet to another; they will believe it, for I have provided for that; otherwise they would see that I had put in this delay on purpose. Monseigneur, I shall commend myself most humbly to your good grace, and pray our Lord to give you a good and long life. From London, the last of June. At The Hague I am not writing to Madame, hoping that the King's letters and yours will serve her; I would only be repeating myself to her. 22 Oct 1529, fr. 3005 f. 165 (Scheurer t. Gallica leaves (BnF fr. 3005, ark btv1b90599952, canvases 259-261 = ff. 165r, 165v, 166r; full resolution through openapi.bnf.fr IIIF, 23 Oct 2026) with the 1529 Bayonne key (`key_p21.tsv`, Tomokiyo's table) and the values listed in `22oct1529_corrections.tsv`. Value transcription by line: `22oct1529_transcription.txt`. Clear words of the leaf are in the text as written. The opening phrase "au cardinal d'York" is carried by one word sign and by Scheurer, *Correspondance du cardinal Jean du Bellay* t. I (1969) pp. 111-112 (Google Books snippets: "la ou je vouldroye ... au cardinal d'York sa requeste qu'il me faict faire par ung sien serviteur italien qui luy est demouré seul feal ...", "bien asseurez d'avoir maint tour de corde"); the rest of Scheurer's text was not seen, so the reading below is the project's own. The clear part of the letter (from "Escripvant ceste lectre", f. 166r) is in Le Grand III pp. 377-379 (`ref/legrand3_p330_400.txt`) and is not repeated. Marks: `[?word]` partly carried (a doubtful sign, or a value from sense only), `[word]` supplied, `[…]` unread, `[ꝏ]` a word sign not identified; `[?Roy]` stands for two word signs read from sense only (ꝑ, five places, Henry VIII; ℋ, two places, Francis I: "il supplye ℋ et madame"). Spelling as enciphered (no modernisation); apostrophes and punctuation are editorial. ## Reading Monseigneur, la ou je vouldroye, si ne me sçauroye je guarder d'accorder au cardinal d'York sa requeste qu'il me faict f[aire] par ung sien serviteur italien qui luy est demouré seul feal de si grant nombre, mais preallablement vous demanderay a entendre [?comme] son afaire. Mardi luy fut osté le seau, faict inventaire de tous ses biens jusques a ung escu, comandement faict a tous ceulx qui ont [?eu] manié quelque chose de luy depuys vingt ans de rendre compte de tout, dont ilz sont bien empeschez, car ne se trouant la sixiesme partie de [?ce] qu'on esperoit, ilz sont bien aseurez d'avoir maint tour de corde. Puys [?luy] fut baillé choix de respondre devant [?Roy] ou le parlement. Il print [?Roy], pensant ce qui est vray, que [?les] seigneurs auroyent mys [?juges] au parlement a leur poste. Toutesfoiz qu'il n'espere de la misericorde du [?Roy] [?complaine] […] si chauldement qu'il est non plus que riens, en sorte qu'il n'actend mains, apres perte de tous biens et honeurs, sinon […] pour tout le myeulx rigoreuse et [?perpetuele] prison, confermee par parlement, et […] par ce irrevocable, ne par roy ne par autre. Les poinctz ou l'on le cherche sont la les pilleries qu'il a faictes, mais tout cela ne le feroit mourir. Ilz [?pressent] pour [ꝏ] lese maieste, qu'il […] de la legation plus de dix ans contre les loix du pays; qu'estant a Amyens il accorda de mectre le duc de Ferrare en la ligue sans le sceu de [?Roy], et qu'il bailla au [?Roy] une cedule obligatoire de sa main sans le comandement, nullement, du dict sieur; et quant […] depuys, il feist intimer la guerre a [?l'Empereur] contre son intention, [et] le maindre de ces poinctz. Somme, ilz pretendent luy faict perdre la teste, et croy bien que si le roy et madame ne l'aydent, elle est en grant dangier de y demourer. Je pourroys bien y avoir d'autres poinctz que je n'entendz pas, mais voy la ce que j'en entendz. La dessus il demande qu'ilz envoyent ung gentilhomme en toute diligence remons[t]rer a [?Roy], qui vous suppliera le plus […] de ce moyens, sans plus avant particulariser, ne […] osera cognoistre [?en] façon du monde qu'il fust, saichant […] ne consentent de ces […] payne de le faire incontinent mourir. Il supplye [?le Roy] et madame pour l'honeur de la passion de Dieu, [?asseurance] par ce moyen, que la fureur des [?ennemys] qui luy ont […] si tranportes ont mais […] a pouvre vieillesse, a la plus honteuse et si [?miserable] fin qui jamais advint a homme, laquelle il voit si prochaine et devant ses yeulx, s'ilz n'ont pitié de luy. Quant a moy, encores que je me desplaise de m'ingerer si avant […] des deux, son advis, ce que […] vous [?en] vouldroye je peu. Car le regrossant les biens que la on [a] afection […], pitié [?regnent], bon jugement […] tourne en son entier. ## Notes - Word signs: ‡ (cross in a box) = "cardinal d'York" (Scheurer's text); R = faict (as on 16 June); V = bien (22 June interlinear); 4 = madame ("si le roy et madame ne l'aydent", as Le Grand prints in the 17 Oct letter "qu'il plaise au Roy & à Madame de l'ayder"); a second 4 ("et [4] par ce irrevocable") does not fit and is left unread. - ℋ: two places ("bailla au ℋ une cedule obligatoire", "il supplye ℋ et madame"): the King of France by sense (paired with madame, Louise of Savoy); flagged, not adopted. - ꝑ: five places (respondre devant, il print, misericorde du, sans le sceu de, remonstrer a); "le Roy" (Henry VIII) fits all five by sense; not adopted as a key value (sense only, flagged for review). - The letters read on look-alike alternates are listed in `22oct1529_reread_log.md` (10 letters). Not a full reading: the second half has unread stretches (see the reading's header and the log). ## Translation My lord, wherever I might wish otherwise, I could not keep from granting the cardinal of York his request, which he has had made to me by an Italian servant of his, the only one left faithful to him out of so great a number; but first I will ask you to understand [?how] his affair [stands]. On Tuesday the seal was taken from him; an inventory was made of all his goods down to a crown; an order was given to all who [?have] handled anything of his these twenty years to render account of everything, which troubles them greatly, for since not a sixth part of [?what] was hoped for is found, they are sure to get many a turn of the rope. Then he was given the choice of answering before [?the King] or the Parliament. He chose [?the King], thinking, as is true, that the lords would have put [?judges] into the Parliament at their pleasure. However, since he hopes nothing from the mercy of [?the King], [?complains] […] so hotly that he is no more than nothing, so that he expects nothing less, after the loss of all goods and honours, than […] at the very best a harsh and [?perpetual] prison, confirmed by Parliament, and […] thereby irrevocable, neither by the King nor by anyone else. The points on which he is pursued are the plunderings he has made, but all that would not bring him to his death. They [?press] for [ꝏ] lese-majesty, that he […] of the legation more than ten years against the laws of the land; that at Amiens he agreed to bring the Duke of Ferrara into the league without the knowledge of [?the King], and that he gave [?the King] a bond in his own hand without the command, in no way, of the said lord; and as for […] since, he had war declared on [?the Emperor] against his [the King's] intention, [and this is] the least of these points. In sum, they mean to make him lose his head, and I well believe that unless the King and Madame help him it is in great danger of staying there. There may well be other points I do not understand, but that is what I understand of it. Thereupon he asks that they send a gentleman in all haste to remonstrate with [?the King], who will entreat you most […] by these means, without going further into particulars, nor […] will dare acknowledge in any way in the world that it was so, knowing […] do not consent to these […] pain of having him put to death at once. He begs [?the King] and Madame, for the honour of the Passion of God, [?assurance] by this means, that the fury of [?his enemies], who have […] so carried away, have but […] to a poor old age, to the most shameful and [?miserable] end that ever befell a man, which he sees so near and before his eyes, unless they take pity on him. As for me, although it displeases me to meddle so far […] of the two, his advice, what […] I would wish you [?of it], I could. For the [?growing] of the goods to which one has affection […], pity [?reigns], good judgement […] turned in its entirety. Key: key_p21.tsv

Six digit-cipher documents of 1744 in the Esterházy archive at the Slovak National Archives, one from Maria Theresa, with no decipherment. Only part of one page is online, a despatch from Moscow of 5 October 1744 in a code of about 2,000 values. The Vienna chancery keys of 1740–1746 on DECODE, the 1745 circular ciphers among them, do not reach its numbers, and the box is not digitised; not solved. 1320. 365. 1700. 1041. 532. 1240. 680. 941. 1512. 624. 636. 913 … key not found: a code of about 2,000 values, 7–1737 and 3018–3297 Moscow → “Votre Majesté” · numerical code · 1744 Esterházy papers, box 636: the cipher letters of 1744 Six cipher documents of 1744 in the Esterházy archive have no decipherment; the one page online was transcribed and tested against every Vienna key of those years on DECODE, and none fits. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 9 October 2026 Method: not solved · Extent: text not obtained not solved At a glance Not solved · text not obtained The documents Six documents of 1744, five in French and one in German, one of them from Maria Theresa to Count Nicolaus Esterházy. The only one visible online is a despatch headed “Moscau ce 5e d’octobre 1744” and addressed to a sovereign (“Votre Majesté”). Where Slovenský národný archív, Bratislava, fond Esterházi – čeklíska vetva, box 636. Not on DECODE or HCPortal. One partial page is printed as Figure 6 of Antal et al., HistoCrypt 2023. The cipher Numbers separated by dots, from 7 to 1737 plus a block from 3018 to 3297: a code or large nomenclator of about 2,000 values. 157 of the 176 numbers occur only once. How it was tried The Vienna chancery keys of 1740–1746 on DECODE were opened, including the 1745 French and German circular ciphers sent to Rosenberg and Esterházy. None reaches the values 1500–1737 or 3000–3297. Why it resists 176 numbers of a 2,000-value code are too few to attack without the key, and the other five documents are not online. Still open Everything. The next steps are scans of box 636 from the Slovak National Archives and the 1744 keys for Russia and Saxony in the Vienna archives.

The Esterházy family archive at the Slovak National Archives (fond Esterházi, čeklíska vetva) was surveyed for ciphers by Eugen Antal, Pavol Marák, Pavol Zajac, Tünde Lengyelová and Diana Duchoňová. Their paper at HistoCrypt 2023 describes box 636 in a paragraph. It holds six encrypted documents, one fully enciphered draft and five letters, five in French and one in German, all of 1744. One letter is from Maria Theresa to Count Nicolaus Esterházy (1711–1764); the other correspondents were not identified. No plain text exists for any of them. The keys kept in the same fonds do not fit, and neither do the Vienna and Hungarian keys the authors tried. The archive has scanned the box at 4160 × 6240 pixels. The scans were meant to go onto HCPortal but are not there yet: up to record 1881, checked on 9 October 2026, HCPortal holds nothing from this fonds. DECODE has no records from the Slovak National Archives. The only image anyone can see is the paper’s Figure 6. The Moscow despatch of 5 October 1744: clear heading and opening, eleven lines of figures, then clear text again. Image: Slovenský národný archív, fond Esterházi – čeklíska vetva, box 636, as reproduced in Antal et al., HistoCrypt 2023, Figure 6 (CC BY 4.0). The page opens in clear: “Moscau ce 5e d’octobre 1744. J’ai reçu avec un tres profond respect les Re- & Postscripts de Votre Majesté en date du 15e Septembre.” Eleven lines of figures follow. The clear text then resumes: “La refutation de l’Imprimé de la Cour de Vienne est trop solide, pour ne pas …”. The Russian court spent 1744 in Moscow, so this is an envoy’s despatch from that court to his sovereign. The Viennese “Imprimé” is presumably the court’s printed answer in the Botta affair of 1743. The writer is not named on the visible part. Count Philipp Joseph Orsini-Rosenberg, Austrian ambassador to Russia from mid-1744, writing to Maria Theresa, would fit, but another envoy writing to his king is not ruled out. It is also unexplained why the letter is among Esterházy’s papers: he was then Maria Theresa’s envoy in Dresden.

The transcription has 176 groups in eleven lines, 157 of them distinct. Four groups are uncertain in the figure: 1056, 1603, 193 and 806. The values run from 7 to 1737, spread evenly across every hundred, with a separate block of twelve groups from 3018 to 3297. Six groups are below 100 (7, 19, 24, 54, 77, 83). The Vienna chancery’s 1745 instruction for its circular cipher (DECODE R1598) tells clerks to scatter two-digit nulls through the text, so these may be nulls. Only 1337 and 536 occur three times, fifteen others twice, and no pair of groups repeats. A few groups are underlined in the manuscript (438, 1000, 1059; 1737 twice). These marks are recorded in the transcription file. This is a code or large syllabic nomenclator of about 2,000 values, of the kind the Vienna chancery issued to its envoys. It is not a small homophonic alphabet.

Every dated key record of 1735–1750 from the Haus-, Hof- und Staatsarchiv on DECODE was listed, and those of 1740–1746 were opened: R1594 , Teutscher Circular Ziffer von anno 1745 zum aufschlüssen , issued to Rosenberg, Wasner, Esterhasi, Colloredo and seven other envoys: German, values 100–1500. R1597 , Französischer Circularziffer von anno 1745 zum Setzen , same list of envoys: the French encipher table, values 101–1355. R1596 is its decipher table (101 W, 102 wa, 103 Wasner …). R1595 , a French and German circular decipher table of the 1740s: values 101–1499. R1598 , Pro Informatione : the instruction for using the circular cipher, with a worked example. R1593 (1746) and R1601 : multi-table keys; R1562 (1743): German, values under 1000; R1574 (1740): German; R1644 (1740) and R1691 (1741): small keys. None covers both 1500–1737 and 3000–3297. The 1745 circulars are closest in style, and both Rosenberg and Esterházy received them, but the Moscow letter is from 1744 and its numbers run beyond theirs. They were ruled out on value range; no key was applied group by group. No reading of box 636 was found in print or online. The search turned up a sibling: a letter in cipher from Maria Theresa to Esterházy, Vienna, 31 July 1744, sold by the Dorotheum on 17 December 2024. The auction house describes a three-digit word code and says a copy of its key survives in the Austrian State Archives. That letter is not in box 636. A three-digit code, as described, would not produce the four-digit groups of the Moscow page. No ciphertext-only attack was run. 176 groups of a 2,000-value code, almost all seen once, give a solver nothing to fit.

Scans of all six documents in box 636 from the Slovenský národný archív (Drotárska cesta 42, Bratislava). The archive already holds them. Box 635 of the same fonds: drafts of 1741 and 1744 with short enciphered passages written under their clear text. If any use the 1744 key, they are cribs. In the Haus-, Hof- und Staatsarchiv: the 1744 Staatskanzlei keys for Russia and for Saxony, and the key that Dorotheum says belongs with the Maria Theresa–Esterházy letters. None of these is on DECODE.

An intercepted letter of the Geertruidenberg peace talks, kept in the Blenheim Papers and endorsed “Mr Blencowe cannot decypher them”: Torcy to the plenipotentiaries, 3 April 1710, 690 groups of a two-part code of 800 or more values. The code was transcribed and checked against the images, and the clear opening of the letter was transcribed. The keys in the same volume, DECODE R587, Tomokiyo’s 1710 Desmarets table and the fr. 6204 keys do not fit; not solved. The French copy is in AE Hollande 223, not online. 47. 435. 423. 5. 553. 17. 255. 411. 110. 316. 508. 127 … key not found: a two-part code of 800 or more values, 1–823 Versailles → Geertruidenberg · two-part numerical code · 3 April 1710 · attempted, not solved Torcy to the plenipotentiaries at Geertruidenberg, 1710 from Jean-Baptiste Colbert, marquis de Torcy → to Melchior de Polignac An intercepted letter of Louis XIV’s foreign secretary during the 1710 peace talks that Queen Anne’s decipherer could not break; its code was transcribed and tested against the keys in the same volume and of the same years, and none reads it. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 9 October 2026 · updated 15 October 2026 Method: not solved · Extent: text not obtained · On the map Credits · Satoshi Tomokiyo (transcription) not solved At a glance Not solved · text not obtained The letter Torcy, Louis XIV’s foreign secretary, to the French plenipotentiaries at Geertruidenberg (the maréchal d’Huxelles and the abbé de Polignac), Versailles, 3 April 1710. It was intercepted. Where British Library, Add MS 61575 (Blenheim Papers), ff. 38–41; DECODE R8755. The letter is endorsed “Mr Blencowe cannot decypher them”. The cipher A numerical code: 690 groups, 285 distinct, values 1–823, a two-part code of 800 or more values with homophones. How it was tried The DECODE transcriptions were checked against the images and corrected. The keys in the same volume (R8766, R8767, R8768), the French two-part code DECODE R587, Tomokiyo’s 1710 Desmarets table and the War-ministry keys of BnF fr. 6204 were tried. None fits. What was added The clear opening of Torcy’s letter, which DECODE’s transcription leaves out, transcribed; the letter identified in Legrelle, who cites the French copy; DECODE’s blank sender and receiver supplied. Still open The cipher passage. The French file copy of Torcy’s letter is in the Archives des Affaires étrangères, Correspondance politique Hollande 223, which is not online.

In the spring of 1710 Louis XIV sent the maréchal d’Huxelles and the abbé Melchior de Polignac to Geertruidenberg, in Holland, to negotiate peace with the Dutch on behalf of the Allies. The talks failed in July. Some of the French correspondence was intercepted and passed to the English, and two cipher letters from it are now in the Blenheim Papers at the British Library, Add MS 61575. This page is Torcy’s; the other, a copy of Villars to Polignac of 1 June 1710, is in a different code: Villars to Polignac, 1710 (a different cipher, with its own page). Torcy to the plenipotentiaries, 3 April 1710 (ff. 38–41, DECODE R8755, seven images). It opens in clear on f. 38r and the top of f. 38v, then turns to figures: 17 lines on f. 38v, then ff. 40r, 40v and 41r, ending in the clear “Je suis &c”. Folio 39r is blank and 39v carries the endorsement. The clerk dated the endorsement “3 April 1709”; a later hand corrected it to 1710, which is right: the letter itself is dated 1710 and Legrelle cites it under that date. Folio 38v: the last clear sentence of Torcy’s letter, then the first eight lines of the code, from 47. 435. 423. 5. 553. Image: British Library, Add MS 61575 f. 38v, via DECODE R8755. The clear part answers two letters from the plenipotentiaries (of 27 and 29 March), says that the long despatch they will have received by their courier answers the main points, and then turns to a request from the Dutch deputy Vanderdussen for the Protestant ministers held in France. Torcy replies that they are not in the galleys but shut up in castles for preaching to the new converts against the King’s orders; that it is a matter of the King’s ordinances in which foreigners have no say; and that priests are treated far worse in England. The opening: A Versailles le 3 avril 1710. Depuis le depart de vre courier, Messieurs, j’ay receu la lettre que vous m’avez fait l’honneur de m’ecrire le 27 du mois dernier; celles que vous m’avez adressée pour le Roy le 29 me fut rendue hier au soir et je les ay lu toutes deux a Sa Mte avec les copies jointes a la derniere. La longue depeche que vous aurez receue par vostre courier repond aux principaux articles de ces lettres, ainsi j’aiouteray peu de chose par cet ordinaire a ce que vous scavez presentement des intentions du Roy. The whole clear part is in torcy_clear.txt . Then the figures begin, and the secret part of the letter is in them. The endorsement on f. 39v, turned upright: “3. April 1709” (1710 pencilled above), an intercepted letter of the marquis de Torcy to the French at Geertruidenberg, and below it “Mr Blencowe cannot decypher them”. William Blencowe was Queen Anne’s decipherer. Image: British Library, Add MS 61575 f. 39v, via DECODE R8755.

DECODE holds a transcription of the letter (Satoshi Tomokiyo’s, the file his Cryptiana article links to, which is dead there). It was compared with the images line by line and agrees with the manuscript apart from notation: “11^0” is 110, “31^6” is 316 and “311^” is 311 (the caret marks a 1 written like a dotted i), and “7*29” is 729, which the repeat “288 729” settles. Struck groups were left out. 690 groups, 285 distinct, values 1–823. The commonest group, 50, is only 1.7% of the text (twelve times), the index of coincidence is 0.0042, and there are only two repeated trigrams (19 523 42 and 46 576 135) and no longer repeats. That is a two-part code of 800 or more values with homophones, the large Foreign-Office type of the period. Its nearest relative in the same volume, the Torcy–Petkum code of 1709 (R8766), has 774 values in a grid ruled to 850. Tomokiyo had already noted that the Villars letter in the same volume uses a different cipher; its values run only to 560.

Before anything else, a search for an existing reading. Tomokiyo’s page on Blencowe’s work ( blencowe2.htm , last changed November 2024) lists the letter as having no decipherment and gives only their frequent groups. No edition or decipherment turned up online. Then every key that could plausibly be the right one: R8766 , the Torcy–Petkum code of 1709, which reads the Petkum letters in the same volume (R8748–R8752). In it “de” is 43 or 140. Torcy’s letter has 43 once and 140 never, and its second commonest group, 42, is “correspondance” in R8766. Not the same assignment. R8767 , a one-part code of 1–996 with English names (Dartmouth, Devonshire, the Church of England), about 1712–14. Its “de” is 215, which Torcy’s letter does not contain, and a one-part code does not produce Torcy’s spread of homophones. DECODE R587 (The National Archives, SP 106/7), a French two-part code of about 800 groups. Applied to Torcy it gives a value for 483 of the 690 groups and the result is word salad about Livonia, Prussia, Berlin and Keyserlingk: a code for the North, not this one. Tomokiyo’s table 11B , the code of Desmarets’s letter of 4 June 1710 on the same negotiations (see Desmarets 1710 ), about 190 values from his published table. Torcy’s letter comes out as nonsense. BnF fr. 6204 , the War ministry’s keys. The “Sixième Clef a Chiffrer” (ff. 31–32) has “de” as 400, 411 and 423; Torcy’s letter has “423 411” twice, which would read “de de”, so it is not that key. For the other keys in the volume and the 1702 Usson code, the values Tomokiyo gives for “de” occur 0 to 7 times in Torcy’s 690 groups, far too few for the commonest word in French. They were not transcribed further. The sibling records were opened as well: all of Add MS 61575 on DECODE, R8746–R8774. The Petkum letters of 1709 are in R8766’s code; the anonymous letter of 10 February 1710 (R8753, R8754), which Blencowe partly deciphered, uses a small code reaching about 409; the other keys in the volume (R8757–R8770) are English or later than 1711. No page of the record is a decipherment. Printed sources give the context but no crib. Alfred Legrelle, La diplomatie française et la succession d’Espagne , vol. 4, p. 546, quotes the clear sentence about the priests in England and cites “Torcy aux plénipotentiaires, 3 avril 1710” in Hollande, t. 223, the French ministry’s file of the negotiation; he quotes nothing from the cipher. Torcy’s Journal inédit for 30 March to 3 April records the council of 30 March and the courier sent on the 31st, which carried the “longue depeche” of the clear text (the King’s letter of 31 March), and the plenipotentiaries’ letter of 29 March read to the King on the 3rd, but gives no wording to match.

Nothing reads, so there is no seed to extend. Torcy’s 690 groups are spread over 285 values of a code of 800 or more, most of them seen once or twice; with homophones and no long repeats there is nothing for a ciphertext-only rebuild to fit, and the printed context gives themes, not words. The Desmarets letter of the same weeks (471 groups) became readable only with a table reconstructed from its own decipherment.

The cipher part (ff. 38v–41r, 690 groups): not read. Blocker: needs physical access. The French file copy, cited by Legrelle, is in Correspondance politique Hollande 223 at the Archives diplomatiques, La Courneuve, which is not digitised. A clear copy or minute there would serve as a crib and recover much of the code. A lead not followed here: Tomokiyo gives “de” = 56 both for the anonymous letter of 10 February 1710 (R8753/R8754) and for the Desmarets code. If those are one code, Blencowe’s partial decipherment on f. 29 could extend the Desmarets table. It does not bear on these two letters.

A clear holograph despatch from Paris with five short cipher runs in the postscript, with no decipherment on the page and not calendared. They were deciphered with Stafford’s letter key, recovered here from a contemporary decipherment and glosses on sibling letters in the same volume (adjacent plaintext). Junius’ son came from Cambrai with papers of his credit with Balagny. x D h x D II · II n n h 6 · f O+ n oo · d x oo 24 O+ w 7 H 6 Junius sonne · from Cambraye 6 = e · w = a · 24 = b · oo = m · h = n · n = o Paris → Walsingham · homophonic letter cipher with codes · 20 August 1586 Stafford to Walsingham, Paris, 20 August 1586 from Edward Stafford → to Francis Walsingham Go to the transcriptions ↓ British Library, Harley MS 1582 ff. 65–66 (DECODE R8500). A clear despatch of the English ambassador in Paris with five short cipher runs in the postscript. There is no decipherment on the page and none was found in print; the letter is not calendared in CSP Foreign. The runs were deciphered with Stafford’s letter key, recovered here from a contemporary decipherment and glosses on two sibling letters in the same volume; all 61 tokens give sense. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 22 September 2026 · updated 26 October 2026 Method: key recovered based on adjacent plaintext · Extent: partial (100% of the cipher) · On the map Credits · Contemporary key or decipherment (key or decipherment used) adjacent text At a glance Key from adjacent plaintext · partial (100% of the cipher) The letter Sir Edward Stafford, Paris, 20 August 1586, almost certainly to Sir Francis Walsingham; clear English with five short cipher runs in the postscript. Where British Library, Harley MS 1582 f. 65v; DECODE R8500, listed with no decryption and an unknown recipient. The cipher A homophonic alphabet of letter forms and graphic signs, plus single-sign and numeric codes; the runs have no glosses. How it was read The key was rebuilt from two sibling letters: f. 73r, with glossed cipher words, and f. 72r, a clear decipherment of the long passages on f. 71. Sign 6 is e , not a null. What it says Junius’ son came from Cambrai with letters from his father; Stafford fears Balagny means them mischief. Still open Nothing, though four symbol values rest on context.

Ff. 65r–65v are in Stafford’s own hand. The clear text reports on Captain Blaize, the Neapolitan with Cesar, his fortifications and dealings in Spain and Naples, on Locatello, and on a book lately printed at Rome by Dr Sanders. A note in the margin of f. 65v forwards a request from “one that was Mr Dennys man”. The address leaf, f. 66v, carries the endorsement “20 August 1586. From Sr Edw. Stafford”. The postscript below the signature holds five cipher runs, written in the same line as the clear words. The signs are a mixture of letter forms and graphic signs ( x D h II n oo O+ w 24 H λ ), the same inventory as Stafford’s other letters to Walsingham in the volume. f. 65v, the postscript: the cipher runs sit inside the clear English lines and give yesterday came hither [Junius sonne] [from Cambraye] and brought me letters from his father … of his [credit with Balagny] … but I am afraid [Balagny] dare them some mischief ; the last line opens with [mayntayne]. Image: British Library, Harley MS 1582 f. 65v, via DECODE R8500.

Harley MS 1582 holds four Stafford despatches of August–November 1586 in the same cipher (DECODE R8500–R8504). Two of them carry the plaintext: f. 73r (R8502). A second hand glossed the cipher words: x D h x D II Junius , d w o o 24 Oo w H 6 Cambray , 24 w a w B h H 6 Balagny , B 6 O+ Oo o w h x 6 Germany , and a sum 10000 crownes . f. 72r (R8501). A whole page of clear text in a small hand, headed a., b. and c. to match the ciphered passages on ff. 71r–71v: the French ambassador’s wife writing to the Duchess of Nemours that the Queen of Scots “is in very ill state”; Villeroy sending the ambassador’s secretary to “make away Nau”. About 480 cipher signs on f. 71 were aligned against it. The alignment gives a letter alphabet with homophones, plus single-sign and numeric codes: letter signs letter signs a w n h b 24 o n c, l d p E e 6 q Δ f ψ r O+, Oo g B s II, #, I h λ t u, A i, y x, H u, v D, ρ k M w D d l a m oo Codes: B alone Villeroy, O+ alone the Duke or Duchess of Nemours, 120 the French ambassador, 47 the King of Navarre; 20, 22 and 54 recur. The earlier interpretation of 6 as a null (from the four runs of R8503) is wrong: it is the commonest letter, e .

The letters are in German, with the secret parts in French code. Where Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz Bibliothek, Hanover, Ms XXIII 1234:29,2 pp. 73–75 and 119–121, online in the GWLB digital library. Kalliope calls both “teilweise dechiffriert”. The cipher A syllabic nomenclator of 863 numbered groups, with homophones, officers’ names, and the control groups “annulle la precedente” and “repete la precedente”. Blank numbers are nulls. How it was deciphered The key table is in another volume of the papers, Ms XXIII 1234:31,1 pp. 386–391 (1745/46). It matches the worksheet the office made for the Steinberg letter, and it reads the unsigned letter, which had no decipherment at all. What it says The King approves the forage instructions, and the troops are to eat the country bare so that the French find “ni fourage ni rien”. Steinberg encloses an extract of the instructions just sent to Lord Stair. Still open One group whose last digit is lost in the binding, and a stray letter before and after it. The unsigned letter of 15/26 February 1743, p. 73. The dateline “866.223” is a null and Londres . Six lines of German clear text are followed by the code, with no decipherment anywhere on the letter. Johann Georg von Ilten (1688–1749) was a Hanoverian lieutenant-general in the Pragmatic Army, which George II had sent to the Austrian Netherlands. His papers, the Sammlunge von Krieges Commissariat undt Landt-Sachen , are Ms XXIII 1234 in the Ilten collection at the GWLB. Kalliope catalogues two letters in volume 29,2 singly, each as “teilweise dechiffrierter Brief”. Unsigned, London, 15/26 February 1743 (pp. 73–75). A German opening says the report of 18 February has arrived and been approved. Twenty-five lines of code follow, 189 groups, and then more German clear text about an affair between Colonel von Hardenberg and a major. Nobody deciphered the code. Kalliope’s “partly deciphered” can only mean the clear parts. Ernst von Steinberg, London, 29 March / 9 April 1743 (pp. 119–121). A German letter with three short code runs, 34 groups. Page 121 is the office’s worksheet, with each group glossed syllable by syllable.

A Kalliope search for “Chiffre” in the Ilten papers finds volume 31,1 (1745–46), whose record lists “eine Chiffre-Tabelle” at pp. 386–391. The key is two-part: pp. 386–388: the enciphering side, in alphabetical order (“a – 25, 61, 244, 301, 467, 720”), with an Additamentum of officers and places, among them Ilten himself as 845. pp. 390–391: the deciphering side, numbers 1–863. Its foot note reads “NB. les Chiffres qui restent ne signifient rien”: blanks and everything from 864 to 1000 are nulls. Groups 101 and 783 mean “annulle la precedente” and 453 “repete la precedente”. The deciphering table, p. 390, entries 1–240: “1 – Car”, “101 – annulle la precedente”, “172 – Duc”, “223 – londres”. Image: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz Bibliothek Hannover, Ms XXIII 1234:31,1 p. 390, via the GWLB digital library (public domain). The table was transcribed in full, 863 entries. The Steinberg worksheet confirms it: every value the office wrote there, 28 of them, is the table’s value. The worksheet has 17 “et” and 294 “re” for être , 472 “Mylord Stair” and 414 “secret”. The table is dated by its volume to 1745/46, but its names (Sommerfeldt, Du Pontpietin, Stair, the Duc d’Arenberg) are the names of 1743. The office worksheet for Steinberg’s letter, p. 121: “344 515 126 15 5 782 644 225 – ex-tra-it de l’in-tra-c”. The table gives 644 as tru , so the word is instruction . Image: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz Bibliothek Hannover, Ms XXIII 1234:29,2 p. 121, via the GWLB digital library (public domain).

The unsigned letter, 15/26 February 1743 Pour ce qui regarde les instructions que Monsieur le general du Pontpietin a donné à Monsieur le Lieutenant general de Sommerfeldt par rapport aux fourages, elles sont aussi approuvées, ainsi que j’ay ordre de le marquer, aussi bien qu’on ne doutoit point du soin qu’on auroit de continuer à tenir toujours une bonne et exacte discipline dans ce pays là. Cependant on souhaite que les trouppes consument avec […] même bonne discipline ce qu’il y a de fourage dans ces quartiers, afin qu’il n’en reste rien si l’envie prenoit aux François de vouloir prendre quartier après vous dans ce pays là, de sorte qu’ils n’y trouveroient point ni fourage ni rien de ce qui seroit necessaire pour la subsistance des trouppes. Vous ferez usage de ce dernier point selon votre prudence ordinaire. In English: the King approves the forage instructions that General du Pontpietin gave Lieutenant-General Sommerfeldt, and trusts that good discipline will be kept. The troops are nevertheless to consume the forage in their quarters, so that if the French should quarter there after them they find neither forage nor anything else to keep an army. Ilten is to use this last point with his usual prudence. The letter is unsigned, but it writes “j’ay ordre de le marquer” and dates itself from London in the code Steinberg used five weeks later, so it probably came from the German Chancery in London. That is not proven. Two control groups are used. 453 (“repete la precedente”) follows trouppes , and 101 (“annulle la precedente”) cancels a mistaken 697 empeche at the end. Steinberg, 29 March / 9 April 1743 Auf Sr. Königl. Mayt. gnädigsten Befehl habe ich nicht nur das heute an den Herrn General du Pontpietin ergehende Königl. Rescriptum… hiebey zu schließen, sondern auch einen extrait de l’instruction qui vient d’être envoyée au Mylord Stair zur Nachricht… mit anzufügen, damit Ew. Hochwollgebohren quoique avec le dernier ménagement du secret bey Sr. Königl. Mayt. généralité allemande Gebrauch davon machen mögen. With the table, all 34 groups read. The worksheet had skipped 278.613 quoique avec and misread 644. In both letters the table’s 172 “Duc” stands for du : “le general Du Pontpietin”, “du soin”, “du secret”.

Unsigned letter, p. 74, line 3: “consument avec 283.75? même”. The last digit of 75? is inside the binding. 751, a null, fits the visible stroke, but 283 ( r ) then stands alone. The sense, “avec la même”, is plain. The same letter, p. 74, line 4: a single 59 ( e ) after discipline , probably a slip. Volume 29,2 is described as partly in cipher throughout. Only these two letters are catalogued singly, so other coded passages in the 1741–46 volumes would read with the same table.

The code Jefferson and Adams gave Barclay and Lamb for the Barbary missions, used by Barclay, Carmichael, Short and Jefferson until 1791. Boyd and successors) (earlier solution) adjacent text At a glance Key from adjacent plaintext · partial (97% of the cipher) The letters Eighteen letters with coded passages, 1786–1791: Thomas Barclay to Jefferson and Adams (Madrid 1786, Lorient 1787), Jefferson to Barclay (4 July 1787), to Adams (28 September 1787) and to William Carmichael at Madrid (1787–1791), Carmichael to Jefferson (1788–89), and William Short to John Jay (Paris, October 1789). Where Library of Congress, Thomas Jefferson Papers, series 1, and National Archives, RG 59, Despatches from US Ministers to France, vol. 1 (microfilm M34 roll 2). Printed in The Papers of Thomas Jefferson (Founders Online). Catalogue no. 483. The cipher A two-part code of about 1,750 numbers for words, syllables, letters and stops, written with dots between the groups, with several numbers for common items. No key sheet survives. How it was deciphered Jefferson decoded Barclay’s and Carmichael’s letters between the lines and kept clear-text sheets of his own coded letters. Every group was transcribed from the images and its value taken only from those decodings: 348 values (key.tsv). What it says Barclay’s arrest for debt at Bordeaux, the Barbary captives, Spanish policy on the Mississippi and the Kentucky settlers, the Russian, Swedish and Turkish wars, and in 1791 the Mississippi and a joint front against the British navigation act. Still open Jefferson’s coded postscript to Adams (the press copy is blotted; the original is at the Massachusetts Historical Society), and about twenty groups that occur only once, among them the editors’ Rayneval , trouble and sea of 4 July 1787. Credit The reading of every passage was first printed by the editors of The Papers of Thomas Jefferson (Julian P. Boyd and successors, 1954–1982); it was used here to align the text and is checked group by group below.

In 1785 Jefferson and John Adams, the American commissioners for treaties, sent Thomas Barclay to Morocco and John Lamb to Algiers. Each carried a copy of a code made for the mission, so that the agents, the commissioners and William Carmichael, the American chargé at Madrid, could write to one another in secret. The Jefferson Papers number it Code No. 11. Lamb never gave Carmichael his copy; the one Barclay left at Madrid, copied by a clerk and handed over by David Franks, turned out to be a different code (Code No. 13), and Carmichael could not read Jefferson’s coded letter of 25 September 1787. Jefferson sent him a checked copy on 1 February 1788, and from May 1788 they wrote to each other in it. In 1790 Jefferson, by then Secretary of State, had to send to Philadelphia for Barclay’s copy because the Department had none, and in August 1790 he replaced it; the editors think he believed the Spanish ministry could read it. The editors decoded every coded passage, “employing a partially reconstructed key”, and printed their guesses in brackets. They never printed the key. Of Jefferson’s letter to Barclay of 4 July 1787 they wrote that they had “only partially reconstructed this code (Code No. 11), for which no key has been found”. Jefferson read Barclay’s and Carmichael’s coded letters with his own copy and wrote the meaning over the numbers, a word over several groups or a syllable over one. For his own coded letters he kept a clear-text sheet, and the State Department clerk wrote the meaning over Short’s numbers in the despatch book. All of this was transcribed group by group from the images, and a value was admitted to the key only from those decodings (grade H), from a clear sheet where the word sits on a single group, or from a pair printed in the editors’ notes from Jefferson’s or Carmichael’s own statements. The editors’ reading of a letter was used to align it, never as evidence for a value. Carmichael to Jefferson, 8 May 1788: “1001 739 1264 1010 1401 1508 1237 1509 950 1509 694 861 221 742 658 233 1017 / 1077 1097”, with Jefferson’s decoding above, “I have no advice of an ral fical ral not e America for many months never ;”. Carmichael garbled “official nature”, and Jefferson quoted the line back to him on 3 June to sort out their copies. Image: Library of Congress, Thomas Jefferson Papers, series 1, William Carmichael to Jefferson, Aranjuez, 8 May 1788, image mtj1 009_0339. The result is 348 values (key.tsv). The code is two-part: the numbers do not follow the alphabet (1196 is the , 1199 to , 1201 back , 1194 si ), so a missing value cannot be bracketed by its neighbours. It has homophones: the full stop is 1013 or 1235, is 1363 or 1306, the 1196 or 1190, their 1365 or 1565, minister 396 or 896. Carmichael’s copy had 1360 where Jefferson’s had 1363 ( is ), and Jefferson’s corrections over Carmichael’s numbers (1567 to 1527 sa , 1396 to 1390 ne , 146 to 140 Sweden and others) are in the transcription notes. About 800 distinct numbers occur in the eighteen letters, so most of the code is still unknown. The printed test line of 15 December 1787, with which Jefferson checked Carmichael’s copy, has two misprints in the edition: the twelfth group is 519, not 515, and the fifteenth 1097, not 1057. Its plaintext is the opening of his letter of 14 June 1787: the first four groups are De-ar Si-r (1420.1250.1194.1307), and groups 14–40 decode as “[go]t back to Paris three days ago, I resume immediately the correspondence with which you have been pleased to”.

Of 1,917 counted groups, 1,868 (97.4%) carry a reading. 1,519 are graded H (a contemporary decoding or clear sheet), 153 C (the value is attested in another letter and agrees), 216 M (the editors’ reading, not checked by any other occurrence) and 16 I (a guess with no support). Jefferson’s quotations of Carmichael’s numbers and groups struck out by the writers (37 in all) are not counted. The brief for this target was to settle the bracketed readings of the July 1787 letters. Each was checked against every occurrence of its groups: Jefferson to Barclay, 4 July 1787. M. 1420. 374. 1139. 1128. is M. de Mon-tmor-in : the same three groups spell Montmorin in the clear-text sheet of 25 September 1787, and 1420 = de is confirmed by the test line ( De-ar ). The editors’ [Rayneval] is 1336.459.1089. The last group ends imperi-al in Carmichael’s letter of 29 May 1788 (Jefferson’s decoding), which fits -val , but it is la in la-t-ter twice in 1791, and 1336 and 459 occur nowhere else. Rayneval, Montmorin’s first secretary, is the likely man, but the code does not prove it (grade I). The editors’ [trouble] is 223, a single occurrence (grade I). The editors’ [sea] is contradicted. “Opposition from another quarter of the 495.”: 495 is the first half of larger in Barclay’s letter of 10 April 1786, “a 495.1243 sum”, with Jefferson’s larger written over it and 1243 = -er (Stadholder, premier, error). Barclay writes 4 as a looped stroke, as in 1458 can on the line above; there is no leading 1. Sea is 1164 in Jefferson’s decoding of L’Oiseau (l-sea-w, the editors’ note). The word Jefferson meant is open: “of the larg-” does not read, so either he slipped in encoding or 495 has a second value no decoding shows. His letter to Jay of 21 June 1787 puts the opposition with the ministry of justice (Lamoignon, the garde des sceaux), not across the sea. Barclay’s footnotes, about 3 July 1787. The dagger note is 265, Congress : Jefferson wrote Congress over 265 in Carmichael’s letter of 26 January 1789, and it is the Congress of Barclay’s 1786 letter. The asterisk note has six groups, not the five the editors’ “The Pro[cu]re[ur]” implies: 1196.1084.758.861.1307.626, with 1196 = the , 861 = e and 1307 = r from Jefferson’s decodings. It reads The [Pro][cur]e r [General?] , the Procureur général Dudon who had Barclay released; 1084, 758 and 626 occur only here. Jefferson to Carmichael, 25 December 1788. “our Kentuck[ians]” is 457.980.913.537.814, and 537 is u (Jefferson’s U-lloa ), so the editors’ [ians] on 537.814 is a wrong split: our Ke-nt-u-[814] , with 814 unknown ( ck , cky or ckians ). Jefferson to Carmichael, 9 August 1789. 1107 is t , the end of Braban-t , so the editors’ [tal]k is t-alk ; the group read 1001 at first is 1111, this (“Is this true?”). “Their” is written 1569, which is you in Carmichael’s letter of 8 May 1788: probably a slip for 1565, their . The eighteen Founders documents that mention Code No. 11 were collected, with the editors’ notes on single numbers. No published key or later study of the code was found. The Library of Congress images were found through the item records and, once those sat behind a bot check, by reading the thumbnails of the image server volume by volume; that is how Barclay’s misfiled letter and the 1791 letter were reached. Short’s despatches came from the National Archives catalogue. Subagents transcribed every coded passage group by group with Jefferson’s decoding or the clear sheet beside it; the doubtful groups named above were re-read on the images at two to four times enlargement. A segmentation solver that cut each passage’s plaintext among its groups was tried and set aside: a few wrong starting values spread through the blotted 1787 press copy. The key was built instead only from the decodings (attested_key.py), and every group was graded (make_reading.py). Each bracketed reading was then checked against all the other occurrences of its groups. The key is recovered from adjacent plaintext: the contemporary decodings and clear-text sheets in the same correspondence, not a key sheet. The statistical test of the project does not apply: words spread over several groups make a quarter of the read groups look polyphonic. The check is that every value in key.tsv is a contemporary decoding.

Humphreys writes me that all Mr. Gardoqui's Communications Communications / while / here while / here tended to impress the Court of Madrid with the Idea that the Navigation of the Missisippi was only demanded on our part to quiet our Western Settlers and that it was not sincerely desired by the Maritime States . Car quand il seroit veritable qu’ilz eussent vingt mil hommes de pied et douze mil chevaux, quand ilz auront divisé leurs forces ou ilz passeront foibles en Flandres sy leur dessein est d’y aller, ou ilz ne demeureront pas dans le Palatinat en estat d’y attendre mes forces, ou ilz passeront foibles en f118r estat d’y attendre mes forces jointes avec celles du duc de Wimar. The archbishop of Patras wrote to his brother-in-law, the lord of Mantua, in clear Latin about the peace of Ferrara, and hid his advice in three runs of letter-like signs (DECODE R1854, image 1). This project could not read them; on 5 November 2026 Mark Vladimir Prizmic, working with Claude from Satoshi Tomokiyo’s transcription, sent a key (a homophonic substitution of Latin with two nulls) and a reading, which decodes here: 307 of 308 signs. Pandolfo asks Gonzaga to keep his men-at-arms and proposes that he become king of the Morea. cc ss 32 33 b3 32 20 9 40 I 26 x … d e s u i s g e n t i b … · de suis gentibus armigeris Rome → Gianfrancesco Gonzaga, Mantua · homophonic substitution, Latin · 22 April 1428 Pandolfo Malatesta to Gianfrancesco Gonzaga, 22 April 1428 to Gianfrancesco I Gonzaga Go to the full text ↓ The archbishop of Patras hid in cipher his advice to his brother-in-law to keep his soldiers together and to make himself king of the Morea; a reader outside the project found the key, and this page checks it. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 15 October 2026 · updated 5 November 2026 Method: read after matching with key from external sources · Extent: complete · On the map Contributed by Mark Vladimir Prizmic (solution, earlier solution) and Satoshi Tomokiyo (transcription) key matched At a glance External key matched · complete The letter Pandolfo Malatesta, archbishop of Patras and brother of Gianfrancesco’s wife Paola, to Gianfrancesco Gonzaga, lord of Mantua, Rome, 22 April 1428. Clear Latin with three cipher runs of 66, 82 and 160 signs. Where Archivio di Stato di Mantova, Archivio Gonzaga. DECODE R1854, image 1; the record was catalogued as one letter of unknown sender and holds four letters in four ciphers. The cipher A homophonic substitution of Latin letters: three signs each for a, e, i, o and u/v, two for r, one for most consonants, two null signs, no word division. The marks first taken for word separators are cipher letters. How it was read Mark Vladimir Prizmic, working with Claude from Satoshi Tomokiyo’s transcription, built the key and the reading and corrected five signs on the image. Here his key decodes his corrected transcription to his text, and the decode scores far above shuffled keys in Latin. This project had tried the letter in September and October and failed. What it says Three days after the peace of Ferrara, Pandolfo asks Gonzaga not to discharge his men-at-arms, and proposes that he be made “rex” of the Morea, “without risk and without great expense”, citing Count Riciardo, who went there with their sister Cleofe, the Despot’s wife. Still open One sign (23, once). The Count Riciardo is not identified. Credit Key and reading: Mark Vladimir Prizmic (with Claude), preprint of 5 November 2026. Transcription: Satoshi Tomokiyo. This letter is image 1 of DECODE R1854, which holds four letters to Gianfrancesco Gonzaga in four ciphers; the other three have their own pages: a Gonzaga agent in Rome, 9 August 1428 , an informant at Forlì, 6 November 1428 and Francesco de’ Cattanei, February 1430 , in which Pandolfo, as archbishop of Patras, appears offering his see’s lordship to Venice.

The letter opens in clear with the news, just arrived in Rome, of the peace between the duke of Milan and the league (the peace of Ferrara, 19 April 1428), “licet nondum publicatam”. Pandolfo writes that he has conceived plans “valde utilia” for his brother-in-law, and the secret parts follow in three runs: after “decrevi ne”, after “quo modo valeat” and after “nolit rem ipsam negligere”. It closes with greetings to Gonzaga’s wife, Pandolfo’s sister. The scan on DECODE carries a notice that the Archivio di Stato di Mantova allows publication only with its permission, so no image of it is reproduced here; the transcription is.

Cipher in bold, spelling as the scribe wrote it (north-Italian x , single l ); letters the scribe left out are in parentheses. Qua de re ipsam premissa rogare ac simul decrevi ne de suis gentibus armigeris cas(s)andis vel quid aliud peragendum [·] delliberet donec sciam; alioquin non possim … Nam sibi tue prepositum(?) me sciat quo modo valeat absque dis(c)rimine et multo dispendio provincie Moree, patrie siquidem fertilis et amene, rex efici ; precor itaque prefatam amplitudinem Vestram, cum se fratrem(?) paratam quoque reperiat posse sibi et natis amplitudinem tantam vendicare, nolit rem ipsam negligere. De eo autem regno magnificum c(o)mitem Riciardum bene informatum puto, quoniam ad illud cum serenissima sorore nostra domina vaxilissa tetendit, et iterum deinde etiam sui ocaxione redivit. Recommendo me prefate amplitudini Vestre … About this, having made the request above, I decided at the same time that he should not decide about discharging his men-at-arms, or about anything else to be done, until I know … let him know, through me, how he could, without risk and without great expense, be made king of the province of the Morea, a country fertile and pleasant indeed ; I therefore beg the said Highness, since he finds me, his brother, ready, and that he can claim so great a dignity for himself and his sons, not to neglect the matter. About that kingdom, I believe the magnificent Count Riciardo to be well informed, since he went there with our most serene sister, the lady basilissa, and afterwards went back there again on her account. The “serenissima soror nostra domina vaxilissa” is, on Prizmic’s reading, Cleofe Malatesta, Pandolfo’s and Paola’s sister, who married Theodore II Palaiologos, Despot of the Morea, in 1421. The timing explains the first run: with the peace made, Gonzaga, a condottiere in the league’s service, would be expected to stand down his companies. Pandolfo also appears in Cattanei’s letters of February 1430 (R1854, images 4–5) offering his see’s lordship to Venice. The complete letter, with the clear parts and the runs together, is under Full texts below.

A homophonic substitution of Latin letters: one sign for most consonants, two for r , three for each of a , e , i , o and u/v , two nulls, no word division and no code groups. The sign 49 stands for x in rex , vaxilissa and ocaxione . The signs are named by Tomokiyo’s labels; the three marks first taken for separators are letters (the double slash is i , the three dots a ). letter signs letter signs letter signs a 12 44 22 i 26 b3 46 r H 21 b x l 8 s 32 c 48 m ss2 t I d cc n 40 u / v 10 24 33 e 9 ss 42 o V 45 50 x 49 f 30 p 52 nulls v g g 20 q 28 unread 23 (once)

How. Prizmic took Tomokiyo’s transcription and the values implied by his CTTS trial as a starting key, ran a homophonic annealing solver scored on a Latin four-gram model with a letter-frequency penalty, and read the result by hand; words such as magnificum , serenissima and basilissa fixed several values at once and showed two signs to be nulls. He then checked every value the reading needed on the DECODE image, which gave five corrections to the transcription (two signs transcribed 30 are the double-c sign, d; two H signs and one mislabelled sign are r, r and o; and the final cc of run 1 is not a cipher sign). Tomokiyo accepted them on 5 November. His preprint is doi 10.5281/zenodo.23969170 ; it says that Claude was used for the solving and drafting. Why this project missed it. Our transcription had 262 signs; the corrected one has 308. The difference is the marks we had set aside as word separators, which are cipher letters. On 5 October we kept five kinds of separator as extra signs and still found nothing, and our annealers, working from the 262-sign transcription, never produced words. We did not find the answer; it reached us. Checks here (5 November 2026), using the key and the corrected transcription he sent: Re-decoding. dec.py applies the key to the corrected transcription: all 308 signs have a value except the unread 23, and the three decoded runs agree letter for letter with his reading, with 66, 82 and 160 signs. A control. Under the Latin model la the decode scores −5.25 per letter, against −6.90 for the best of 300 keys of the same shape with the letters shuffled among the sign classes (mean −7.88); the language check names Latin ahead of every other language. The clear text. The reading fits the Latin round each run: run 2 follows “me sciat quo modo valeat” and leads to “amplitudinem tantam vendicare … sibi et natis”; “ne … delliberet” takes “amplitudo Vestra” as its subject, in the third person like the rest of the letter. The clear text is this project’s transcription; the preprint does not say whether Prizmic used it as cribs, so the fit is evidence of sense, not an independent test. Our own transcription. The beginning and the end of run 1 ( cc ss Z K bz Z and cc ss g cc ss 8 vb 8 bz x n H y I in our labels) read d-e-s-u-i-s and d-e-l-l-i-b-e-r-e-t with one sign each for the repeated letters, as the key says. These checks do not make the reading independent: the key was built together with the reading, and the control shuffles a key already fitted to this text. What carries the reading is that 308 signs of 33 kinds decode to whole Latin clauses that agree with the clear text round them, and that Prizmic checked each value on the image and Tomokiyo accepted the corrections.

Sign 23, once, before delliberet : the sentence is complete without it, so it may be a null. Count Riciardo, who went to the Morea with Cleofe and returned for her, is not identified, and whether Gonzaga was ever offered the Morea is not established. The clear text round runs 1 and 2 rests on the DECODE image and this project’s transcription (“prepositum(?)”, “fratrem(?)”, “sensu(?)” stay doubtful); a better image would settle them. No contemporary decipherment has been looked for in the Archivio Gonzaga. Falcioni’s 2004 note on Malatesta chancery ciphers was not seen. Pandolfo’s ciphered letter of 1 March 1438 (ASMn, AG, b. 1081, c. 159–160, with the contemporary translation in b. 840, c. 95) may use the same cipher; this key could be tried on it if its cipher is ever imaged.

News has just been brought here that peace has been concluded between the illustrious ducal dominion and the lord duke [and the league(?)], though it is not yet published. Since then I have conceived and thought out several things that are very useful for us, by which Your Highness could advance your own position and ours not a little. About this, having made the request above, I have decided at the same time that **[RUN 1] he should not decide about discharging his men-at-arms, or about anything else to be done, until I know**; otherwise I could not, which by God's favour I hope will be within twenty days if the news of the peace is confirmed. For let him know, through me, **[RUN 2] how he could, without risk and without great expense, be made king of the province of the Morea, a country fertile and pleasant indeed.** I therefore beg the said Highness, since he finds me, his brother, ready, and that he can claim so great a dignity for himself and his sons, not to neglect the matter. **[RUN 3] About that kingdom, I believe the magnificent Count Riciardo to be well informed, since he went there with our most serene sister, the lady basilissa, and afterwards went back there again on her account.** I commend myself to the said Highness, whom I wish well from the heart, with your magnificent consort, my honoured sister, and your sons. Pandolfo de' Malatesti, archbishop of Patras, Rome, 22 April 1428. Notes: "ne ... delliberet" takes "amplitudo Vestra" as its subject, in the third person like the rest of the letter. Where Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 15572 f. 276, fr. 15571 f. 179 and fr. 15573 ff. 379–381 (Gallica). The two slips were part of catalogue item 12 with the Mayenne–Forget despatches, which are in other ciphers. The cipher Matignon’s Cipher-3: invented signs and figures for letters, a few signs for whole words ( de , la , que , et ) and a null. How it was deciphered Satoshi Tomokiyo published a partial table of the key. alejandrozarco checked it against a sibling leaf and its contemporary decipherment, then read both slips sign by sign, twice and independently. f. 179 also carries Tomokiyo’s own decipherment, written over his image of it. The despatch reports on the Garonne trade the Huguenots tax, Castillon, Marmande and the King of Navarre. Still open On the slips, three one-sign code words, two blots and a few faint signs; with them f. 179 reads at 90.6% of its words (measured 24 October 2026), under 95%. In the despatch, the code signs and about 45 words whose signs are clear but give no word under the key; after two re-readings on 23 October 2026, 36 of its 61 sentences are clean (0.59, the bar is about 0.60), so the despatch stays decoded, not read, with a partial reading and English. Credit The slips are alejandrozarco’s work (pull request 25, October 2026); the despatch is Brett Burford’s (issue 44, October 2026). Both were reviewed and re-measured here. Other ciphers The Mayenne–Forget despatches filed with these slips use Cipher-1; that entry is still in progress ( targets/matignon1586/ ). Matignon’s despatch of May 1586 from Monségur is in Cipher-2, with its own page: Mayenne–Forget’s Cipher-2 .

BnF fr. 15572 and fr. 15571 hold the papers of the Guyenne war of 1585–86 round Mayenne, Matignon and Forget de Fresnes. Satoshi Tomokiyo (cryptiana, Henry III’s Cipher with Ambassadors ) lists ten leaves there with no known decipherment, in two ciphers: Mayenne–Forget’s Cipher-1 and Matignon’s Cipher-3. Until 14 October 2026 the project kept them as one entry. Each cipher is now its own entry, and this page covers the two Cipher-3 leaves. A third Cipher-3 document, a six-page despatch in fr. 15573, came in with Brett Burford’s reading in October 2026 (section 04).
