Tomokiyo’s partial table is a homophonic letter substitution with word signs: 60 faire , a β-like sign de , 20 la , 18 le , a p with a stroke pour , a C with n que , ∴ qui , and plain v a null. alejandrozarco checked it on a sibling that was deciphered at the time: ff. 277r–278r, whose decipherment is on ff. 279–280. A transcriber who never saw the values copied f. 277r by shape, and a hard-EM alignment matched that copy to the clear text. 1,271 signs aligned to letters and 55 word signs to their words, and for every frequent sign the table’s value is the one the alignment picks. The two slips added values that the table lacks. Three crossed strokes, ### , are et : the sign occurs eight times, always between words. Some columns of the table split in two (a z-topped hook is i, a reversed hook o). A hooked ρ is i, a dotted v is u, and a C with ε inside is q.

f. 276 , in alejandrozarco’s reading (16th-century spelling, word division his): La Guiolle est en doubte du Puy pour les amis de La Rousiere, [qui] sont en grand nombre avec luy, dont il y en a qui veullent mal a Polidor. La Saussaie a soing de lui […] a secouru de ce qu’il a peu vos amis de la Madeleyne. … Le Pui est ennuyé de la guerre, et neaulmoins redoute la […] … It is a Poitou intelligence note on the Catholic factions round La Roussière, Henri III’s governor of Fontenay(-le-Comte) from 1582 to 1587, and on a priory promised to one Aubois. Its first line matches the opening Tomokiyo published. fr. 15571 f. 179 continues with the same people. Frontin will come to terms with La Roussière’s children; the plan is now to attack Pons, il se poura prendre en ung mois . The writer fears the sickness among the foot will spread, and a long rest would then be needed before the army could serve again. Iehan Durant is to be written to pour employer Lansac en … l’armée de mer; il n’y est propre . The siege and the sickness fit the plague in Mayenne’s and Matignon’s army round Castillon in August–September 1586, but that is not established.

BnF fr. 15573 ff. 379r–381v is a despatch of autumn 1586 written wholly in cipher over six pages and addressed to the King. Tomokiyo lists it as having no known decipherment and as written in Matignon’s Cipher-3, and he prints its first line. The sender’s name is not in the readable text, so “probably Matignon” rests on the cipher and the content. The first four lines of f. 379r. In Burford’s reading they begin a ce qu’il plaist a vostre maieste , which matches the opening Tomokiyo published. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 15573 f. 379r (view 740), via Gallica. Brett Burford published a decipherment of the whole despatch on 18 October 2026 (his search of code hosts, cryptiana, Cryptoole and the web found none earlier beyond Tomokiyo’s first line) and brought it to version 0.5 the next day. Claude Opus 5.5 named every sign under a reference sheet of 50 shapes cut from the sibling f. 277r. Five passes were voted, and a correction was kept only where two blind asks agreed and the image showed the sign. On a stretch of f. 278r with a known answer, the voted reader got 96% of signs right. The key is Tomokiyo’s table, checked against the decipherment of ff. 277–278 on ff. 279–280. Burford also aligned another Cipher-3 letter that was deciphered at the time, fr. 15570 ff. 271–272 of September 1585, against its decipherment on f. 273. That gave six new values: a long zigzag is ss , a circled 9 is par , a d is vostre , and three more are marked doubtful. A word decoder chose one value at each two-valued sign, and his files record every choice. The readable stretches are a military report on the Guyenne campaign. They cover the Garonne between Toulouse and Bordeaux, where the Huguenots tax the river trade, and Caumont and the Mas de Verdun. They also name Castillon, the Isle and the Dordogne, the King of Navarre, “your sister” at Agen, the artillery brought out of Navarrenx, Marmande, and fifteen to sixteen thousand crowns. The reading was re-measured here with the same rule as the two slips: 2,540 of 2,836 signs (89.6%) fall in runs of period French, against a median of 6–10% for shuffled keys. Runs of French are not sentences. Read as sentences in the reading audit of 22 October 2026, Burford’s unpunctuated decode had a garbled word in nearly every sentence and no translation, so it was classed decoded, not read. On 23 October 2026 the decode was divided, punctuated and translated word by word, every departure from the key’s letters bracketed ( f379_381/ff379-381_reading.md , ff379-381_en.md ). A second pass the same day re-read every break on the full-size views 740–745: one label corrected (a “p” on f. 379v l. 3 is bleed-through), five second values that recur across the despatch and a few look-alike alternates (28 letters of about 2,300), and a word-by-word check that each unbracketed word is carried by its signs. The neighbouring folios (views 724–757) hold no clear copy or decipherment. The partial reading opens: […] a ce qu’il pliaist a vostre maieste me […] luy doner advis pour lettre de vostre armee […] veu la saison qui est proche de l’iuer, et que il n’y a rien qui incomode tant c[e] pays que les places qui sont sur la riuiere de Garone entre Tolouse [?et] [?Bourdeaulx], dont ceulx de la [?nouuelle] religion tirent de grandes daces sur les marchandises It names Sainte-Bazeille, where the King of Navarre’s commissions levy tolls, Caumont and the Mas de Verdun, and Bergerac, Sainte-Foy and Castillon, and advises clearing the river before besieging a strong place. Scored as sentences, 36 of 61 are clean (0.59, with 0.60 the bar). Other documents at 0.59–0.597 were kept unread, so this one stays decoded, not read : f. 379r and the end build sentences, while f. 379v ll. 17–21 and f. 380r ll. 1–2 and 18–22 are weak. About 45 words have clear signs that give no word under the key; Matignon’s minutes (Monaco, J 41) have not been looked at.

Two independent reads of each slip. Two readers worked sign by sign, each with only the table. They agree on 693 of 739 signs on f. 276 (93.8%) and 472 of 516 on f. 179 (91.5%). Every disagreement that changes the sense was settled on the image. Measured coverage. A sign counts as read only inside a run of at least three words of a period lexicon, the shared model fr-1600-letters . f. 276 gives 706 of 734 signs, f. 179 gives 473 of 509. Both figures were re-run after the split and are unchanged. Counted word by word on the written-out reading (24 October 2026), f. 179 reads at 90.6%: its sentences hold, but under the 95% a complete reading needs. Shuffled keys. With the letter values shuffled, 50 random keys give a median of 6.9% on f. 276 and 3.5% on f. 179. External agreement. Tomokiyo’s published opening of f. 276 and his magenta decipherment of f. 179 agree with the reading. So do the contemporary glosses over two lines of f. 276, where they can be read.

Three one-sign code words, each used once: on f. 276 a large K ( redoute la [K] : paix ? Ligue ? Royne ?) and a C with o inside ( en temps de […] ), and on f. 179 an ω with an overbar, probably a person. The deciphered Cipher-3 siblings (f. 189 in f. 190, f. 282, fr. 15570 ff. 271–273) have not been searched for them. Two blots (f. 276 line 4, f. 179 line 18), the closing of f. 276 and de la D[…]use on f. 179, and a few short spans. In the despatch: five rare code signs that occur in no deciphered Cipher-3 letter found so far, five short runs of clear signs not yet deciphered, and doubtful words and names (Burford’s list explains 110 of 115 items). Who wrote the two slips, and to whom; whether Matignon wrote the despatch.

Decryption SOLUTION.md # Matignon's Cipher-3, BnF fr. 15572 f. 276 (1586): read Catalogue item 12, the Cipher-3 leaf. `targets/matignon1586/NOTES.md` listed it as "blocker: not-attempted; not transcribed" (coverage table: 0 / ~27 lines). This contribution is dated 6 Oct 2026. **Result: f. 276 deciphered with Tomokiyo's key (method: read with known key): 706 of 734 signs (96.2%), measured.** - **Measurement.** `scripts/measure.py` follows the `targets/matignon1586/measure.py` rule: lines are joined; a sign counts as read only inside a run of at least 3 lexicon words totalling at least 10 letters; a word is lexical if it occurs at least 20 times in the corpus of the shared `lang/` model `fr-1600-letters` (source `fr-henri4`, Berger de Xivrey, *Lettres missives de Henri IV*, t. I–V), normalised with the model's `early` scheme, fetched through `lang.corpora`. - **Unkeyed signs.** An unkeyed sign (`?`) inside a run is the rule's CONTEXT token: it doesn't break the run and is never counted read. `targets/matignon1586/measure.py` lets the language model supply its letter; here it simply passes through, which is an approximation. - **Control.** The scrambled-key floor is 6.9% (median of 50 shuffles; maximum 29.3%). Chance-corrected, that is 95.9%. - **Agreement.** Two sign-by-sign readings, made independently, agree on 693 of 739 signs (93.8%, `scripts/compare_reads.py`). - **The measured text.** `read_final.txt` is read 1 with the image-checked corrections listed under Method. - **What stays open** is listed at the end: a blot, two signs not in the table, the closing, and a few short spans. - **Sibling leaf.** fr. 15571 f. 179 is in the same cipher and names the same people; see `../f179/SOLUTION.md`. The leaf is Gallica `btv1b9061879d`, canvas 285 (right page). It is a small slip of **22** cipher lines. The coverage table's "~27" was an estimate. Images are not included. ## Clear text (16th-c. spelling; word division and punctuation ours; […] unread, [?] doubtful) > La Guiolle est en doubte du Puy pour les amis de La Rousiere, [qui] sont en grand nombre avec luy, dont il y en a > qui veullent mal a Polidor. La Saussaie a soing de lui […] a secouru de ce qu'il a peu vos amis de la Madeleyne. > [Ils] font courir le bruit que la Chambre et frere de la Mare ont ausi bone intelligence qu'ils l'eurent iamais, et se > doibuent bientost assembler au preiudice de Front[enay?]. Le procureur et son fils ont promis Aubois le remettre en > possession du prieuré, ce que La Saussaie ne peult croire, encor qu'ils se escriuent, s'en asseurant que les sieurs > de la Fontaine, la Chaie et Mirebeau et son procureur, ausquels il se fie, ne voudroient permettre mesmes en temps > de […] qu'il feust deposedé du prieuré; et surtout il supplie que le Bois et lui n'[…]aient que de se mesler > ensemble […]. Le Pui est ennuyé de la guerre, et neaulmoins redoute la […]; quelque chose qu'il se face, il est besoing de > le bien de maistre Iehan Durant, soit paix ou guerre, que l'on esloigne la Mar[e?], car c'est le logis que desirent > les amis de la Mare et de la Rousiere […]. **English, loosely.** - **Factions.** La Guiolle is unsure of Le Puy because of La Roussière's friends, who are many, and some of whom wish Polidor harm. - **La Saussaie.** He has taken care of him […], and has helped your friends at la Madeleine as far as he could. - **Rumour.** They are spreading word that la Chambre and la Mare's brother are as thick as ever, and will soon gather to the prejudice of Frontenay[?]. - **The priory.** The procureur and his son have promised Aubois to restore him to the priory. La Saussaie cannot believe it, even though they write to each other. He trusts that the sieurs de la Fontaine, la Chaie, Mirebeau and his procureur would not allow him to be dispossessed, even in time of […]. - **A request.** Above all he begs that le Bois and he […] mingle together […] (the sense of this line is unsure). - **Le Puy.** He is tired of the war, yet fears […]. Whatever he does, for maistre Iehan Durant's good, in peace or war, la Mare should be kept away: "car c'est le logis que desirent les amis de la Mare et de la Roussiere". **Context.** A Poitou intelligence note among the Catholic factions round La Roussière, Henri III's governor of Fontenay(-le-Comte) 1582–87. He surrendered the town to Navarre on 1 June 1587. ## Key S. Tomokiyo's partial Cipher-3 table (cryptiana, *Henry III's Cipher with Ambassadors*). It is a homophonic letter substitution with word signs: - 60 *faire*, a β-like sign *de*, 20 *la*, 18 *le*, p-with-stroke *pour*, C with n *que*, ∴ *qui*; - v is a null. **Checked on the deciphered sibling ff. 277r–278r → 279r–280r.** We blind-transcribed the 37 cipher lines of f. 277r by shape only: the transcriber never saw values (`crib/BRIEF_transcriber.md`, `crib/f277r_all.txt`). A hard-EM alignment then matched that transcription to the contemporary decipherment (`crib/plain_all.txt`): ``` python scripts/align_em.py --cipher crib/f277r_all.txt --plain crib/plain_all.txt --iters 10 ``` - **Overall.** 1,271 signs align to letters and 55 word signs to their words. The table's value is the top emission for every frequent sign column; examples follow. | sign column | table value | aligned as | |---|---|---| | C05r1 | e | e 106 of 149 | | C16r1 | r | r 49 / 65 | | C17r1 | s | s 40 / 48 | | C19r2 | u | u 37 / 41 | | W02 | de | *de* 26 / 31 | | W03 | la | *la* 13 / 15 | - **Agreement with the table.** 58% of all aligned events carry exactly the table value. The rest are mostly transcription noise between similar rows (the blind transcriber's row ids are inconsistent), not key errors. **Additions to the table, found on f. 276 and checked on the image:** - **`###`** (three crossed strokes) = **et**. - It occurs 8 times, always between words, and "et" fits every place: *la Chambre et frere*, *le procureur et son fils*, *la Chaie et Mirebeau et son procureur*, *prieuré et surtout*, *guerre et neaulmoins*, *la Mare et de la Roussiere*. - Tomokiyo has a # in his r column, which this leaf does not support. - **Split columns:** ζ (z-topped hook) = i but ɤ (reversed hook) = o; ꝫ (9 with a bar) = u but ʒ (closed 9) = t. - **Other signs:** a small o with a diagonal tail = y; the crossed-A / ※ sign = i (L04, L16). - **The f column's ∂ is f**, not o: *de Front…* in L08, against δ = o elsewhere. - **ϱ with a hook below = i**, in five places: *il i en a* (L03), *de lui* (L04), *ausi bone* (L06), *lui n'…* (L16), *le Pui* (L17; *du pu* in L01). - **The dotted v = u** (*vos amis*, L04), although plain v is Tomokiyo's null. - **Two-stroke # = i** (*Rous|iere*, L22), as against three-stroke `###` = *et*. ## Method 1. **Line crops.** The slip was deskewed (−5.25°). We cut 22 lines at a 134-px pitch into three overlapping crops each. 2. **Read 1 and read 2.** Read 1 was done by hand for L01–02 and by two agents for L03–22. Read 2 was done by a third agent that never saw read 1. - Both used `BRIEF_reader.md`: the table, sign conventions verified on this hand, and the L01–02 worked example, which matches Tomokiyo's published opening. - Output is one letter per sign, with no smoothing into French. - Files: `read1.txt`, `read2.txt`. 3. **Comparing the reads.** `scripts/compare_reads.py` gives the letter-level agreement and lists every disagreeing span (44). We checked the spans that change the sense against the deskewed image: - *et* (8 places); - *sont en grand nombre* (y = n), not *et grand*; - L03–04 *a soing de* (hook = o, ※ = i, y = n, 23 = g); - L08 *Front…* (∂ f, ⊥ r, hooked o, y n, a t, then null v and *que*). 4. **A second image pass** made `read_final.txt`. They are presumably local gentry and officers, for the Vendée or Deux-Sèvres archives or the *Archives historiques du Poitou*. ## Open - **The 28 unread signs:** - L04: a blot after *de lui*; - L14: *en temps de* [one sign not in the table: a C with o inside]; - L18: *redoute la* [a large K, not in the table]; - L16: the last three signs; - L22: the closing, with one or two signs, then plaintext *ou…* and a flourish; - L08: one sign of *Front[…]*. - The rest are words the period lexicon holds fewer than 20 times: *prieure, escriuent*. - **L20:** *la Mar[e?]*, or Mareuil. - **Next target:** fr. 15571 f. 179, the other Cipher-3 leaf. Beinecke Mellon MS 136, catalogued on DECODE as a ciphered letter of Johann Arndt, is a 129-page alchemical manuscript on a “magical machine” of burning glasses. Its 31 passages in a Rosicrucian pigpen cipher were deciphered with the key drawn in the book on p. 83, applied unchanged: 1,545 signs, two left open. DECODE and the Unsolved Catalogue list it as a ciphered letter from Johann Arndt to an unknown recipient. It is an alchemical manuscript book, Das zweyte Silentium Dei in Königs Salomonis des Weisen paradiessischen Lustgarten . It describes a “magical machine” of three burning glasses, and hides its working details in a Rosicrucian cipher. The key is drawn in the book on p. 83 and was applied unchanged; the work was transcription. All 31 passages were deciphered, with two signs left open. The long passage on p. 24 had been decrypted online in 2022, and a blog comment gave most of the short passages. The title page reads Das zweyte Silentium Dei in Königs Salomonis des Weisen paradiessischen Lustgarten … des Theophrasti Paracelsi Himmels Schlüssels 2ter Theil . It says the text came “von dem Patriarchen und grossen R. Rosen” out of Arabic and Spanish into High German, with its secret script, “durch Johann Arndt”. Arndt is the Lutheran author of Wahres Christentum , and here his name is a borrowed authority. The Yale record dates the copy 18–25 September 1798 at Glücksbrunn, “by Gottfried Klaussen(?)”. DECODE turned that into a sender, a date and a place for a letter, and gave it an “unknown recipient”. The book has 129 numbered pages. The plates on pp. 21–23 show the machine: a stand with three conical glasses aimed at the sun, a sand-capel, a glass globe of water, a distilling flask. The text runs from the mineral kingdom (calcination, the “Aurum potabile”, the “Alumen plumosum”) through the vegetable (distilling plants and wine) to the animal, the seven metals and a “Secretum secretorum”. Page 16 says the use of the machine is written “in unserer geheimen Sprache, so Crucis Rosen[kreuzer]”. Page 83 prints “Die Figur unserer geheimen Schrift”, under a verse: “Wer allhier diese Figur recht versteht, der sieht, wie unsre Schrift darinnen steht”.

Page 83: “Die Figur unserer geheimen Schrift”. Each cell’s walls are its sign. The second letter of a cell is the same sign with a dot. On the right is the table of ligature signs (ae, oe, ui, ch, ck, sch, ss, st, th, und, ll, lich, nn, tz). The last five triangle signs, for v, w, y, x and z, are a later pencil addition. Image: Beinecke Rare Book and Manuscript Library, Mellon MS 136 p. 83, via Yale Digital Collections (image 45). The figure is a circle crossed by two diagonals and a noughts-and-crosses grid. That makes nine square cells and four triangles where the diagonals cross the centre. Each cell holds two letters in alphabetical order, and the second is marked by a dot: sign ┘ ⊔ └ ⊐ □ ⊏ ┐ ⊓ ┌ V > < Λ plain a c e g i l n p r t v z dotted b d f h (k) m o q s u w y (x) The table beside it adds single signs for common German letter groups. A double stroke over any sign doubles it ( ll , tt , nn ). It is a textbook pigpen, the kind the eighteenth-century Rosicrucian and masonic societies used. The key has the same shape as their alphabets. It hides nothing from anyone holding the book, and the key fits every passage without a single change.

These are the recipes that carry the deciphered passages, translated whole from the clear German around them. Words written in the secret script are in bold . Pious asides and the attacks on apothecaries are cut to […]. (?) marks an uncertain reading of the clear hand. The German transcription is in targets/mellon136/clear/ . The figures of the machine are on pp. 21–23, and p. 24 above gives the letters used for them. 1. The spirit of mercury (pp. 25–26) To begin using the machine, make the spirit of common mercury, which cannot otherwise be brought into its prima ens . Put common mercury into a cucurbit, as the machine shows. Set a still-head on it and attach a receiver. Behind the receiver place the water-globe No. F. NB this globe must stay there the whole time. It must not be closed, and if the water runs low it must be topped up. Then point the machine exactly at the sun, so that the third focus reaches the mercury in the flask. Its heat drives the mercury over the still-head as a spirit. NB: too quick and sudden a fire does harm. Set the stand with the machine somewhat farther off than the focus reaches, and move it up to the focus little by little. The mercury then rises with force into the receiver and turns into a spirit or aqua viscosa . This spirit leads all metallic bodies back into their prima materia , making a spiritual thing out of a bodily one. 2. The philosophical glass stone: silver, gold and a medicine (pp. 26–28) Coagulate the spirit of mercury again in an open glass dish before the machine into a metallic stone. Then melt it with the same fire into a glass, a “salamander”: this is the philosophical glass stone. Silver. Melt 1 part of the ground glass with 100 parts of fine silver. This gives a white, brittle matter that grinds easily to powder. Add 1 part of this to 1,000 parts of common mercury in open glass dishes, once the fire has taken hold and the mercury begins to smoke, and it is fixed into the best silver. This silver is too compact, as heavy as gold, so alloy each Mark of it with 4 Loth of raw copper. The copper’s sulphur “opens its pores”, and it stays good silver. Gold. Done the same way with gold, “the profit could well run higher, for it is one and the same work”. Medicine. The stone must never be taken raw. Put a small piece into a glass of wine for 12 hours, drink the wine and wait for the sweat. It purges by stool and urine, and in plague time it is “a universal medicine”. 3. Improving ores and minerals, in four operations (pp. 28–32) The book says this works for all tame and wild ores (gold, silver, iron, mercury, tin, copper and lead ores) and for the wild minerals: pyrites, blende, bismuth, glance, cobalt, marcasite, spar, vitriol earth, calamine, ochre, feather alum, tin-stone, sands and coloured mineral earths. The main rule. Take a tame or wild mineral and assay it on the mine hundredweight. Stamp it crude, as it comes from the mine, and wash off as much of the rock as you can. Set up the machine. Dry the slimes and spread them, not too thick, on a broad smooth grinding- or marble-stone . Let the machine calcine them, stirring all the time with a piece of wood, or better a glass rod, so that they take the heat evenly. Weigh the calcined mineral again and you will find “a rich increase”. The book's explanation is that the spiritus mundi gathers in it, and the wild ores ripen and fix themselves without any addition. Second operation. Put the calcined mineral into a wide, strong glass dish and let the fire work into its middle at full strength. It soon melts without any flux. Take the machine away and let it cool. Third operation, refining. Take a strong, thick glass dish of suitable size, shaped like a capel but hollowed deeper. Lay the melted metal in it and add lead, as in ordinary cupelling. Set the fire on it: the lead fumes away and leaves the finest bead, “far higher than on a capel”. An ordinary bone-ash capel will not do, because the spiritus mundi would sink into it and spoil the work. Fourth operation, parting. If the bead holds gold and silver together, lay it in a glass dish, moderately deep and not too wide, and melt it before the machine. Throw a little powdered glass on it bit by bit. The gold separates, and the silver goes with the glass into a slag. Then cupel the slag with lead in the glass capel described above. You now have the silver and the gold, each refined separately. 4. Aurum potabile, drinkable gold (pp. 43–44) Melt a ducat’s weight of fine gold in a glass dish before the machine and keep it molten until it begins to smoke. Then draw it quickly away from the machine, so that it has only a calcining heat. Throw a small piece of common sulphur on it and let it burn off, and the gold turns brittle and quite red. Stir it round with a glass rod and calcine it until it no longer smokes. Turn the machine away and let it cool. The gold is now a brittle matter, “spread with many thousand beautiful colours”, and the text claims it has gained half its weight in “astral salt”. It dissolves in wine at once, tinges it deep red and rises with it over the still-head, so it can never be turned back into gold. Boil it all down before the machine into a sweet salt. The dose is one drop, or half a Gran by weight, in wine. It works by sweating, and the book says it cures every disease and keeps a man healthy to the term God has set. 5. Feather alum (p. 45) Take feather alum ( alumen plumosum ) crude, as it comes from the mine, and treat it before the machine in such a glass dish , the same way as the pearls earlier in the book. It gives “a very noble stone” of many colours, “our true electrum”. This is the root of the tincture that raises lesser gemstones to perfection. The next page claims the same treatment makes talc, “invincible in fire”, fluid and turns it into a like tincture. 6. Oil of talc (pp. 47–48) Put common talc in the glass dish before the machine. Bring it up little by little , so that the heat only calcines it. Calcine it until it falls into a blue powder and no longer smokes. Then draw the machine back gently, little by little, so that for about 13 (?) hours it gives only a digesting heat. The calcined talc then draws the spiritus mundi to itself and dissolves into a flesh-coloured oil and spirit. Every metal, mineral, stone, coral and pearl is brought to spirit and oil the same way. The more a mineral has been calcined, the more strongly it draws the world-spirit. In a stronger fire the solution coagulates again and fixes itself “in the very highest degree”, for health and for improving metals and gemstones. 7. Drawing down the Star of the World, and a water that multiplies seed (pp. 53–55) The vegetable tinctures are of two kinds, one for multiplying plants and one for health. The multiplying tincture needs the Astrum Mundi first. Attractio Astri Mundi. Take purely melted-down nitre , spread it thinly in the glass dish, as at K. , and calcine it very gently before the machine until all its moisture has fumed off and the saltpetre turns yellow and reddish. Then draw it little by little away from the machine until it has only a little digesting [?] heat. It now draws the spiritus mundi to itself, “its very nearest blood-relation”. In a few hours one can collect “many measures” of the world-spirit. Set the collected spirit nearer to our magical fire , so that it little by little boils down into a bright-red powder , or one of the yellow kind. The author breaks off here: three words more, he says, would show the philosophers’ stone to the whole world. Throw a small part of this powder into a great deal of fresh water. It rises and ferments, and the froth is skimmed off. Sprinkle grains of wheat or any other seed with this tinging water before sowing: the book promises a thousandfold increase and fruit of unheard-of size. For plants, trees and shrubs, wet their roots with it a little. 8. The vitrified stone of the Astrum Mundi (p. 56) Take the Astrum Mundi caught by means of the saltpetre . After calcining it, melt it before the machine into a vitrified stone, which takes 4 to 5 (?) hours. “All the forces of nature” are said to be in this stone, for wonders “in all three kingdoms”. A curse on anyone who misuses it (Deuteronomy 28:59) runs on to p. 59. 9. Distilling flowers downwards (pp. 59–61) What the machine drives up over a still-head is only a clear spirit, though it is “a thousand times better” than what a coal fire gives. With plants, what is driven down ( per descensum ) is far finer. Fill glass No. O (the glass for the flowers) heaped full with rose petals or other flowers, and close the stopper on top. Lute the glass No. S. underneath , set the whole in a ring on a stand before the machine, and let the fire work very gently. It drives first the spirit, then the oil, down into glass No. P. One drop of it is worth more than a thousand of waters distilled the common way. The cipher has “No. S.”, but on p. 24 the glass to be luted is P, and the clear text on p. 61 calls it P. 10. The “cure” of all flowers and herbs (pp. 61–62) Put the spirit and oil driven down above into the open glass dishes and let the fire shine on them gently. They draw the Astra Mundi to themselves and boil down to a very fine powder of the same colour as the flowers. Of this, 1 grain to 1 Maas of fresh water tinges it all into the best rose water, or the water of whichever flower it came from. 11. Concentration of wine: the stone that turns water into wine (pp. 62–63) The vegetable universal is made from the noblest wine. It lets a person “carry about with him two hundred and more Ohm of wine”. Choose the wine you find best to drink. Fill the open glass dishes with it and set the machine so that the rays strike down on it steadily. It begins to simmer. Do not let it boil hard, but let it boil down to half and keep adding more, or let it drip in from another vessel, no faster than it boils away. Go on until three or four Maas or more have been boiled down to dryness. Then strengthen the fire and hold what is left in fusion for an hour, which increases it by a third. Turn the machine aside and let it cool: “you then have a stone that turns water into wine”. To raise it higher, crush the stone, calcine it and melt it in an open glass dish over a very gentle fire into a liquor. 12. The electrum of the seven metals and the magic mirror (pp. 69–71) No one can work wonders with characters, sigils or electrum amulets without first making an electrum with this fire, in the right conjunction and course of the planets. Take all seven metals in equal weight, fine and refined, and melt them one after another in a wide and strong glass crucible, each at the time of its rule and in its own planetary hour . Gold goes on Sunday in the hour of the Sun, silver on Monday, iron on Tuesday, mercury on Wednesday, tin on Thursday, copper on Friday and lead on Saturday. Each will be found heavier. Then melt all seven together on a Sunday in the hour of the Sun into an electrum metallicum . Cast it in a mirror mould and have it polished. The polisher must never look into the mirror with bare eyes, but always through spectacles (“Renien”, the green glasses of p. 24): whoever first looks into it is its master. It then shows whatever is asked of it. A little bell cast from the same electrum is said to put a whole army to flight. 13. How to set the machine for each fire (pp. 75–76) The larger the burning glasses, the greater their power […] but for the works described here, glasses of M., O. and Q. inches, up to 7 inches, are large enough. Too much power overdrives the work. Each operation needs its own fire: Melting: make the largest glass stand in front, facing the sun . It throws the rays together onto the matter into one joint . Distilling: turn the machine round so that the smallest glass faces the sun . The rays spread and warm the whole glass, as in the machine with the Spiritus Mercurii (recipe 1). Digesting, or a still weaker fire: either draw the machine and the matter set before it somewhat further apart, or set a large glass globe filled with fresh water between them . Melting, calcining and fixing: set it so that the fire casts its central rays exactly onto the matter . “This is, NB NB, the chief rule in all the works.” The book then turns to the “receptacle No. 2” for catching the Astrum Mundi (pp. 76–78): a helm and counter-flask made in one piece, pierced with sixteen holes the width of a little finger, four to each quarter of the sky. The world-spirit is driven through them into a round receiver.

Nils Kopal told Klaus Schmeh about the book, and Schmeh put it on his Encrypted Book List as no. 00114. His post on Cipherbrain (4 March 2022) links a video by Kopal. In it Kopal decrypts page 24 from a transcription by George Lasry and shows how CrypTool would break it without the key. The post prints the p. 24 plaintext and points to the key on p. 83. On 10 March 2022 a reader, Christof Rieber, commented with readings of most of the short passages. The search that found these came after the key on p. 83 had been identified here, but before any passage was transcribed. They were then used as a check. Page 24 agrees with the published text except for small points: Stöpsel (not “Stopfel”), Löchlein , zu lit. b. muss lutirt werden , arbeitet , and the open sign after “No. M. ist ein gläserner”, which the published text passes over. Rieber’s list has gaps and some misreadings. He gives “rotiere das Glass noch unten” for lutire das Glas No. S. unten (p. 60) and “noch” for the cipher No. (pp. 25, 60). He gives “nachtnach” for nach und nach and “einige raschen” for einige sta-cken (p. 75). The p. 75 word is still doubtful. Rieber does not have the second passage on p. 47 ( nach und nach ), the third on p. 53, the one on p. 56 ( durch den Salpeter ), or seine centralische Strahlen … auf die Materie werffe on p. 76.

The Yale Digital Collections site blocks scripted requests, so the manifest was opened in a browser and the 69 images were then fetched from the IIIF server. Contact sheets of every opening located the cipher: p. 24 and pp. 25–76. No page before 24 or after 76 has cipher, except the key on p. 83. Pages 84–87 give a cabbalistic letter-number table in clear. Each passage was cut from the full-resolution image, transcribed sign by sign and decrypted with the p. 83 key. The transcription is kept as key values with ligature signs bracketed, and a short script maps it back to signs and counts it: 1,545 signs, 345 words, two open.

Open (2 signs). p. 24, No. M.: one sign after “ein gläserner” that is not in the key, probably a pictogram of the vessel. p. 54: the word after “ein wenig dig” runs into the gutter, probably digerirende (Hitze). Yale’s image is the only one available. Doubtful (C). p. 24 “steig der Spiritus” (or steigen ); p. 24 “No. K. ist d gläserne” (one sign, perhaps short for die ); p. 53 “nach K.” (a clear capital after the cipher; sense unclear); p. 75 “einige sta-cken zu enden”, decrypted letter by letter but obscure. “Renien” (p. 24, No. S.) decrypts cleanly but is an obscure word. On p. 60 the cipher has “lutire das Glas No. S.”, but the glass to be luted is P on p. 24 and on p. 61. The copyist probably slipped, or the S is an unusual P; the decipherment keeps the S. Everything else is H: decrypted sign by sign with the book’s key, gives sense, and consistent with the clear text and the plates.

BnF Espagnol 144 f. 22, an unsigned Spanish instruction for the Fronde plot, enciphered in the numbers 2–34 in runs inside clear text. NoAutopilot (GitHub issue 16) recovered the key from the ciphertext alone; here the transcription was checked on the images and corrected in eight places (four “codes” are digit pairs), and the name sign and the Elector of Brandenburg’s chamberlain were identified from the clear instructions on the leaves before. 98.5% of 529 tokens read. 34 28 10 32 16 29 6 · 7 34 6 · 5 34 30 6 a l a n d o s e · e s t a s · a r m a s Barneton → the abbé (baron) de Mercy · homophonic digits in clear Spanish · 6 June 1648 · key recovered ciphertext-only Archduke Leopold Wilhelm’s instruction to the abbé de Mercy, 6 June 1648 from Archduke Leopold Wilhelm Go to the full text ↓ An unsigned copy at the BnF of a Spanish instruction for the Fronde plot, enciphered in the numbers 2–34; an outside contributor broke it, and here it is checked against the images and 98.5% of it reads. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 1 October 2026 · updated 23 October 2026 Method: key recovered from ciphertext-only · Extent: partial (98% of the cipher) With NoAutopilot (new cipher with solution) ciphertext-only At a glance Ciphertext-only break · partial (98% of the cipher) The letter Archduke Leopold Wilhelm, governor of the Spanish Netherlands, to his chaplain Mercy, from the camp at Barneton, 6 June 1648: whom to see, what to ask the Elector of Brandenburg, and how fast. Where Bibliothèque nationale de France, Espagnol 144 (formerly Supplément français 1257C, tome III) f. 22r–v, finding-aid item 11, “Autre instruction chiffrée pour l’abbé de Mercy”. Not in the catalogue and not on DECODE; it reached us as GitHub issue 16. The cipher Letter by letter in the numbers 2–34, one to three numbers for each letter, no word division, in runs inside the clear Spanish; one extra sign (a square with a dot) for a name. How it was deciphered NoAutopilot (cipher-lab) recovered the key by annealing on Spanish n-grams, with no plaintext. Here the transcription was checked on the images and corrected in eight places, and the name sign and a named official were identified from the clear instructions on the two leaves before. What it says Get a categorical answer from the duchesse de Chevreuse and have Saint-Ibal come back with Mercy; then go to Cleves and ask the Elector of Brandenburg and his chief chamberlain whether 3,000 infantry can be raised in his lands, in two or three regiments, and by whom. Still open Eight tokens in the middle of the verso (code 15 twice, “t non”), and the letters lost where the right edge of f. 22v is trimmed. Credit The transcription, the key and the reading of the cipher runs are NoAutopilot’s ( issue 16 , cipher-lab ); the corrections and the identifications on this page are ours. f. 22r, lines 6–9. Runs of numbers stand between clear lines. The small square with a dot is the name sign, twice: “y del [Santibal] y porque qualquiera ora de tardança”, and “que el [Santibal] uenga con uos para que nos informe della”. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, Espagnol 144 f. 22r, via Gallica (btv1b10035717h).

Item 11 of Espagnol 144 is the last of a small series for the abbé (baron) de Mercy, the Archduke’s chaplain and agent in the intrigue between the Spanish Netherlands and the French malcontents of the early Fronde. Item 8 is a French memoir of September 1647 on his journey to Holland with the comte de Saint-Ibal and the duchesse de Chevreuse; items 9 and 10 are two instructions in clear Spanish, of 8 February and 13 April 1648, written for him from Brussels. The third, the one in cipher, is dated “Barneton a seis de Junio de 1648”, from the field, the summer the Archduke took the army out. The two clear instructions matter here, because they name the same people in clear. On f. 20r (8 February, signed “Leopoldo Guillermo” and by his secretary Juan de Galarreta) Mercy is to meet the duc de Longueville on his way home from Münster, where “el Conde de S. Ibal” may come with him. On f. 21r (13 April), for the journey to Kerpen to meet “la Duquessa de Cheurossa y el Conde de Sant Ibal”, the Archduke writes the sentence that settles the first open question of the cipher: f. 21r, 13 April 1648: “Despues de oydo a la Duquessa con Santibal, desearia si fuese possible que este viniese con Vos incognito (si pareciere) para que me hiciese relacion de las noticias que hubieren traydo las personas que despacho a Francia”. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, Espagnol 144 f. 21r, via Gallica (btv1b10035717h). That is the sentence the cipher repeats seven weeks later: “que el [box] uenga con uos para que nos informe della”.

The numbers run from 2 to 34 and each is a letter; the same letter has up to three numbers, and the vowels a, e, i, o, u have three each: a b c d e f g h i l m n o p q r s t u y 10 17 34 12 14 16 18 19 33 20 22 24 21 26 31 28 30 32 2 23 29 3 4 9 5 6 7 8 25 27 13 There is no letter for j, k, ñ, v, w, x or z (u is written for v), doubled letters are written twice, and the runs have no word division. One extra sign, a square with a dot, stands for a name. The Spanish clerk, as on the clear leaves, wrote “Cheureuse” for Chevreuse and “Cleues” for Cleves, and spelled them out letter by letter. The table above is NoAutopilot’s, recovered from the numbers alone; every value reads in Spanish in the text below, and the common ones (18, 5, 32, 6, 10) are the commonest numbers in the leaf.

The 522 tokens of the contributor’s transcription were compared with the full-resolution Gallica images line by line, with crops at native resolution for every doubtful glyph. They agree except in eight places: Where They had The image Reading f. 22r line 24 65 6 5, touching t re s r egimientos: s, r f. 22r line 17 52 5 2 came r o : r, o f. 22r lines 17, 20 48 4 8 para qu ien se os embian; qu e si se permitira f. 22r line 16 72 7 2 burgs to rf: t, o f. 22r lines 18, 24 26 2 6 se os embian; regimient os y f. 22v line 1 19 an open 14 y al c amarero The key has values 2 to 34 only, and 2 to 9 are single digits, so a token above 34 can only be two digits written together. The contributor’s four “uncertain codes” (48, 52, 65, 72) are therefore not codes at all, and with them the number of tokens goes from 522 to 529. 26 stays a letter, i, where it reads ( propondreis , pais , permitira , que si se ). The contributor had already seen five more places where a 14 with an open 4 looks like 19, and settled them by sense; the image supports each. Two more tokens are re-cut by sense and graded M: in line 10 a tight 25 as 2 5, and a 2 and an 8 that stand apart as one 28, which turn “infume de oulay” into “informe della y”. Every line of f. 22v is also cut at the right edge, by about four or five digits; the clear lines are cut too (“no con[venga]”, “encargar p[ara]”). Where the loss falls inside a word, the sense restores it ( camare[ro] , encarga[r s]e , por su [ma]no , pag[an]dola , cons[ig]uiese , tener [tan]ta gente ); these 18 letters are marked and not counted as read.

Spanish as the clerk wrote it, the cipher in bold, brackets for letters lost at the edge or supplied: Baron de Mercy mi Sumiller de Cortina deseo tener Resolucion de la negociacion que fuisteis por lo que conviene saver lo que se puede esperar della Respeto de las operaciones que se deven saver: 24. (H)alandose estas armas en campagna y asi Holgare me digais lo que en esta razon saueis entendido de la duquesa de Cheureuse y del [Santibal] , y porque qualquiera ora de tardança en la coyuntura presente es de summo perjuicio procuraveis sacar Respuesta Cathegorica en la materia. Y que el [Santibal] uenga con uos para que nos informe della y sepamos Con fundamento lo que nos podemos prometer y Caso de no estar en estado y que es necesario esperar algun tiempo para poder dezir determinadamente el que tiene esta negociacion y lo que se puede confiar della, pasareis a Cleues a veros con el elector de Brandenburg y con Conrad von Burgstorf su camarero mayor para quien se os embian cartas de creencia que uan con esta y les propondreis que si se permitira se leuanten en aquel pais tres mil hombres de infanteria en dos o tres regimientos y con que condiciones y al camarero mayor si querra encargarse della y que corra por su mano no la dire?t non y si i u? a sera mas conuenient[e …]ar otra tanta gente de […] que a leuantada pag[an]dola y en su lugar leua[nt]ar otra. Y Caso que le paresca que esta materia no convenga Corra por su mano le preguntareis a que persona se podria encargar para que se pudiese caminar en ello sin perder tiempo, y se cons[ig]uiese el fruto de tener [tan]ta gente . En todo os encargo la brevedad porque qualquiera dilacion que aya es summamente danosa y de nuestro zelo fio aten… a ello con el Cuydado que Conviene vos encargo. Barneton a seis Junio de 1648. In English: Baron de Mercy, my chaplain: I want a decision on the negotiation you went on, because it is important to know what can be expected of it concerning the operations … The armies being in the field, I shall be glad if you tell me what you have understood on this matter of the Duchess of Chevreuse and of Saint-Ibal; and because any hour of delay at this juncture is most harmful, get a categorical answer on the subject, and have Saint-Ibal come with you, so that he may inform us of it and we may know firmly what we can promise ourselves; and if it is not ready and one must wait some time before saying what this negotiation holds and what can be trusted of it, go to Cleves to see the Elector of Brandenburg and Konrad von Burgsdorff, his chief chamberlain, for whom letters of credence go with this, and put to them whether it will be allowed to raise in that country three thousand foot in two or three regiments, and on what conditions, and whether the chief chamberlain will take charge of it and have it run through his hands … [if it is more convenient to … as many people again as he has raised, paying them, and raise others in their place]. And if it seems to him that this matter does not suit, ask him to whom it could be entrusted, so that one can go ahead without losing time, and the fruit of having so many people be got. In everything I charge you with haste, because any delay is most harmful, and I trust in your zeal that you will see to it with the care it needs. Barneton, 6 June 1648. The substance matches the one printed source that the contributor found: Lonchay, Cuvelier and Lefèvre, Correspondance de la Cour d’Espagne IV no. 183 (1933) calendars the Archduke’s dispatch to Philip IV of June 1648 as reporting that someone had been asked to ask the Elector of Brandenburg whether 3,000 infantry could be raised in his states for a corps to operate in Flanders. The text of the instruction itself is in neither.

The box. A square with a dot occurs twice, both times after “el”, in the sentence that Mercy is to bring “the [box]” back with him; the clear instruction of 13 April asks exactly that of Santibal. The sign is the comte de Saint-Ibal , the duchess’s partner in the plot (item 8 of the volume is the memoir of the journey “entre luy, le comte St Ibal et Madame la duchesse de Chevreuse”). Grade C, adjacent plaintext. The duc de Longueville, the subject of f. 20r, is not named in this instruction. The chamberlain. After “el elector de Brandenburg y con” the cipher gives copurad lon burgsto rf su cmarero mayor (with 5 2 read as r o). That is Konrad von Burgsdorff (1595–1652), Oberkammerherr, “camarero mayor”, of Elector Friedrich Wilhelm from 1642 and his closest adviser: burgstorf is exact but for d written t, rad and on are exact, the part before is two letters off ( copu for con , l for v ), and the writer drops an a in cmarero . The same title comes back at the top of the verso, “y al camare[ro] mayor si querra encargarse della”. Grade I.

The middle of the verso, “no la dire?t non y si i u?” (line 4, eight tokens): code 15 occurs twice and has no value; a Spanish word model finds “no la direct- … y si una sera mas conveniente” at best, by moving two glyphs, which is not accepted. At two line ends on the verso (“conuenient[e ?]ar otra”, “gente de [?] que a leuantada”) two to three letters are lost with the edge and cannot be restored. 27 tokens are graded M: the 14 for 19 glyphs, the re-cut tokens, and the first two letters of “co p u r a d” in the chamberlain’s name ( copu for con ). The name sign is grade C; the other 498 are I, from the ciphertext-only key. “Saint-Malo” and “Péronne” for the governors on f. 21r are guesses, and do not touch the reading.

And because any hour of delay in the present juncture is of the greatest harm, you should try to obtain a categorical answer on the matter, ⟨and that [_] come with you so that he may [?inform us of it] and we may know⟩ on good grounds what we can promise ourselves. And in case it is not ready, and it is necessary to wait some time to be able to say definitely what footing this negotiation has and how far it can be trusted, ⟨you will go on to [?Cleves] to see the Elector of Brandenburg and [?Konrad von Burgsdorff], his [?chief chamberlain], [?for whom] letters of credence are [?sent] you, which go with this, and you will propose to them [?whether] it would be permitted that three thousand men of infantry be raised in that country, in two or three [?regiments], and on what conditions; and to the [?chief chamberlain] whether he will be willing [?to take charge of it] and have it go through his [?] no the [?dirent non] and if [?iun] a will be more fitting [?] as many people again of [?] that has raised, pay [?] it, and in its place rai [?] another⟩; and in case it seems to him that this matter should not go through his hand, you will ask him to what person it could be entrusted, [so that] one could proceed in it without losing time ⟨and [?obtain] the fruit of having [?so much] people⟩. In everything I charge you with speed, because any delay there may be is extremely harmful; and from your zeal I trust [you will] atten… …to it with the care that is fitting. I charge you. Where Biblioteca Nacional de España, MSS/20213/12 (BNE Digital “Carta 9”). On DECODE as R1191, filed without an author. The cipher A homophonic substitution of Spanish letters, with a few code groups. Method A pencil note points to volume XXIV of the Colección de documentos inéditos (1854), which prints the secretariat’s decipherment. The 442 signs were transcribed and aligned with the print; the key recovered from that alignment decrypts the one gap. What it says The gap: Bourbon, through Monsieur de la Mota, asked Moncada que le lleuase a España , to carry him to Spain in the galleys. Everywhere else the print agrees with the cipher. Still open Three short code groups that the print does not give, and two signs at the end of a line. Credit Tomokiyo’s Cryptiana (June 2026) noted the pencil note but could not find the decipherment; the 1854 print is its source. Cipher lines 1–4. Line 2 ends with the credence the 1854 print leaves out: after es que , the signs read me rogaua que le lleuase a España ; line 3 continues diziendome muchas razones para ello. Yo le he … Image: Biblioteca Nacional de España, MSS/20213/12 f. 1r, via DECODE R1191.

One leaf. The recto carries the letter, with about seventeen lines in which cipher runs alternate with clear Spanish; the verso carries the close in clear and the signature Don Hugo de Moncada . The folio stamp reads “20213/12-9” and a later hand has written “Monago 6 octubre 1524” at the head. Moncada was then captain-general of the galleys, at Monaco with the fleet that had supported Bourbon’s siege of Marseille; he became viceroy of Naples only in 1527. The catalogue’s “from the viceroy of Naples” followed Tomokiyo’s gloss. DECODE has the letter as R1191, “NLS_MSS_20213_12”, dated 1524, with no sender or receiver, symbol set “Graphic signs” and status “Decrypted”, though no decipherment is attached. The BNE Digital viewer sits behind a Cloudflare check that a script cannot pass; the DECODE images (970 × 1395 px) were used. The pencil note beside cipher lines 3–5: “Descifrada en t.° 24 Col. Doc. inéd.” Image: Biblioteca Nacional de España, MSS/20213/12 f. 1r, via DECODE R1191. The 1854 editors printed the letter under the heading “Carta de D. Hugo de Moncada á Carlos V, avisándole que el ejército había llegado á Niza… Monago 6 de octubre de 1524”, from the original then in the Salazar collection (“Salazar, C. V., 1524, p. 3”). Before the cipher passage they note that it “sigue en cifra, y descifrado después de letra de la secretaría de Carlos V”, on a following leaf headed CLARO , and they mark its end “Hasta aquí la cifra”. That leaf is no longer with the letter at the BNE.

Each cipher run was transcribed sign by sign from the image, deskewed and enlarged three to eight times: 442 signs in seventeen runs, 54 distinct sign forms. Each run was then aligned with the printed text by an EM aligner that lets a sign stand for a letter, two letters or nothing, and lets the encipherer skip a letter; the result was checked by hand. It is a homophonic substitution of Spanish letters: e is written with the angle ∟ (44 times) or an upright 8 (17); a with ɼ, ƶ, 9 or A; n with ꝑ or β; s with δ, -σ or ʃ‡; t with = or ∥; u/v with ʒ. There are no syllable signs. A double cross written after a base sign makes a different sign: ʃ is q (in ʃʒ∟ que ), ʃ‡ is s or z ; ƶ is a , ƶ‡ is i or y . A few code groups are written in Latin letters: lay = yo (twice), ne = duque in “el duque de Genoua”. The full table, with counts and proof words, is KEY.md . Moncada’s key is not the one Lope de Soria used at Genoa in 1523–24 (three-letter code groups), nor any of Kolosova’s.

The cipher runs are in bold; cleartext is roman. The text follows the 1854 print except the marked passage, which the print left as dots and which was decrypted with the recovered key. Spelling is the letter’s. Mossior de la Mota me es venido esta noche, que es tres oras de noche, con vna letra de crehenna, la qual sera con esta, del ‹=D·› duque de Borbon ; la crehenna es que ‹P‡D› me rogaua que le lleuase a España, diziendome muchas razones para ello. Yo le he respondido que vna vez ponga el exercito de V. Md. en seguro, y que estas galeras no tienen pan para dos dias, como lo tengo escrito a V. Md., y es forçado yr a Genoua a vituallarlas, y que despues de vitualladas se ha de veer si el duque de Genoua querra dexar yr las galeras, y el visorey de Napoles las de aquel reyno, que solo quedan las de España mal en orden; y que en caso que su persona ouiese de yr, que querria que fuese fuerte , lo que siendo en Genoua yo sere con el, y que alli se entendera mas largamente sobre esto. Yo deterne esta yda por no saber en que V. Md. sera mas seruido. V. Mag. con presteza enbie a mandar lo que se ha de hazer por el. Tornando a este negocio viene muy mal contento , segun el dicho mossior de la Mota me ha significado ‹=P‡D·f›. Translation. Monsieur de la Mota came to me tonight, at three hours of night, with a letter of credence, which goes with this, from the Duke of Bourbon. The credence is that he asked me to carry him to Spain , giving me many reasons for it. I answered that once he puts Your Majesty’s army in safety — and these galleys have no bread for two days, as I have written to Your Majesty, and must go to Genoa to be victualled, and after that it remains to be seen whether the Duke of Genoa will let his galleys go, and the viceroy of Naples those of that kingdom, since only the Spanish ones are left, in poor order — if his person is to go, I would want it to go in strength; when he is at Genoa I will be with him, and there we will discuss it at more length. I will hold back this voyage, not knowing how Your Majesty will be best served. May Your Majesty quickly send orders what is to be done for him. He comes back from this business very discontented, as the said Monsieur de la Mota has told me. The clear parts of the letter, before and after, report that the imperial army reached Nice on 6 October, having crossed the mountain by the Genoese riviera with its artillery broken up and carried on mules; that the brigantine carrying Bourbon’s man was taken by the French at Toulon; and that Francis I was said to be at Saint-Maximin. The full text is in reading.txt . The gap is the only content missing from the 1854 print. After the failure before Marseille, Bourbon wanted to go to Spain, to the Emperor, in Moncada’s galleys, and Moncada stalled for want of bread and orders. Cipher lines 13–17, from largamente sobre esto to de la Mota me ha significado and the code group =P‡D·f , which has no value. Image: Biblioteca Nacional de España, MSS/20213/12 f. 1r, via DECODE R1191.

Three code groups , 12 signs, each once: =D· after “del” and before the ciphered “duque de Borbon”, P‡D opening the credence, and =P‡D·f after “me ha significado”. The print has no counterpart for them; they are titles or names (the Duke, the Emperor), but nothing in the letter fixes which. Graded I. Re-examined 30 Sept 2026: two of them share the element P‡D and all three contain D ; P‡D stands where the subject of me rogaua would be (the Duke of Bourbon, I), but none of the three is in the key or recurs, so they stay unread. 99 at the end of cipher line 2, set apart at the margin between a España and diziendome . Re-examined on the image (30 Sept 2026): the sentence is complete without them ( que le lleuase a España, diziendome muchas razones ), a a makes no Spanish there, and the two signs stand apart at the right edge after the last letter of España , so they are read as line-end nulls and left out of the text above. Graded M. Readings graded C rather than H because the scan is small: diziendome (the second sign, ʒ, is u everywhere else), para ello (six signs for eight letters) and galeras in line 8 (five signs). Measured on the transcription: 428 of 442 cipher signs have a value (96.8%).

Despues de auer escrito la de 5 del presente y no auer hecho tiempo al bergantin para se partir, es llegado el campo de V. Md. a Nica oy, que son seys del dicho mes, de donde me escriuen que pasara la montaña por la ribera de Genoua el otro dia siguiente sin auer auido ningun ympedimiento. La artilleria que trayan la hizieron pedaços y la traen encima de azemilas. El rey de Francia dize que ha estado en Sant Maxemin, pero no se sabe de cierto. El bergantin que venia en compañia del que se tomo por franceses, en el qual venia el del duque de Borbon, que no se hallaua, aporto en Tolon pensando que estaua por V. Md., de manera que amos a dos han aportado en manos de franceses; y asi me ha sido referido. Mossior de la Mota me es venido esta noche, que es tres oras de noche, con vna letra de crehenna, la qual sera con esta, del <=D.> {duque de Borbon}; la crehenna es que <P#D> {me rogaua que le lleuase a España [here], <99 = line-end nulls, 30 Sept 2026> diziendome [here] muchas razones para ello. Md., y es forçado yr a Genoua a vituallarlas, y que despues de vitualladas se ha de veer {si el duque de Genoua querra dexar yr las galeras, y el visorey de Napoles las de aquel reyno, que solo quedan las de España mal en orden; y que en caso que su persona ouiese de yr, que querria que fuese fuerte}, lo que siendo en Genoua {yo sere con el, y que alli} se entendera mas {largamente sobre esto. After having written that of the 5th of this month, and the weather not having served for the brigantine to leave, Your Majesty's army has arrived at Nice today, which is the sixth of the said month, from where they write to me that it passed the mountain by the Riviera of Genoa the following day without having had any hindrance. The artillery they were bringing they broke into pieces and are carrying on the backs of mules. The King of France is said to have been at Saint-Maximin, but it is not known for certain. The brigantine which was coming in company with the one taken by the French, in which the Duke of Bourbon's [man] was coming, who could not be found, put in at Toulon thinking it was held for Your Majesty, so that both of them have fallen into the hands of the French; and so it has been reported to me. Monsieur de La Motte came to me tonight, at three hours of the night, with a letter of credence, which will be with this, from the <=D.> {Duke of Bourbon}; the credence is that <P#D> {he begged me to carry him to Spain [here], <99> giving me [here] many reasons for it. I have answered him that, once he puts Your Majesty's army in safety, and that these galleys have no bread} for two days, as I have written to Your Majesty, and it is necessary to go to Genoa to victual them, and that after they are victualled it must be seen {whether the Duke of Genoa will be willing to let the galleys go, and the Viceroy of Naples those of that kingdom, for only those of Spain remain, in bad order; and that, in case his person had to go, I would want it to be strong}; which being at Genoa, {I shall be with him, and there} it will be dealt with more {at length. I shall hold back this journey because I do not know} in what Your Majesty will be best served. Let Your Majesty send orders with speed of what is to be done {for him. Turning to this business, he is coming very ill content}, as the said {Monsieur de La Motte} has given me to understand <=P#D.f>. The weather being good for the brigantine to leave, I have not waited for letters from the Duke of Bourbon or the Marquis of Pescara, since their men who stay here have not been willing to go with him. Sacred Caesarean Catholic Majesty, may God our Lord keep and exalt Your Majesty's royal person and estate for very long times, as Your Majesty desires. From Monaco, 6 October 1524. Of Your Sacred Caesarean Catholic Majesty the slave and servant who kisses your royal feet and hands, Don Hugo de Moncada Key: KEY.md

Three cipher letters and a postscript of Willem Lodewijk of Nassau, stadtholder of Friesland, to his brother Johann VII on the defence of the Palatinate, in a nine-cell shape grid whose key sits in the family key book. Brice Dudout transcribed and read them: 96.4% of 1,388 cipher words, the nomenclator signs still open. D. U:? N D. F F. J:? C: L: J N. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 5 November 2026 Method: read with known key · Extent: partial (96% of the cipher) · On the map Contributed by Brice Dudout (solution) · Also credited · Daniel Bourdeau (pointer to a source) known key At a glance Known key applied · partial (96% of the cipher) The letters Three letters (1, 3 and 5) and a postscript from Willem Lodewijk of Nassau, stadtholder of Friesland, to his brother Johann VII of Nassau-Siegen, February to May 1620. The dates are in cipher and not broken. Where Hessisches Hauptstaatsarchiv Wiesbaden, Abt. 171 Nr. S 995, fols. 20r–21v, 41r–41v, 44r–44v (cipher part) and 53r. Not on DECODE. The cipher A letter is the shape of its cell in a 3×3 grid, with no, one or two dots; capitals and symbols stand for names. The grid is written in the family key book, Abt. 171 Nr. C 667, image 55. How it was deciphered The upper grid of the key book was frozen, then tested on eleven cipher words of the file that carry a contemporary gloss: 0.860 against 0.185 for the other grid and at best 0.442 for 20 permuted grids. Each page was transcribed sign by sign before decoding. What it says Johann is thinking of giving up his command. Willem Lodewijk urges him to keep it, or if age weighs on him to withdraw as an “emeritus miles” as he does himself, and answers Johann’s plan for defending the Lower Palatinate. Still open The nomenclator signs (names of persons and rivers), the ciphered dates, the end of the postscript, and 25 unresolved words. Credit Brice Dudout (Europe chiffrée) transcribed and read the letters, working with Claude Opus 5.5 agents. The entry comes from Daniel Bourdeau’s Archivportal-D sweep (catalogue no. 566).

In the spring of 1620 the Bohemian war was spreading into the Empire. Spinola was gathering in the Netherlands the army that would invade the Palatinate at the end of the summer, and the Protestant Union was preparing its defence. Willem Lodewijk of Nassau (1560–1620) wrote from Leeuwarden to his brother Johann VII of Nassau-Siegen (1561–1623), the theorist of defence by militia, who had been commissioned to defend the Palatinate. Willem Lodewijk died at the end of May 1620. The four pieces are almost wholly in cipher. A neighbouring letter in the same channel (fols. 22r–23v) has “1620” in clear and answers a letter of Johann of 23 February, which dates the group to February–May. The signature is in clear: “E. L. trewer bruder Wilhelm Ludwig graff zu Nassaw”. Two letters of the file (fols. 22–23 and 42–43) are in clear and not part of this reading.

The cover of the file says “Die Schlüssel sind zu C. 667 gelegt”. Image 55 of C 667 holds two 3×3 grids, a worked example dated 1620 and the nomenclator. The upper grid (AKT·BLV·CMW / DNX·EOY·FPZ / GQ·HR·IS) reads the 1620 letters; the lower one reads the letters of 1606 and 1609. The key was therefore not reconstructed here, and it is not claimed. The grid was frozen by SHA-256 and tested before any letter was decoded, on eleven cipher words of fols. 25 and 29 that carry a contemporary gloss (“vnion”, “werbung”, “monatlich”, “künfftig”, “feindt”…). Mean agreement was 0.860, against 0.185 for the second grid and at best 0.442 for 20 permuted grids. Each transcription was frozen before decoding as well, so the key was never adjusted to a reading.

The reading is counted by script on the published text, with the statuses certain, probable, restored and unresolved. All four pieces together come to 1,388 cipher words: 1,184 certain, 154 probable, 25 restored and 25 unresolved, which is 96.4% certain or probable and 98.2% with the restored words. Letters 1 and 5 and the postscript pass the 95% bar; letter 3 does not without its restored words (92.6%), so by the repository’s rule the group counts as partial. Willem Lodewijk writes “[A] and I” for himself and a person left unresolved. In letter 1 he calls a plan for the command of the relief forces “nicht practicabel vnd gantz immature”. Letter 3 answers Johann’s defence plan for the Lower [Q], very probably the Lower Palatinate: militia plus a regular corps, muster by Circles rather than one assembly of the Union, no invasion towards the Weser expected that year, provisions first. Letter 5 hopes Johann will continue in his charge and finds it dangerous to write such things “ohne chifer”. The postscript concerns officers’ pay fixed by the late Elector and table money in the field. The German text and an English translation of each piece are under Full texts.

The nomenclator capitals and symbols are printed as they stand, without a conjecture. From the sense only: [A] and [B] are persons or authorities, [Q] is feminine and very probably the Lower Palatinate, [O] and [⊙] look like rivers. The list of capitals in C 667 (images 20–54) has not been seen. The dates are in cipher with number signs that are not resolved; the dating rests on context and on the neighbouring letter dated in clear. The transcription of letter 5 does not record word spaces; the division was made from the sense. Letter 1, fol. 21v, lines 23–24, were not redone at high magnification. The last line of the postscript runs to the edge of the leaf and its continuation has not been seen. Most probable words come from a dot misread in the transcription. For letter 3 a blind re-reading of 22 shapes confirmed 21; the other pieces had none. Prior work: a pencil slip on fol. 1, in an unknown modern hand, gives a partial alphabet and no decoded word. No edition of these letters was found (Groen van Prinsterer, Briefe und Akten, the finding aids). Three studies were not seen: Wolf 1937, Paul 1966 and Hahlweg 1973. If one of them holds an earlier reading it will be credited here. The scans were used for research only and are not reproduced.

[A] and I have read Your Dilection’s letter with care and attention and weighed it thoroughly, [to see] what we might best advise you in such weighty matters. We hold, first, that no one is fitter or more capable for this service than Your Dilection, since you understand the work of territorial defence (Landrettungswerk) thoroughly, have put it into practice for many years in a praiseworthy and most profitable way, and know better than anyone the state of the country and the temper of the whole levy (Auszug) and of the other levies, on which the preservation of the Lower [Q] will partly depend; without your presence, direction and government little could be expected, and the common good, and the [B] above all, might suffer irreparable harm, which could be laid at Your Dilection’s own door, as if in the hour of need you had despaired of the common good and abandoned the [B] for private considerations — which we should be sorry to see. For [A] and I hope that the [B] has not the least thought of taking the general command from Your Dilection in the absence of the [A̅] and the [A·], after declaring you [∇] in your commission themselves; not only in view of equity and of the great difference in experience of war between Your Dilection and the others, who cannot be supposed to be preferred to you, but above all in view of necessity: the [B]’s own service and profit depend in the highest degree on Your Dilection being maintained in the command (“beim commendo maintenirt”). We also think that [A] and [A°], because of their particular interest, since they cannot be assisted by anyone as well as by Your Dilection, for the reasons given, must not be wronged. Therefore [As] and I hold that Your Dilection’s person and presence cannot be done without, without notable harm to the common good, and that the [B] will face the matter and give Your Dilection, for your own profit, a fair satisfaction; in that case we do not doubt that Your Dilection will weigh everything in good conscience and on your side know how to comply for the common good, since the other burdens are such that you can accommodate yourself to them; [As] and I are subject to the like ourselves, but with discretion and patience have overcome much and brought it to the best. Above all, if Your Dilection, in remonstrating your case, has done what the matter required, you cannot fairly be blamed in your person if the lord’s own service suffered and no hand was offered to you, or if it must be laid to the lord himself, who will not give better order, or to impossibility. Yet if, against all expectation, Your Dilection’s [∇] were not granted outright in the absence of the [A] and the [A°], neither [A] nor I could hold it against you that you keep to your resolution and resignation (“vfkündigung”), the more so as it would be not only most belittling for you but impossible to discharge your service properly, and you alone would remain answerable for what had been badly done, had turned out ill and might be another’s fault. If Your Dilection, because of age, from weakness of memory as well as infirmity of body — as I find in myself — felt too weak for so laborious and difficult a work, or noticed that the [B] or other directors of this work had doubts about it, I would advise you to do as I do myself: to count yourself an emeritus miles and withdraw in time from such danger and reproach, from which one must expect far more than thanks or reward, and leave the toil to those who want the thanks all the same. That the [A] will grant Your Dilection no command beyond having the mere watch ordered is signum imperitiae, and in keeping with the custom and capitulation of the old Germans, by which we make ourselves unfit for the service of all lords; yet they had to dispute the like with the Prince of Parma himself; this can be remedied with discretion, and these times will give occasion to correct many things. Your Dilection’s proposal concerning the command over the relief forces of these parts, [A] and I find impracticable and wholly premature (“immature”); and he who will command over the [A] might already be […] of the [Am] himself; they will gladly acknowledge Your Dilection in your charge and obey you. This, from good brotherly intent, as the advice of [As] and myself, I wished to convey to Your Dilection herewith, as quickly as was possible. [A] and I find the proposal that Your Dilection made to the [B] about preparing for war in the Lower [Q] weighty and well founded, and hold it a necessity to rely in part on the country militia (Landvolk), since good foreign troops are hard to get and such costs are more safely spent to the profit of the levy (Auszug). We think, however, that a good corps [M] would be most necessary in so extraordinary an expedition and against the multitude of different nations on the other side; this has been thought of […] from afar. It would also be desirable that, as soon as the enemy begins to assemble, all members of the Union should likewise bring their assistance together in one place; but we hold it impossible to achieve, because no one will let his troops go unless assured that it will not fall on himself, and also because of the great distance between the quarters, and before one knows which course the enemy will take. Things should therefore be arranged so that the Circles hold their muster on their own ground and send one another the help they owe, once it is seen where the enemy is marching. In our opinion no invasion and no march towards the Weser is to be feared this year; so the Lower Saxon and Westphalian Circles will have only the defence of the country [2̲] and the Westerwald to provide for, and can send their help without any suspicion once the enemy has taken his route beyond the [O] or the [⊙]. If, when the enemy has joined at the general rendezvous, one could march against him instead of awaiting him on our own ground, that would be a thing to wish for, and Your Dilection is [master] […]; but whether it can be done will be decided by the state of our own affairs, the difference between our troops and the enemy’s, and other circumstances besides, as they turn out. In any case I think one must above all seek […] how to hamper the enemy most in his provisions, and that provisions can follow our camp conveniently for all its needs, and that this be always almost […]; […] can have; as Your Dilection has also prudently reminded, that provision be made, for a [∇], for the crossing of the [O], the artillery train and its order, the victuals and whatever else the camp needs, so that in the end one is neither taken by surprise nor cut short.
