BnF fr. 3977 no. 96 is a cleartext French digest of League and Spanish letters intercepted in September and October 1589; the ciphered letters are not in the volume, so the item has no ciphertext. The same volume holds eleven other intercepted ciphered letters of 1589, each with its contemporary decipherment between the lines. They are located, not yet transcribed. 83 b2b9b792 43 b0399932 b11792 96 b7 138 45592 b2505797 b0925592 the decipherer’s words, written above the figures: de Mendoza · a los xv de Abril intercepted League and Spanish letters → the duc de Nevers · cleartext digest · September–October 1589 Intercepted letters summarised for Nevers, 1589 to Duke of Nevers BnF Français 3977 no. 96 · a digest of “plusieurs lettres escriptes en chiffre par les ennemis du Roy” , sent to Nevers “pour estre interpretées” · catalogued with the ciphertext’s survival unknown The summary is in clear French and the ciphered letters it describes are not in the volume, so there is nothing to decipher under no. 96. Eleven other intercepted ciphered letters in the volume carry their 1589 decipherments between the lines. Arya Sanketbhai Patel · posted 21 September 2026 · updated 26 October 2026 Method: not a cipher Contributed by Arya Sanketbhai Patel (solution) closed At a glance Not a cipher The document A Recueil sommaire : a digest in fifteen numbered points, in clear French, of the principal points of letters the King’s enemies wrote in cipher in September and October 1589, sent to the duc de Nevers to be interpreted. Where BnF fr. 3977 f. 318r–319r (canvas 520), no. 96. The catalogue (item 31) did not know whether any ciphertext survives. How it was tried The sweep checked fr. 3977 around no. 96: every piece dated September or October 1589 is in cleartext, so the ciphered originals are not in the volume. What it says Mercoeur asks Spain for help; powder and money reach Nantes via Diego Maldonado “avec le chiffre général d’Espagne”; Mendoza at Bayonne writes on Arques and Dieppe. What was added Points 1–9 are transcribed. The sweep also located eleven other intercepted ciphered letters in the volume, February to August 1589, each with a contemporary decipherment above the cipher; they are not transcribed.

The catalogue entry states what it does not know: “Only the ‘Recueil sommaire’ of the interpreted letters is described; whether the intercepts survive in the volume is unknown” , scored “unknown whether there is any ciphertext to attack” , with the instruction “sweep fr. 3977 around no. 96 for cipher leaves” . The task is to settle whether any ciphertext exists. BnF fr. 3977 is btv1b9060546p , 715 canvases, a volume of the Collection Mémoires de la Ligue . Its catalogue notice carries a piece-by-piece dépouillement : 138 pieces, nos. 2–143, folios 3–423. Canvas labels are all NP , and the folio offset drifts: f. 125 is canvas 229, f. 318 is canvas 520.

Folio 318 is canvas 520. The piece is headed, in a large chancery hand: Recueil sommaire des principaux poincts contenuz en plusieurs lettres escriptes en chiffre par les ennemis du Roy — En Septembre et Octobre 1589 — et envoyées à S.A. pour estre interpretées en decembre aud. an. fr. 3977 f. 318 (canvas 520): the digest and its first points. It is in clear French throughout; the ciphered letters it summarises are not in the volume. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3977 f. 318, via Gallica (btv1b9060546p, canvas 520). It is in clear French , a digest in fifteen numbered points running fol. 318r–319r. The first nine: The duc de Mercœur has asked Spain for help; the King of Spain has sent powder and money by Diego Maldonado , despatched to Nantes “avec le chiffre g[e]n[er]al d’Espagne” , who arrived on 18 October 1589. Mendoza has lent the Prévôt des marchands a sum, to his master’s satisfaction; the Prévôt has since repaid it, and Mendoza is cautioned against gratifying him too promptly “à cause des envieux et calumniateurs” . The sieur de Mauléon is aggrieved at not being employed by Spain; Mendoza renews the signal agreed with him, “par tant la lettre escripte du chiffre qu’ilz ont ensemble” . The master of the posts of Bordeaux passes Spain’s advices, and what Matignon orders him for the King’s service. Villeroy has complained to Mendoza that the help the League expected never came. Mendoza writes repeatedly from Bayonne on what passed at Arques and Dieppe , “jusques a dementir les advis et les memoires du Roy” ; the sornettes Madame de Montpensier tells him; and the King reproves him for not reporting particularly enough on the Cardinal de Bourbon , the duc de Guise , d’Elbeuf and the archevêque de Lyon . The commandeur de Diou presses his suit at Rome, and what the consistory means to allow him. The King of Spain presses the Pope , and has his adherents press him, to renew the excommunication against subjects who obey the King. Spain resolves to maintain the war in France , to continue the Leaguers’ agreed annual payments and to have them paid in full; Parma to send his forces into France; Moro , captain of light horse; Balagny . fol. 318v, points 7–9: the commandeur de Diou at Rome, Spain pressing the Pope to renew the excommunication, and the resolution to maintain the war in France. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3977 f. 318v, via Gallica (btv1b9060546p).

Every piece in fr. 3977 dated September or October 1589 (nos. 81, 84, 85, 89, 90, 91, 92, 94, 95, 96, 97) is in cleartext . None is ciphered. The letters behind the digest were sent to Nevers to be interpreted and are not bound in this volume; what was kept is the interpretation. Catalogue item 31 therefore has no ciphertext , and the item should be scored as answered. The scoring note “unknown whether there is any ciphertext” can be retired.

The same volume holds eleven intercepted ciphered letters, each with a contemporary decipherment . They are working papers of the same royalist deciphering service, three to seven months earlier: piece folio letter no. 29 79 Governor of Milan → Bernardino de Mendoza, Milan, 16 Feb 1589 no. 31 83 P. de Acuña → Mendoza, Turin, 28 Feb 1589 no. 38 115 Governor of Milan → Mendoza, Milan, 4 Mar 1589 no. 39 117 Bernardino de Yssunça → Martin de Yssunça, Brussels, 18 Mar 1589 nos. 43–45 126, 128, 130 three letters, Mendoza → the duke of Parma, April 1589 no. 47 135 news of the duc de Mayenne → Claude Maumarché, for Pierre Letelier, 21 Apr 1589 no. 48 137 a Leaguer to a royalist he is trying to win for the Union, Paris, 21 Apr 1589 no. 49 139 Mendoza → Juan de Moreo, Paris, 21 Apr 1589 no. 71 191 Robert, marquis de La Vieuville → the duc de Nevers, 13 Aug 1589 Three letters in one catalogue entry. The three Mendoza–Parma letters are the longest of the group. The dépouillement files them in a single multi-folio entry, “Fol. 126, 128 et 130 • 43 à 45” , which a search for single entries of the form “Fol. N • M” misses. They are not described as ciphered in any single-folio line, and folio 125 shows no cipher in the catalogue at all. fr. 3977 f. 126 (canvas 229), “Copia de la carta escrita al Duque de Parma por Don Bernardino” : the cipher runs in continuous strings mixing figures and letters, and the French decipherer has written his plaintext word by word above every group . Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3977 f. 126, via Gallica (btv1b9060546p, canvas 229). His decipherment of the opening: El Vizeseneschal de Montelimart, que V.A. conoce … aqui me escriva … un billete de Monsieur de Vienna en su creancia … y lo que por [Ma…] me ha dicho es el yr a dar intelligencia a V.A. de los abisos que tienen del Coronal Fifer … la leva que el haze por los de la Liga, y la que el Rey levanta de los 12.000 que los Cantones hereies le han acordado … puntos en que no me alargare, pues ellos … ha de referir a V.A. These are eleven ciphertexts with their plaintext for Spanish ciphers of 1589, enough to rebuild the keys. They have not yet been used.

Points 10–15 of the digest, on fol. 318v–319r, are not transcribed. None of the eleven deciphered intercepts has been transcribed, and no key has been reconstructed from them. They are located and one is photographed. Rebuilding the keys from them is a separate task, and a feasible one, since each leaf carries its own plaintext. Whether the September–October 1589 originals survive elsewhere , in another Mémoires de la Ligue volume or among the Nevers papers, was not checked. The digest says they were sent to Nevers in December to be interpreted, so they were in his office at some point.

BnF, Département des Manuscrits, Français 3977 , btv1b9060546p , 715 canvases. No. 96 at canvases 520–522 (ff. 318–319); the Mendoza–Parma leaf at canvas 229 (f. 126). BnF archives et manuscrits , Collection Mémoires de la Ligue, notice ark cc504266 (fragment cd0e4184), for the dépouillement that gives piece → folio. Image rights: Bibliothèque nationale de France. Working notes, the parsed piece list and the fetch script are in targets/nevers1589/ .

Where Bibliothèque nationale de France, français 3151 no. 33, ff. 59–60v (Gallica btv1b9059865k, views 60–62); catalogue item 10, with two other letters. BnF fr. 3151 f. 60r (Gallica btv1b9059865k, view 61): Noailles’s two cipher blocks, with the court’s decipherment in the inner margin, partly hidden in the gutter. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3151 f. 60r, via Gallica btv1b9059865k view 61. The letter is in clear (the Levant galleys, Candia, Corfu) with three cipher blocks: two of three lines each on f. 60r, and one of seven lines on f. 60v, which Michael Brackx found (issue #113) and our first notes missed. The court’s decipherment is written beside each block, so the letter was deciphered when it arrived. On f. 60r it stands in the inner margin, and only part of it is legible, because the start of each line runs into the binding: « … mauluaise … e pauur[eté] … [cond]uitte q[u’il] donne a … affaires », « [gr]and seigneur … [entre]prend sur luy et le … de la Tou[ss]aint ». (Our earlier reading of these glosses had « gouvernement », « ne luy » and « de la fortune »; Brackx corrected them.) On f. 60v the gloss stands in the outer margin and is nearly complete.

The hidden start of each gloss line. It needs the volume opened flat, which only the BnF can do. The cipher itself. 262 symbols in three blocks. Michael Brackx reports a key recovered from the glosses and a French language model, with 246 of the 262 symbols given a value; we have asked for his files and have not yet reproduced it. Where the f. 60v gloss is legible over unread groups, it gives cribs for the gaps. The printed edition of Noailles’s embassy (Vertot, 1763) has not been searched.

A one-page cipher letter in French, catalogued on DECODE as homophonic with no decipherment. It is a polyalphabetic cipher of five alphabets changed line by line; the key sheet filed with it (R2235) decrypts the whole letter once the order of the alphabets was found by trial. The writer reports on Salm’s hussars, Barthélemy and the French armies. gasoez ma 12: eoemmav, ea q ye syz hado ga wiz giowammaz → depuis le 12 juillet je n’ai pas reçu de vos nouvelles · D: a→y e→a s→z Basle → William V in exile · polyalphabetic cipher, five alphabets changed line by line · 17 August 1796 An Orangist at Basle writes to the Stadholder, 1796 to William V Go to the full text ↓ Koninklijk Huisarchief, The Hague, Prins Willem V, inv. 339 (DECODE R2234, catalogued as “homophonic” with no decipherment). One page in letters, dated in clear “30 thermidor an 4 de la Rép. franç. / 17 août vieux style”. Decrypted in full with the key sheet R2235 filed in the same inventory number; the order in which its five alphabets are used, one per line, was found by trial. No earlier decipherment was found. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 21 September 2026 · updated 26 October 2026 Method: read with known key · Extent: complete Credits · Contemporary key or decipherment (key or decipherment used) · DECODE database (pointer to a source) known key At a glance Known key applied · complete The letter An unsigned letter from a writer at Basle to William V, in French, under Republican dating; he asks for a reply by 4 September and a bill of 50 louis each quarter. Where DECODE R2234 (listed as homophonic, no decipherment). The pencil note “Tollius” is an archival attribution that was not tested. The cipher Polyalphabetic, with five alphabets D, G, L, N, R that change line by line; a capital in the margin restarts the cycle. DECODE’s “homophonic” label is wrong. How it was read The key is R2235, a printed pair of tables in the same file. Trying all five alphabets on lines 2–5 gave the line-by-line rule, and the whole letter decrypts to French. What it says The Prince of Salm is raising hussars for Prussia on condition they pass to the Prince of Orange; the Prussian ministers are being lulled by the French; the armies of Italy and the Rhine may join. Still open A few words are doubtful because of the transcription, and the clear signature is not made out.

The head of R2234 (rotated): the section capital D, the date in clear, and the first lines. Image: Koninklijk Huisarchief, The Hague, Prins Willem V inv. 339, via DECODE R2234. The key, R2235, has two sheets. The Schrijf Tafel (writing table) gives, for each of D, G, L, N, R, the cipher letter for each of the 25 plain letters a–z without j. The Translateur Tafel is the same five rows as inverses. The rows are built in pairs: D and R undo each other, G and N undo each other, and L is its own inverse, so the second sheet is the first with its labels swapped. DECODE R2235, the Schrijf Tafel : five enciphering alphabets. Image: Koninklijk Huisarchief, The Hague, Prins Willem V inv. 339, via DECODE R2235. The letter uses the key in a way the tables do not state. The first line of the first section decrypts under D (“gasoez ma 12” = “depuis le 12”), but the second line does not. Trying all five alphabets on lines 2 to 5 showed that they decrypt under G, L, N and R, in that order. Each line starts with a dash, and a new capital in the margin (D, G, L, N, R, D, G) restarts the cycle at that alphabet. Word division, figures and punctuation stay in clear. DECODE’s “homophonic” label is wrong. The cipher is polyalphabetic, with five alphabets that change line by line.

The corrected French, one line of the letter to a line; the alphabet of each line is in brackets. […] marks words spoilt by my transcription. [D] Depuis le 12 juillet je n’ai pas reçu de vos nouvelles; quel silence! J’attends [G] sans faute une lettre pour le 4 septembre, […] ou à [L] renoncer ou à reprendre ma maison pour 3 mois, mon bail finissant le 4 octobre. [N] Il me faut aussi vers ce temps-là une nouvelle lettre de change de 50 louis, et cela de 3 en 3 [R] mois, pour subvenir à l’horrible cherté de ce séjour; et j’en suis aux derniers […] [G] […]. Un officier d’état-major venu à Bâle dit qu’il est [L] d’un régiment de hussards que le prince de Salm lève pour le roi de Prusse [N] sous condition de rentrer au service du prince d’Orange quand il retournera en [R] Hollande; c’est une imprudence d’en [parler] ici. Mandez-moi ce qui en est; je me recommanderais [L] pour y en faire autant. Par contre on assure que le prince aura Hambourg(?), le pays […] [N] de […] Osnabruck. Cela est-il vrai? J’ai peur que les ministres prussiens ne se laissent [R] endormir comme à l’ordinaire par les belles paroles des Français, qui n’ont pas le [dessein de] voir [N] autre chose que bien s’ancrer sur les 2 rives du Rhin. […] et Barthélemy [R] ne m’invite plus, depuis que l’on m’a mis, je ne sais pourquoi, dans la gazette de Hambourg du 5 [R] juillet, ou depuis 2 malles prises. Son secrétaire me disait hier que dans un mois on [D] s’attendait à la jonction de l’armée d’Italie à celle du Rhin par le Tyrol; cela ne ressemble [G] pas à la paix. Degelmann n’y croit pas et ne sait rien. [L] Il est venu hier un courrier français d’Italie; rien n’a transpiré: donc [N] mauvaise nouvelle pour eux. Ce qu’on écrit de Bâle de passages de courriers […] [R] d’envoyer des mensonges. Mais s’il y avait un congrès, je ne pourrais y rien faire sans [G] être aperçu. [in clear] Salut et fraternité [signature] In English, in brief. No letter since 12 July; he needs an answer by 4 September on whether to keep his house for three more months, the lease ending on 4 October, and a bill for 50 louis every quarter, Basle being ruinously dear. A staff officer at Basle says he belongs to a hussar regiment the Prince of Salm is raising for the King of Prussia, on condition that it pass into the Prince of Orange’s service when he returns to Holland. It is said that the prince will have Hamburg(?) and the country about Osnabrück. He fears the Prussian ministers will again be lulled by the French, who want only to hold both banks of the Rhine. Barthélemy, the French envoy, no longer invites him since he was named in the Hamburg gazette of 5 July; Barthélemy’s secretary expects the Army of Italy to join the Army of the Rhine through the Tyrol within a month, which does not look like peace; Degelmann, the Imperial envoy, does not believe it. A French courier from Italy has come and nothing has leaked, so the news is bad for the French.

The single DECODE image and the two key sheets were downloaded with the project’s DECODE session. I transcribed the key rows from full-resolution crops and the letter from rotated bands (1,321 cipher letters). A short decoder applies the inverse of each Schrijf row. Only the line cycle had to be found, and it came from four trial decryptions. The raw machine output keeps my transcription slips (n/r/u/v, c/e, i/y); the text above corrects them by sense, and no key value was changed.

End of line 5 and start of line 6 (“aux derniers …”): transcription too corrupt to settle. Line 10–11: the prince’s share, “Hambourg” (M) and the word before Osnabrück (not settled). Line 13: two words before “et Barthélemy” (not settled); “Barthélemy” itself is H (w for b is a slip). Line 19: the verb after “passages de courriers” (not settled); line 20 “aperçu” is C. The signature, in clear, is not made out. The writer is unidentified; the pencil “Tollius” (Herman Tollius, the princes’ former tutor, named in the DECODE note) is an attribution, not tested.

Words in italics are those reading.md marks as deciphered with a bracket in reading.txt; [...] = unread; (?) = doubtful. --> # R2234, an Orangist correspondent at Basle to William V, 17 August 1796: English translation [Basle,] 30 Thermidor, Year 4 of the French Republic (in clear) / 17 August, old style (in clear) Since 12 July I have had no news from you; what a silence! I expect without fail a letter by 4 September, so as *to make up my mind* either to give up or to take my house again for three months, my lease ending on 4 October. Around that time I shall also need a new bill of exchange for 50 louis, and so from three months to three months, to meet the horrible dearness of living here; and I am down to my last ones, [...] [...]. A staff officer who has come to Basle says that he is from a regiment of hussars which the Prince of Salm is raising for the King of Prussia, on condition of returning to the service of the Prince of Orange when he goes back to Holland; it is imprudent to *speak* of it here. Tell me what there is in it; I would put myself forward to do as much there. On the other hand it is asserted that the Prince will have Hamburg(?), the country [...] of [...] Osnabrück. Is this true? I am afraid that the Prussian ministers are letting themselves be lulled, as usual, by the fine words of the French, who have *no intention* of seeing anything other than anchoring themselves firmly on both banks of the Rhine. [...] and Barthélemy no longer invites me, since I was put, I do not know why, into the Hamburg gazette of 5 July, or since two mails were taken. His secretary was telling me yesterday that within a month the junction of the Army of Italy with that of the Rhine through the Tyrol was expected; that does not look like peace. Degelmann does not believe it and knows nothing. A French courier from Italy arrived yesterday; nothing has leaked out: so, bad news for them. What is written from Basle about couriers passing [...] to send lies. But if there were a congress, I could do nothing there without being noticed. Greetings and fraternity (signature, in clear, not read)

A letter-book copy of Burghley’s letter to Walsingham in Paris, clear English with 15 code and cipher tokens. Context and Walsingham’s reply identify code [3] as the French King; no key survives, and the rest is not deciphered. Some that are come home bear us in hand that [3] reneweth the m o R. d A. [4] whereby the last matter ⅋B [5] is hindered Westminster → Paris · name codes in a clear letter · 5 July 1572 Burghley to Walsingham, 5 July 1572 from William Cecil → to Francis Walsingham British Library, Harley MS 260 f. 262 (DECODE R8358), a later copy in Walsingham’s Paris letter-book. DECODE lists it as “William Burleigh to unknown recipient, Jul 1572, short parts encrypted only”. The recipient is Walsingham, ambassador in France. The cipher items were transcribed. One code, [3] = the French King, was identified from context; the rest are not deciphered because no key survives. No earlier decipherment is known. Where British Library, Harley MS 260 f. 262r–v, the fair-copy letter-book of Walsingham’s embassy; DECODE R8358, two images in reverse order. The cipher Boxed name codes [2], [3], [4], [5], a monogram, the single letters A and F, and a five-letter run “m o R. d A.”: 15 cipher tokens of 11 kinds. How it was tried Digges (1655) printed it with the codes left in cipher; CSP Foreign has neither letter; no key survives. The setting and Walsingham’s reply of 13 July identify [3] as the French King. Still open Of 15 cipher tokens, the 2 uses of [3] are identified; the rest are not deciphered. They need the lost key or a signed original with a clerk’s decipherment.

Harley MS 260 is a fair-copy letter-book of Walsingham’s embassy in France, 1570–73, the book Digges printed from. DECODE R8358 has two images, in reverse order: f. 262r (DECODE P2): the end of an earlier Burghley letter (“I am sorry for them, and so would you also yf you thought the suspicion to be true”), signed William Burleigh and addressed “To his very frend M r Frauncis Walsingham Esquire Ambassador Resident for the Queenes Ma tie in Fraunce”. Then the ciphered letter begins: “My Lord Ambassador, this day my Lord Admirall came to the Queenes speech”. f. 262v (DECODE P1): the end of the letter, “From Westminster the 5 th of July 1572”, signed “Yo r assured frend William Burleigh”. Then the address of Walsingham’s reply to Burghley, which begins “Your Lordship’s of the second and 5 th of July”.

I am sorry that the opinion groweth here of the French King’s recoil from the Flanders enterprise; it breedeth coldness here. Some that are come home bear us in hand that [3] reneweth the m o R. d A. [4] whereby the last matter ⅋B [5] is hindered. I marvel much thereof; indeed [3] is more given to Milan [4] then to [2] . … I see no means by worldly means A but Florence with F. [2] ; God send it some way. F. 262r: “some that are come home bear us in hand that [3] reneweth the m o R. d A. [4] whereby the last matter ⅋B [5] is hindered … indeed [3] is more given to Milan”. The boxed numbers and letters are the cipher items the copyist carried over; [3] is probably the French King (grade C); the rest is not deciphered. Image: British Library, Harley MS 260 f. 262r, via DECODE R8358. Digges set the same passage as “[3 | reneweth the in o A. D. F. [4] whereby the last matter Bl5! is hindred … indeed 3| is more given to Millane 4] thentoſs|”. The transcription counts 15 cipher tokens of 11 kinds.

[3] is the French King, Charles IX (grade C). Both uses come in the paragraph that opens with “the French King’s recoil from the Flanders enterprise”. Walsingham, writing from the French court on 13 July, answers: “I find the conjectures touching the [3] reneweth the … altogether false and vain, whereof I am assured of the contrary many ways”. Digges misprints “vain” as “Fain”. “Milan [4]”. In this book a box written after a word marks a cover-name (see the November 1572 letter-book pages ). So “Milan” is probably a cover-name, perhaps for Spain, and [4] its marker. This is not graded.

Print. Digges 1655 prints both letters with the cipher as figures. CSP Foreign x, July 1572 (nos. 452–492), includes neither letter. The signed originals were not seen. Keys. There is no key record from Harley 260 on DECODE. Tomokiyo’s survey of Elizabethan ciphers has no key for Walsingham’s Paris embassy. The Cecil–Norris table of 1568 already failed on a sibling group ( Walsingham to Burghley, January 1573 ). Siblings. Records R8356–R8364 from the same volume are being worked in this project. None of them holds a key or a gloss. Context. Every token was regraded against the letter, the reply and the rule for cover-names. Only [3] is fixed.

“m o R. d A.” is not deciphered. It is five letters of an unknown cipher, too short for cryptanalysis without a key. It is probably what [3] was said to “renew”. [2], [4], [5], the monogram ⅋B, A and F are not deciphered. They need the lost key, or Burghley’s signed original with a clerk’s decipherment, if one survives in SP 70 or at Hatfield.

Two leaves of one record in the Munich key volume, in two sign ciphers. A Bavarian agent’s report on the Pressburg talks between Ferdinand and John Zápolya, with a Turkish embassy, Imre Czibak and Alvise Gritti, was broken from the ciphertext alone with a language model of sixteenth-century German; a faint gloss of the time agrees, and six lines are deciphered clean. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 15 October 2026 · updated 23 October 2026 Method · f. 263 (pp. 3-4), report on the Pressburg talks: key recovered from ciphertext-only (partial) · f. 262 (pp. 1-2), a servant's letter to his duke: read from existing decipherment (complete) Credits · Contemporary key or decipherment (key or decipherment used) ciphertext-only At a glance Ciphertext-only break · partial · f. 262 read; f. 263 six lines clean, the rest decoded, not read The documents Two leaves of one DECODE record. f. 262: a Bavarian servant to his duke, “eritags nach Jacobi” (the Tuesday after 25 July). f. 263: a report on the Pressburg negotiations between Ferdinand and John Zápolya, about 1533–34, probably its enclosure. Where Bayerisches Hauptstaatsarchiv, Munich, Kurbayern Äußeres Archiv 4591 ff. 262–263; DECODE R9416, part of catalogue entry 161, “partially decrypted”. The ciphers Two different sets of invented signs. f. 263 is a homophonic substitution with about 23 frequent signs and word division, and a few codes for persons. How it was deciphered f. 263: a solver (simulated annealing) with a language model built for it from German prints of 1472–1609 gave running German on its first run; a faint gloss of the time over the first lines, read afterwards, agrees word for word. f. 262: the key rebuilt letter for letter from the clerk’s decipherment over page B, and page A read from its signs (23 October 2026). What it says The diet at Pressburg, Ferdinand’s party arriving “mit grossem Pomp”, a Turkish embassy on Shrove Tuesday, Imre Czibak offering the Sultan tribute, Alvise Gritti dispatched; dated at Buda (“datm ofen den 12 marcij”). The servant reports Turks up to four thousand strong and Italian and Spanish foot on the move, and asks for seven years’ pension and the office of Oberrichter at Straubing. Still open f. 263 beyond recto lines 11–16: a reading of the whole leaf exists (23 October 2026), but about 4% of its letters rest on signs with two values chosen by sense, unconfirmed beyond the glossed lines, so it stays decoded, not read. Codes +L and Ω on f. 263, and X, ⊼ and a G-sign on f. 262. Until 15 October 2026 this record was filed on one page with thirteen other ciphertexts of the same key volume. They are different ciphers, each with its own page; the largest group is System A′ of the dukes’ agents in Hungary. The two leaves here are in two ciphers of their own and are kept together as one record, with a part for each.

3,150 signs, word-separated. The solver, held to the frequency limits of a homophonic cipher, gave German at once with the new model: “…uon beden kunigen zu entlicher handlung gen Pressburg gesetzt… der tag zu Pressburg erfolgt ist… mit grossem pomp… dem turkischen kaiser… tribut… zu geben…”. The faint gloss on the first lines (“nunmen tag uon beden kunigen zu entlicher handlung gen bresburg gesetzt”) agrees with it word for word, which confirms the break independently. The report concerns the negotiations between “beden kunigen”, Ferdinand and John Zápolya, and their commissaries; a Turkish embassy; “der Emrich beeche” (Imre Czibak) offering the Sultan tribute and “tausent tucaten”; and “den hern Griti abgefertigt” (Alvise Gritti, killed in September 1534), so about 1533–34. (These are the solver’s first-run words; the reading of 23 October 2026 has “dem Emrich Besche [?hundert] tausent” and “der Khö. den hern Griti ab gefertigt”.) Lines 11–16 of the recto were deciphered word by word at the image (30 September 2026). One transcription code covers two shapes: the zig-zag with one bar is e , the dagger with two bars is s ; another covers d and l . In normalised spelling: … daraus der Tag zu Pressburg erfolgt ist, dahin auch des [Ferd.] Tail mit grossem Pomp kummen sint, auch volmechtigen Gwalt anzaigt, und sich zu beden Tailn entliche Vertrage versehen. Es hat sich aber zutragen, das am Ertag in der Fasnacht von dem turkischen Kaiser ain treffliche Botschaft ankummen … (“… from which the diet at Pressburg followed, whither also [Ferdinand’s] party came with great pomp and showed full powers, and on both sides a final treaty was expected. But it came about that on Shrove Tuesday a distinguished embassy arrived from the Turkish emperor …”) [Ferd.] is a code sign identified only by the faint gloss; three signs after “Tail”, passed over by the gloss, are not rendered. The whole leaf, 23 October 2026. f. 263 turned out to carry its own faint interlinear decipherment over recto lines 1–12 and the last lines of the verso, not only the first two lines ( r9416/f263_gloss.txt ). It writes “fg” over the hourglass X ( E. F. G. , Your Princely Grace), “Khö” over the barred T (the King, by the context Zápolya) and “Ferd” over g, which settles the person codes. Every line (39 recto, 43 verso) was then read on its crop with the extended key ( r9416/f263_reading.md , English f263_en.md ). One sign serves both k and b , so the place the solver had as “Kreekurg” is Bresburg ; the embassy came “mit vij scheffe”; Imre Czibak offers tribute “und darzu das ganz widisch lannt, welches doch nit sein ist”; on the verso the King dispatches Gritti, the commissioners are recalled from Pressburg, and the last line is “datm ofen den 12 marcij” , Buda, 12 March. The f. 262 key does not apply: the two leaves use different sign sets. Outside the glossed lines, however, about 4% of the letters rest on the second value of a multi-valued sign (z e/s , b d/l , p b/w , K k/b ) chosen by the word, with no gloss or print to confirm them, so beyond recto lines 11–16 the leaf stays decoded, not read .

The letter is glossed over every line in German by a hand of the time, so it was deciphered when it arrived. The gloss is faint, and the reading audit of 22 October 2026 found that page A did not build sentences from it. On 23 October the key was rebuilt letter for letter from the decipherment of page B (a simple substitution with homophones and three code signs, r9416/f262_key.md ), and page A was deciphered from its signs on the full-resolution image, all 25 lines, including three the gloss leaves bare (“minkwicz und ander geferden halb durch slesi”). Both pages were then transcribed sign by sign ( r9416/f262_signs.txt , 1,498 signs) and decoded again, which changed 17 words to what the signs give. The servant writes of troops in Austria and Styria, of “die turcken bis in vier tausent stark”, of the Italian and Spanish foot (“italische und spanischen kne[chte]”) to move through Styria and by the Danube into Hungary, and of “bartlen von eschelkamb”, and asks for seven years’ outstanding pension and the office of Oberrichter at Straubing. It is dated “eritags nach iacobi”. The reading ( r9416/f262_reading.md , English f262_en.md ) builds sentences throughout; three code signs stay open.

f. 263 beyond recto lines 11–16: re-keyed line by line on 23 October 2026, but the letters on the multi-valued signs (3.9% of the reading) are chosen by sense with no gloss or print to confirm them: decoded, not read. f. 263: the codes +L (6 times, always beside Ferdinand) and Ω (7 times, a lord with an instruction), the dotted-circle cluster (recto ll. 12, 21, 34) and the groups at recto ll. 8–9 and verso ll. 27–28, 38–40. The person codes X, T and g are now fixed from the gloss. f. 262: the code signs X (3 times), ⊼ (twice) and a G-sign (twice), the first group of A04, the end of A03 and one sign in B01.

DECODE R4330 and R4331 are two letters of Johann Friedrich, archbishop of Bremen, to Salvius at Hamburg, of 27 November and 2 December 1631, in German. The figure runs sit inside the clear text, and a clerk of the time wrote his decipherment above most of them. A few small numbers stand for words: 4 = wir / uns , 5 = Herzog Christian, 7 = Herzog Georg, 32 = the Stift Minden, 59 = Salvius.

R4330, the letter of 27 November 1631: figure runs inside the clear German, with the decipherer’s words above (“Gronsfeldische”, “Colonien”, “troupen”). Image: Riksarkivet, Stockholm, letter of 27 November 1631, via DECODE R4330. Thirty-five glossed words were set against their numbers one letter to one number. Twenty-three matched in length, and the numbers for each letter came out as runs of four: 8–11 for a , 16–19 for n , 72–75 for e , 96–99 for s . The runs are not in alphabetical order. The alphabet is written in six columns (a b c d e f / g h i k l m / n o p q r s / t u w x y z) and read downwards, so the bands go a g n t, b h o u, c i p w, d k q x, e l r y, f m s z: 8 a · 12 g · 16 n · 20 t · 24 b · 28 h · 32 o · 36 u · 40 c · 44 i · 48 p · 52 w · 56 d · 60 k · 64 q · 68 x · 72 e · 76 l · 80 r · 84 y · 88 f · 92 m · 96 s · 100 z No gloss covers k, z, m, w or y. The unglossed groups fix them: sincken , schantze , kommen and dem accord mitbegriffen , etwas and wir , weyter and Reuterey . Once they are in place, the grid predicts q and x without a single example. Small numbers stand for words: 4 = wir/uns, 5 = Herzog Christian, 7 = Herzog Georg, 32 = the Stift Minden, 59 = Salvius.

The archbishop, Johann Friedrich of Holstein-Gottorp, wants Swedish help, and quickly. In the letter of 27 November he fears that the enemy will be in the Stift before relief comes, “ und in die euserste gefahr kommen würden ”, and asks that “ mit schleunigem hulf und succurs ausgeholffen werden möchte ”. His people have taken die Burg and are attacking die schantze . They cannot hold without more men. The letter of 2 December is more urgent. The Reuterey ranges up and down the country, laying waste one place after another, and he fears an einfal by Bönninghausen und Gronsfeldischen troupen from the Westphalian border. He hopes to be “ mit etlichen tausend secundiret ”, or at least to get etwas fusvolckes und theils dragoner . A postscript asks that, if the garrison of Newenburg marches out on terms, his ertzstift be in dem accord mitbegriffen . The full decipherment, line by line with the glosses, is in bremen_decoded.txt . The remaining errors are transcription slips from the phone photographs ( occupireh , feldlsihen ); no group is left undecrypted.

Words in brackets with `?` are uncertain in the German; `[...]` unread; `[31]` etc. unidentified name numbers. ## Translation ### R4330, Bremen, 27 November 1631 By the grace of God Johann Friedrich, elected and postulated archbishop and bishop of the sees of Bremen and Lübeck, heir to Norway, duke of Schleswig-Holstein. Our gracious greeting with especial [?well-disposed] goodwill first, noble, steadfast and most learned, especially dear [friend]. We do not doubt that you will have duly received our last letter, and what we asked in it about the succour that might be sent to us in haste, you will have learned from it. When we are then informed whether [?the Landgrave of Hesse] should, by [?His Royal Majesty's order], with his army from the Westphalian [...]. And [?therefore] not [?...] [?now] the town [would be] summoned. And we then [?...], because the Count Gronsfeld's [troops] at [31] and the Minden folk and [19] troops otherwise have no resistance to fear on that account, [?as] ours are also advised from Minden, that they will [?join forces] and also press upon us, whereby [?the Landgrave] [18] [82] would go, and [we] would come into the utmost danger. If not [?thus] [...] the actual help follows in haste, especially since we would be surrounded by enemies on both sides. Therefore it is herewith our [?gracious] request to you that, in this consideration, you will promote with especial diligence and [?order] and [?arrange] the most gracious provision in haste, as soon as ever possible, that we be not abandoned but helped out with speedy help and succour, so that General Tott's and Colonel Dumeine's troops be sent over now without delay and sent to us with all speed, so that the work be not made harder by delay and we [over that ...] [82] with [?pressing]. We have exerted ourselves so far and brought it so far that our own and [42] troops have at the same time attacked the sconce at the castle and are engaged in the work; also, as we now receive report, [it is] already occupied. [?We] cannot, however, advance further unless we receive assistance. Therefore we earnestly desire that Salvius will take it to heart that the succour not tarry too long but follow with all speed. We rely wholly on you for this and remain in return well disposed to you with especial grace in all good things. Given in our town of Bremen, 27 Nov. 1631. Friedrich. ### R4331, Bremen, 2 December 1631 [Title as above.] Our gracious greeting with especial [?well-disposed] goodwill first, noble, steadfast and most learned, especially dear [friend]. We have no doubt that you will have received our last letter about speedy succour and troops' [?help-sending], since the [?sconce] castle has now also been occupied and taken. And although we have quartered the cavalry there, Reinach nevertheless raids hard here and there through [?our] lands and lays waste one place after another, and we cannot prevent it. For we must secure ourselves of the passes along the Westphalian borders first of all, of necessity, against the feared invasion of Bönninghausen's and Gronsfeld's troops, of which a strong [rumour] is spread, so that no greater [86] and [82] may befall and come upon us from that quarter. But as we take every comfort [?in this] and rely on it, that we would be seconded, as promised, with some thousands and helped out, so we still have the firm confidence that one will send us in haste some troops to our help and [?not] leave us so any longer, or hold us off only with good promises, whereby we, together with land and people, would be wholly endangered and might come into [?misfortune] [?utterly]. And we therefore, because the highest need demands it, graciously request of you once more that you will make the definite arrangement and order and [?provision] that, if the full number of which you lately wrote to us cannot be, at least some foot and partly dragoons, as many as one can at all muster in haste, be sent to us with all speed at the first opportunity for succour, and [?usefully] come to us, so that we see ours, that [...] succour is nevertheless at hand, and do not let our hope sink greatly; also that Tilly's [men] in [...] be not made bolder. And we remain graciously disposed to you with all grace and especially well-inclined goodwill. Given in our town of Bremen, 2 Dec. Anno 1631. Friedrich. ### R4331, postscript Could Salvius also, since he [...] anyway, [...] [?go] to Celle, [and] so dispose and direct the work with Duke Christian and Duke Georg that we [?therefore] in that quarter not only may expect all good assistance and have cause to rejoice, but also may surely obtain that the enemy, where [he would come] [?down] from Neuenburg and otherwise over the Aller, through the land of Lüneburg, [be] granted passage of war, [but rather be] [?blocked], [lest] from there harm of war [82] and danger befall and meet us and also Minden, [?all the less] if the garrison of Neuenburg should march out on accord, [?it be] not allowed to come into our archbishopric, but rather that we be included under the accord on that account, we would graciously [?like it]. And it would be especially dear and agreeable to us, and we have therefore graciously [?to desire] in this, as we also do not doubt that you will take it especially to heart to promote it. Otherwise it is also our [?gracious] wish that Salvius come as soon as possible nearer to [?Stade] and to us in person. That will be done to our [?gracious] pleasure. Key: key.md

Twenty-two English telegrams between Sun Yat-sen and Soong Ching-ling (“Rosamonde”), copied for the Japanese Foreign Ministry and never translated. Brice Dudout found them in the JACAR volumes and, with Claude, recovered the key from the cipher alone: a reciprocal letter substitution, twelve swapped pairs with d and p unchanged, used from February 1915 to May 1916. From 1913 to 1917 the Japanese Ministry of Communications had the telegrams of Sun Yat-sen’s circle in Tokyo copied for the Foreign Ministry. The copies form the series “inquiry into the mail of designated persons” (特定人ノ発受郵便物取調), now digitised by the Japan Center for Asian Historical Records. Most are in Chinese telegraph codes; the project’s page on Sun Yat-sen’s intercepted telegrams, 1916–17 covers the condenser systems, a different cipher. In the 1915 volumes Brice Dudout noticed a separate family: ten-letter words with no pattern of consonants and vowels, but recurring groups such as hea . They leave Tokyo in the name of Tōyama Mitsuru (頭山滿), Sun’s neighbour and protector, for two Shanghai addresses, “Laisaosang, 445 Chaoufoong Road” and “Rosamonde, 628 E. Yuhang Road”. In May 1916 the same words travel between Shanghai and “Rosamonde Tokio”. Tokyo to “Laisaosang, Shanghai”, 26 February 1915, 10.40 am, signed 頭山滿. Read across the two columns, the twelve words begin myovonoiho coohavbhea = “whenever ye see Yung you”. Image: Diplomatic Archives of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Japan, JACAR B03050087600 image 52, via Brice Dudout’s wenmi repository.

The plaintext is telegraphic English with the spaces removed, cut into ten-letter words. Each letter is replaced by its partner in a table of pairs, so the same table enciphers and deciphers: a↔u b↔g c↔s e↔o f↔j h↔y i↔r k↔z l↔t m↔w n↔v q↔x · d and p unchanged You becomes hea and love becomes teno ; several clear telegrams of March 1915 to Rosamonde are simply signed “teno”. Names, sums and reply addresses stay in clear, and so do a few words ( happy , Inuzuka , iron , trunk ). The last word stops at ten letters, which cuts husba[nd] twice in May 1916. On 6 March 1915 the form twice has qq where pp is expected; Brice renders it [pp] and leaves the table as it is. How the key was recovered. On Brice’s account the letter index of coincidence is 0.062, a natural language and not a code; f and q never occur and hea comes ten times. Simulated annealing over all substitutions, then over reciprocal ones only, scored with an English quadgram model, gave the key; the same search recovers an English control text enciphered with a random key. No crib or outside plaintext was used. The key taken from the 1915 telegrams alone then scores the 1916 forms, transcribed blind before the key was found, far above 2,000 random reciprocal tables (z = 7.5), and Brice’s own blind re-transcription of 1915 likewise (z = 10.9). A telegram in another system stays at chance (z = 0.6). The forms were transcribed twice and independently, by Claude and then by Brice without seeing Claude’s transcription; 89% of the letters agreed. Checked here. The cipher words of three forms whose scans are in Brice’s repository (20 and 26 February, 7 July 1915: 20 words, 200 letters) were transcribed again from the images and deciphered with the table unchanged. The result agrees with his edition letter for letter, including the letters he corrects and the unreadable xa ins of 7 July; the statistical test in docs/_validate.py passes on these 200 letters. Two small points: the scan gives abon (g, not p) in “[u]pon”, a second slip that his brackets leave out, and the cipher has “for our soul are mingled” where his edition prints “souls”.

No form names either party; the attribution is Brice’s, built from independent facts that agree. “Rosamonde” (or Rosamond) was Soong Ching-ling’s English name, and in 1916 “Rosamonde Tokio” was a telegraphic address of Sun’s household. The dates. Ching-ling was in Shanghai from 28 October 1914 to 17 March 1915. The Tokyo–Shanghai telegrams run from 17 February to 12 March, and on 15 March one goes by wireless to the steamer Korea , which brought her back (“Are you land Kobe or Yoko?”). She left again on 3 May; the run resumes on 10 June. The relay. Zhu Zhuowen (“Chu”), Sun’s man in Shanghai, wrote on 2 and 4 February 1915 that he had set up an office for Miss Soong beside his own room, out of her mother’s sight, where she could be written to. On 20 February Tokyo wires “Must answer cable to Chu’s yesterday.” The rumour of March 1915. On 9 March clear telegrams from Shanghai ask after Sun’s health, one of them to Rosamonde signed “teno”. Tokyo replies in the cipher, “I a[m] well and sound usual”, and the next day Sun asks Shanghai, in a condensed Chinese code, what rumours are going round about his safety. Yung. A suitor named, with another, in a letter from her father Charlie Soong to Sun of 3 August 1915, published by Yang Tianshi; the telegrams name him five months earlier. May 1916. The messages are signed “devoted husband” and addressed to “my own wife”; the iron trunk, Inuzuka Shintarō, Canton, Zhang Ji and the liner Porthos recur in Chinese-code telegrams of the same days. Ching-ling joined Sun in Shanghai on 19 May 1916. The 11 March telegram is itself a lesson in the system’s weakness: encipher at home, never in the office, “You don’t use code book, so they can get our secrets by guessing.” Japanese officials copied every form but did not decipher them.

In the eleven complete telegrams of the first 1915 sample, about 45 of 750 letters are corrected (6%), nearly all copying confusions. The brackets in the table show each one. Not deciphered: eight words in the middle of 9 March 1915; one word after “throw of[f]” and the end of “de[vou]t” on 25 February; one group on 7 July (the key gives lovesickxa instorture ). The key is complete; these fail on the copies. Probable, not proved: “Chang Ki” as Zhang Ji, “Tai” as Dai Jitao, Ching-ling as sender of 7 July, 8 and 13 May. Unidentified: who stood behind the address “Laisaosang”, and Yung’s Chinese name. Brice found the telegrams neither in the work on the 1916 intercepts nor in the studies of the marriage he checked (below); other works remain to be searched. This project checked three of the twenty-two forms against the scans; the other nineteen rest on his transcription. May 1916: Brice Dudout’s blind transcriptions of the seven forms (made on 15 October 2026, before the key was known), the decryption word by word and the table of every emendation are in the repository folder ( dudout/ ). The emendations fall into a few cursive pairs: n/v 23 times, i/r 18, r/i 7, y/h 6. That makes them copying confusions rather than guesses, but they are still 109 of 627 letters, so the telegrams stay decoded, not read, under the rule that a reading may rest on at most 3% of look-alike letters.

Three draft telegrams of a general of Huerta’s federal army to the Minister of War, from Lampazos (18 July 1913) and Zacatecas (13 and 18 March 1914), in the numerical Clave núm. 109 whose printed key sheet is filed with them (CEHM-Carso, fondo DLXXIII). Brice Dudout checked the sheet on a contemporary pencil pair (1.000 of words against 0.111 for permuted tables) and read the cipher passages, 67 words: the Laredo garrison courted by the Carrancistas, an old general at San Antonio in touch with revolutionaries, and a railway to Torreón the rebels are destroying. The fonds’ other “en clave” pieces use other tables and stay unread. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 30 October 2026 Method: read with known key · Extent: complete Contributed by Brice Dudout (solution) known key At a glance Known key applied · complete The telegrams Three signed drafts of General Guillermo Rubio Navarrete, a general of the federal army, to the Minister (Secretary) of War and Navy in Mexico City: 18 July 1913 from Lampazos (Nuevo León, incomplete), 13 March and 18 March 1914 from Zacatecas. Where Centro de Estudios de Historia de México (CEHM-Carso, Fundación Carlos Slim), fondo DLXXIII, Manuscritos del General Guillermo Rubio Navarrete: DLXXIII.1.30.16-49, 2.41.9-41 and 2.41.13-41. The key: DLXXIII.1.28.14-23. The cipher "Clave núm. 109, Secretaría de Guerra y Marina, con el General Guillermo Rubio Navarrete": a printed table of 160 numbers for letters, syllables and military words. The numbers stand inside the plain text, joined by dashes. How it was deciphered The printed sheet was transcribed with nothing added, frozen, and checked on a contemporary pair: a typed telegram of 30 March 1914 and its pencil draft, where Rubio wrote the plain text above the numbers. The held-out part came back 1.000 of characters and words, against at most 0.111 for permuted tables. What it says The garrison at Laredo is courted by the Carrancistas and its commander cannot be fully trusted; an old general in San Antonio, Texas, is in touch with revolutionaries; at Zacatecas Rubio is waiting for material and troops to rebuild the railway to Torreón while the rebels destroy it. Still open Nothing in these three telegrams. The other "en clave" pieces of the fonds use other tables, which are not in the file, and are not read here. Three words are probable. Credit Brice Dudout ( Europe chiffrée ), working with Claude Opus 5.5: the identification of the key sheet, its test on the contemporary pair, the transcription of the three telegrams, the Spanish text and the English translation. His write-up .

After the coup of February 1913, General Victoriano Huerta's federal army fought Venustiano Carranza's Constitutionalists. Rubio Navarrete commanded first in the Northeast, at Lampazos (Nuevo León) in the summer of 1913 against the troops of Pablo González, then at Zacatecas in the spring of 1914, as Villa marched on Torreón. His drafts of telegrams to the Minister of War are partly in cipher, and what the cipher carries is what he would not leave to the telegraph clerks. The telegram of 18 March 1914, first leaf: the plain words "con toda atención que", then the cipher runs 2-86-74-37-147-34-46-60-149 ( urge so-be-ma-ne-ra ), with pues con and de que left in clear. Image: Centro de Estudios de Historia de México (CEHM-Carso), fondo DLXXIII, DLXXIII.2.41.13-41 image 1, via the CEHM public viewer (crop; the viewer's watermark is partly visible). The three drafts: DLXXIII.1.30.16-49 (Lampazos, 18 July 1913, incomplete), 2.41.9-41 (13 March 1914) and 2.41.13-41 (18 March 1914). The fonds holds other telegrams "en clave", but they use other tables, among them an alphabetical numerical syllabary from 1 to 255 for the traffic with General Téllez and the División del Bravo, a two-figure code, a presidential code and a "Clave nº 99". Those pieces are not read here.

Clave núm. 109 is a printed grid. Letters have several numbers for the vowels (1–3 for u , 13–15 for o , 25–27 for i , 37–39 for e , 49–51 for a ) and run on to 61 d up to 93 z ; syllables ( pa , pe … ta , te , ti ) fill the upper numbers, and a few military words have a number of their own (98 Gobernador , 106 tropa , 107 fuerza , 112 vía , 132 General ). Rubio wrote the numbers inside the plain text of the draft, separated by dashes, and spelled out the words that were not in the table, so a name such as Téllez comes out as te-e-ll-e-z.

The key is the sheet itself: the printed table filed with the telegrams (DLXXIII.1.28.14-23). Every number of the three telegrams is on it, and no value was added or corrected. The transcription of the sheet is the project's key.tsv . To test it, Brice Dudout used a telegram that survives twice: the typed telegram of 30 March 1914 (DLXXIII.2.41.18-41) and its pencil draft (DLXXIII.1.29.9-30), on which Rubio wrote the plain text above the cipher numbers, "… la ha dado guarnición de dicha plaza por conferencia tenida hoy. Espero fuerzas". The key and the protocol were frozen and hashed before the measurement, and the first ten groups, which had been checked by eye, were left out. On the held-out part (9 words) the key gives 1.000 of characters and 1.000 of words; 200 control keys, with the table's values permuted, give at most −0.021 and 0.111. The thresholds, 0.85 and 0.75, were met. The rest of that telegram, which has no contemporary plain text, reads "para poder seguir mis trabajos al norte".

The clear words that the writer left around the numbers are in angle brackets and do not count; braces mark a probable reading. Lampazos, 18 July 1913 <Hónrame comunicar a Ud. personas de confianza me informan que> guarnicion laredo es muy solicitada <por> carrancismo <y que jefe de la plaza> no merece toda confianza <, así como que general> treviño <está en> san antonio texas <en> relaciones <con revolucionarios. Permítome indicar conveniencia de la estancia del Sr. Gral.> teellez en laredo <, así como mandar persona de confianza> a san antonio <, pues> general treviño <por su> edad <se ha hecho muy maleable y siempre está de acuerdo con la última persona con quien habla. En la entrevista que […]> Persons he trusts tell Rubio that the Laredo garrison is much courted by Carrancismo and that the commander of the place does not deserve full trust; also that General Treviño is at San Antonio, Texas, in relations with revolutionaries. He suggests that General Téllez should stay at Laredo and that a trusted person be sent to San Antonio, since Treviño, because of his age, has become very pliable and always agrees with the last person he talks to. The leaf breaks off there. Zacatecas, 13 March 1914 <Hónrome participar a Ud. que> unicamente espero {material} <y> fuerzas para comenzar <la> reconstruccion <de> la via <que> esta terminada <en> dos meses <. Respetuosamente. Gral. de División G. Rubio.> He is waiting only for material and troops to begin rebuilding the railway, which will be finished in two months. Zacatecas, 18 March 1914 <Me es honroso participar a usted con toda atención que> urge sobemanera el envia de fuerzas a esta {plza} <, pues con> el solo anuncio <de que> vengo a <reparar la vía> a torreon los rebeldes se estan dedicando <con gran actividad a> {destruirla} <totalmente, lo que> es imposible evitar <con el> escaso <efectivo de fuerzas> que existen en esta <. Respetuosamente. G. Rubio.> It is extremely urgent to send troops to this place, for at the mere announcement that he is coming to repair the railway to Torreón the rebels are busy destroying it completely, which cannot be prevented with the few troops there are. The spelling of the cipher is kept: teellez , sobemanera (the r of sobre omitted), envia for envío . Cipher parts of the three telegrams: 67 words; 64 certain (95.5%), 3 probable (4.5%), none restored or unresolved. To Brice Dudout's knowledge nothing in the cyphersolver repository, in Cryptiana or in Roberto Narváez's open-access articles reads them, and Narváez's book Criptografía diplomática, política y militar en México 1813-1926 (SRE, 2019) could not be consulted.

{material} (13 March 1914): the second 159 ( te ) is badly formed; the value is required by ma-te-ri-a-l . {plza} (18 March 1914): group 93 ( z ) is written over another figure, and the cipher gives p-l-z-a without the second a , which is not restored. {destruirla} : the middle figure of 153 ( ru ) lies under the CEHM watermark; de-s-t-ru-i-r-la is what the sense requires. The people. General Joaquín Téllez commanded the federal forces in the Northeast. The elderly "General Treviño" at San Antonio is probably Gerónimo Treviño (born 1836), former military chief of the Northeast under Porfirio Díaz; the identification was not checked in the sources. The rest of the fonds. The other "en clave" pieces (one of 19 July 1913, DLXXIII.1.30.17-49, carries a pencil interlinear decipherment) use other tables that are not in the file. Catalogue no. 1468 stays open for them.

Ferrara’s envoy to Matthias Corvinus writes in a substitution of graphic signs with homophones. The key was recovered by aligning two letters with their contemporary clear copies in the same file; two of the four DECODE targets proved to have contemporary decipherments. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 19 September 2026 · updated 26 October 2026 Method: key recovered based on adjacent plaintext · Extent: partial (50% of the cipher) · On the map Credits · Contemporary key or decipherment (key or decipherment used) adjacent text At a glance Key from adjacent plaintext · partial (50% of the cipher) The letters Despatches of Nicolò Sadoleto, Este envoy to Matthias Corvinus, from Buda and Pozsony in 1482, written when Venice attacked Ferrara; never printed. Where Archivio di Stato di Modena, Ambasciatori, Ungheria b. 1/9; DECODE R1101–R1106, four listed as partly decrypted; images also on Vestigia. The cipher Graphic signs with word divisions kept and clear words mixed in: about twenty-five signs, with homophones for the vowels and n , r . How it was read The alphabet came from aligning two letters (15 July, 31 August) sign by sign with the chancery’s clear copies. It then read the seven cipher lines of 16 July, which have no copy. What it says On 16 July Sadoleto learnt in secret that Venice had offered the King Veglia, a fleet command for his natural son and a hundred thousand ducats a year; he urges the League to match that sum. Still open The faded block of 17 August gives fragments only; a few words of 16 July lie under stains or the binding fold; the 27 November decipherment sheets are not aligned with the cipher. The twelve 1483 letters were all deciphered at the time.

The file holds forty-seven reports of Sadoleto, June 1482 to November 1483, most in his own hand, with a handful of ducal minutes in reply (Mátyus 2020). Vestigia catalogues all of them with images; DECODE has eighteen of those with cipher. The ones that matter here: Item Date, place Form Status found DECODE R1101 · b. 1/9 no. 7 (Vestigia 1284) 15 July 1482, Pozsony four pages, long cipher passages no. 7a (Vestigia 1283) is the full contemporary clear copy: read at the time ; used as a crib DECODE R1102 · no. 8 (Vestigia 1286) 16 July 1482, Pozsony clear letter; seven cipher lines at the foot of p. 2, more on pp. 3–4 no clear copy: deciphered here in gist DECODE R1103 · no. 11 (Vestigia 1294) 17 August 1482, Pozsony copy for Ercole of Sadoleto’s letter to King Ferrante; four faint cipher lines on p. 2 no clear copy: fragments only DECODE R1104 · no. 13 (Vestigia 1298) 31 August 1482, Pozsony one page, mostly cipher “Decrypted”: clear copies 13a and 13b (Vestigia 1295, 1297); used as a crib DECODE R1106 · no. 26 (Vestigia 1318) 27 November 1482, Pozsony four pages, partly cipher two sheets of decipherment, 26a and 26b (Vestigia 1319, 4004): read at the time ; here decoded, not read (26b faded on the photographs) DECODE’s “partially decrypted” on R1101 and R1106 reflects that the decipherments are filed as separate items and were not attached to the records; the chancery deciphered both letters at the time. For R1106 the decipherment slips survive only in photographs whose right halves are faded. On 23 October 2026 slips 26a and 26b were transcribed as far as the photographs allow and a partial reading was built on them, following the cipher where its read spans differ ( R1106_reading.md , English R1106_en.md ): the two paragraphs of p. 2 that 26a covers (the Queen, the King of Hungary’s moves, the League’s spending, Venice) build sentences, but the p. 3 cipher that 26b covers keeps holes in most sentences, so R1106 stays decoded, not read. The faded right halves of 26b and of p. 3 are the blocker. The seven cipher lines of 16 July 1482 at the foot of p. 2. Line 1 reads essendo in Buda per partire per venire a Posonia ; the last line per mare, et gli voleva dare ogni anno cento milia . Image: Archivio di Stato di Modena, Ambasciatori, Ungheria b. 1/9 no. 8, p. 2, via DECODE R1102.

No Este key for this embassy is known. The archive’s Cifrario series holds a key “per corrispondere con Nicolò Sadoletti a Napoli tra 1479 e 1480”, rebuilt by nineteenth-century archivists (Cremonini 2017, n. 39), but it is not digitised. The key was therefore rebuilt from the letters. The cipher keeps word divisions, which makes alignment straightforward. The clear copy 7a of 15 July runs “… volesse unirse e pigliare questa impresa, e non lassasse pretermittere questa opportunità laquale mai più fo, né forse sera, e che lo facesse per lo amore …”, and the first lines of the cipher on the original’s second page match it word for word. The one-page letter of 31 August and its clear 13a confirm it: “epsa me dice che è certa che la liga non … perchè Millano et Fiorenza non voriano …”. One habit shows up at once: where 13a has perchè the original writes quid in ordinary letters, which works as a code word. It is a plain alphabet with a few alternative signs for common letters; no syllable signs were needed. The nomenclator is small or rarely used: one group in the letter of 16 July does not spell out and is almost certainly a code word (below).

The letter’s clear part is routine news of the court. The last seven lines of p. 2 are in cipher, and the cipher runs on into p. 3. From the reading ( R1102_reading.md , English R1102_en.md ; [U..] an unresolved sign label): Essendo in Buda per partire per venire a Posonia, sapi per gran secreto da dom Francesco como [Signoria di Venetia] haveva scripto ad Francesco Quirino, che e qua, fosse a [Re di Hungaria], gli facesse offerta como [Signoria di Venetia] voleva havere seco bona amicitia, et voleva dargli Vegla, et voleva lo figliolo (e bastardo) per loro capitaneo de l’armata per mare, et gli voleva dare ogni anno cento milia ducati; ma voleva potere soldare et [U20] cauare gente de questo regno. Et questo l’aveva saputo sua [U03] per subtile via, et non volse per cosa del mondo che io monstrasse saperne cosa alcuna. “Being in Buda about to leave to come to Pozsony, I learnt in great secret from dom Francesco that [the Signoria of Venice] had written to Francesco Quirino, who is here, to go to [the King of Hungary] and make him the offer that [the Signoria] wanted to have good friendship with him, and wanted to give him Veglia, and wanted his son (the bastard) as captain-general of the fleet at sea, and would give him a hundred thousand ducats every year; but it wanted to be able to hire soldiers and draw men from this kingdom.” The reading of 19 September had [X] and gaps where the text above now stands; the second pass below supplied them. The words that fix the decipherment could be nothing else: Buda , Posonia , Francesco twice, Quirino , Vegla , capitaneo , per mare , ogni anno , cento milia . The sense fits the moment. Veglia (Krk) had been taken by Venice from Count Giovanni Frankopan in 1480, and the count was at Matthias’s court that summer (13a: “le qui lo Conte Zohane da Vegla”). The “son, the bastard” can only be János Corvin, Matthias’s natural son and intended heir. The sum links this letter to a later one. Six weeks later, in the letter of 31 August, Sadoleto told Ercole that Matthias “per cento milia ducati ogni anno pigliaria la impresa”, that is, would enter the war for the League for a hundred thousand ducats a year. The cipher of 16 July shows where that price came from: it was the figure the other side had already put on the table. [X] is a five-sign group that occurs twice, after como both times, as the subject of haveva scripto and of voleva havere seco bona amicitia . It does not spell a word in the letter key, so it is a nomenclator entry, and the context makes it the Venetian side, most likely “la Signoria”. The informant’s title before Francesco is another three-sign group (see the second pass below). Second pass, 20–21 September 2026 A second pass corrected the text above and found more cipher. The informant’s title spells out in the ordinary alphabet as dom , so the name is “dom Francesco”. Group [X] turns up again in the letter of 27 November, where the contemporary decipherment 26b renders it as the Signoria of Venice. A six-sign group K is aligned with the King of Hungary’s title in the 15 July clear copy. The doubtful end of line 3 and start of line 4 give fosse a [K] / gli facesse offerta . The sign for ss is checked against facesse and imparasse in the 15 July letter, and the sign for ff against affinita . Those corrections are in the reading quoted above. The cipher does not stop there. The sentence continues on p. 3 (quoted above): Venice also wanted the right to recruit soldiers in Hungary, and the informant made Sadoleto promise to show no knowledge of it. Further down p. 3 comes a mixed passage of clear and cipher in which Sadoleto argues his own case to Ercole: … ⟨per ogni modo disponerse⟩ ad dare a questo [Re di Hungaria] cento milia ducati ogni anno sino a sei o septe anni, che seri[a] questa suma che li domanda; et non seria gran suma alla liga, considerata la [?indubitata] victoria che sua m[aesta] … [?prome…] ⟨est lo modo che mai fo la migliore opportunita⟩ … Non scio percio se sua maesta [?atentasse] … monstra desiderare et haver piu bisogno in questo principio. Ma [U15] alla liga [U16] tractare, et non e da perder tempo; et se [?volen]o [?spen]dere dinari a questo tempo et fare la bona spesa … “… to make up [the League’s] mind at all costs to give this King a hundred thousand ducats a year for six or seven years, which would be the sum he asks, and it would not be a great sum for the League, considering the certain victory that His Majesty … he shows he wants it and needs it more at this beginning … there is no time to lose, and if they mean to spend money, now is the time to spend it well …” So the letter sets the Venetian counter-offer beside Sadoleto’s advice to match it: a hundred thousand ducats a year from the League. Page 4 carries one more cipher line, “se bene non la mandato a questo [U11]”. Sections A–C of the letter build sentences; the monetary passage keeps unresolved labels in its last lines.

R1103 is the copy, sent to Ercole, of Sadoleto’s letter to King Ferrante of Naples. Four lines of cipher in the middle of p. 2 have faded almost to the colour of the paper. Contrast stretching on the blue channel brings out perhaps half the signs, and they give fragments only: “… se tener che … et … lo credo …”, “… suoi …”, “… vostro … meco … che …”. The clear text around the block concerns the King’s price for joining the League and the hundred thousand ducats, so the block probably says something about that, but no reading is offered: R1103 is decoded, not read. Re-cropped line by line on 23 October 2026, the block gave no word beyond vostro that could be accepted, and DECODE R1103 carries only the page images. It needs better imaging (ultraviolet or multispectral) of the original in Modena.

DECODE lists twelve more Sadoleto letters of 1483 from Buda and Zagreb (b. 1/10, R1107–R1118), several as partly decrypted. None is open. Four have clear copies filed beside them (nos. 4a/4b, 20a, 21a, 24a on Vestigia); two of the DECODE records are those copies themselves (R1108 = 9a, R1113 = 20a, R1115 = 24a); and the three letters with no filed copy carry the chancery’s decipherment on slips pasted to the leaf: R1109 (4 April, to King Ferrante) over both cipher pages, R1116 (Zagreb, 3 October) and R1118 (30 November) at the foot, keyed to the cipher by a caret. The slips show on DECODE’s photographs; on Vestigia’s later ones they have been lifted, which is why the pages appear to have no decipherment. The 1482 key decrypts the cipher of R1118 in agreement with its slip (“ma come scripsi a V.S. non gli [s]panza questo accordo col turcho”).

All images are 4320 × 3240 two-page spreads, fetched from DECODE with a logged-in session and from Vestigia, which needs no login. The cipher lines were cut into strips, glyphs segmented by connected components and numbered on the strip (the segmentation script is the one written for the Milanese letters of 1489, see Buda 1489 ), and transcribed by eye against the clear copies. The pairs of signs most easily confused were settled on high-magnification crops: the two Δ forms ( p and q , which differ only in the loop at the apex), the stemmed and flat-topped sixes ( e and n ), and the long ſ against Γ.

16 July, line 1 and lines 5–7 (Buda, Posonia, Veglia, the son, the fleet, the hundred thousand): H . 16 July, lines 2–4 as corrected ( dom , fosse a , facesse offerta ): C . [X] = the Signoria of Venice, from 26b: C for the referent; the exact wording of the code group is not known. K = the King of Hungary, from 7a: C for the referent. Page 3: subtile via , soldare et cauare gente , victoria , in questo principio , dinari a questo tempo , spesa : C . seri[a] , indubitata , atentasse , vol[e]no spen[dere] : M . Still without a reading in the 16 July letter: the word after epsa non scia che ; a clear word and a cipher word ( piacede ?) after ma ; a form of promettere (?) with an unassigned K-shaped sign; the last word of the page-4 line ( effecto ? A Spanish churchman’s private letter, copied into Oldenbarnevelt’s papers (Nationaal Archief 3.01.14 inv. 2442), hides its secrets by writing the vowels as digits. The key came off the first cipher line and about 97% of 1,447 cipher words read. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 23 October 2026 Method: key recovered from ciphertext-only · Extent: complete ciphertext-only At a glance Ciphertext-only break · complete The letter Juan Gara de Senisteros, newly a canon and rector of a college at Alcalá, to his patron Juan de la Peña, 23 December 1605. An early seventeenth-century copy. Where Nationaal Archief, The Hague, 3.01.14 (Johan van Oldenbarnevelt), inv. 2442, 11 scans online. Found by a title search of the archive’s inventories; not on DECODE. The cipher Consonants stay in clear and only the vowels are replaced: 4=a, 8=e, 3=i/y, 7=o, 2=u, with 5 and 6 as forms of s and b. Word division is kept. How it was broken The first cipher line of page 1 gives the key by itself: l4s m3sm4s p4l4br4s can only be las mismas palabras . The rest was deciphered with it. What it says How he forged his patron’s signature on a blank sheet to win his posts, the sees of Sigüenza and Pamplona, money troubles with a student, and a rumour about the Inquisitor Salcedo’s ancestry. Still open About 46 scattered words where the copyist’s hand is cramped. Pages 4R–11 were deciphered directly, without a sign-by-sign transcription.

The Oldenbarnevelt archive catalogues inv. 2442 as “Missive van Don Juan Gara de Senisteros aan Juan de la Pena van 23 december 1605; afschrift (begin 17e eeuw)”. It is a copy in one hand on eleven scanned pages: a single page, then two-page openings, the folios numbered from 54. How a Spanish churchman’s private letter came to Holland’s Advocate is not stated; it reads as an intercepted letter copied for him. The text is Spanish, mostly clear, with long enciphered stretches on pages 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 7 and 10. There is no decipherment on the leaves. It was found by the project’s sweep of the Nationaal Archief inventories for cipher words ( research/nationaal_archief/ ). Haak and Veenendaal’s edition of Oldenbarnevelt’s papers (RGP, 1934–67) does not print it, and no other reading was found. Page 1. After “la brevedad que desseo y espero,” the cipher begins: 8l s8cr8t4r37 Fr4nc3sc7 G7nc4l8z , “el secretario Francisco Gonçalez”. Image: Nationaal Archief, The Hague, 3.01.14 inv. 2442, scan 1 (f. 54r), via the archive’s IIIF service.

Every consonant stands in clear. The five vowels are replaced by digits, always the same digit: Plain a e i, y o u Cipher 4 8 3 7 2 Two further digits are only letter forms: 5 for s ( 53n7 = sino , 53 4c4s7 = si acaso ) and 6 for b or v ( 468r = haber , q2864n = que van ). A looped sign that the transcription calls {G} is the copyist’s l in lo and los . Words are separated as in the clear text, and once or twice a clear gloss is written above a cipher word ( hablar , en secreto ). There is no nomenclator: names, titles and places are spelled out. With the consonant skeleton visible, the key is fixed by the first stretch of cipher. On page 1, l4s m3sm4s p4l4br4s qu8 s7n p4rt3c2l4r8s has only one reading, las mismas palabras que son particulares , and that gives four of the five vowels. The fifth comes from 2 in p4rt3c2l4r8s .

The cipher hides what the writer did not want read by others. In order of the pages: The new bishops. Siguença went to Fr. Mateo de Burgos and Pamplona to Antonio Venegas of the Council of the Inquisition. Mucho temo que se debe de aber dado alguna occasion para la voz levantada : he fears money changed hands. The forged signature. To get the canonry and the rectorship, Gara needed a letter from de la Peña to the Cardinal of Toledo that had not come. Yo hice una firma de V.S.ª en un pliego de papel lo mejor que pude, y hice a un criado mio secreto que escribiesse la sustancia de la carta, diciendo que V.S.ª me avia dexado algunas firmas en blanco. He did the same for a letter to the abbot, and asks to be forgiven: estas cosas he hecho por ser tan convenientes en esta occasion . The regent’s canonry was to be resigned into the Cardinal’s hands, with powers sent to the Licentiate Gomara or Agustín Mexía, and Gara asks his patron to support him. The Lerma collegiate church the Duke was founding, and a plan to aim at its abbacy. The student Chaves , who had been given a cassock, borrowed forty reales and asked Gara not to tell; Gara asks what to charge. Page 10. The Inquisitor Salcedo’s grandmother was said to be the daughter of a cleric and a married woman whose husband, a smith, tiene opinion de confesso . Salcedo had nonetheless become a collegial at Oviedo and an inquisitor, and families of standing (don García de Medrano’s among them) had married into the line. Gara will do nothing sin el parecer de V.S.ª . Page 10, right: the passage on the Inquisitor Salcedo’s grandmother. c4s4d4 c7n 2n h8rr8r7 , “casada con un herrero”. Image: Nationaal Archief, The Hague, 3.01.14 inv. 2442, scan 10 (right-hand page), via the archive’s IIIF service. The full readings are in the repository: the literal transcription of pages 1–4 left ( transcription_A.txt ) with the key applied by script ( decoded_A.txt ), and pages 4 right–11 read directly with the cipher passages marked ( reading_B.md ).

The scans were fetched at full resolution through the Nationaal Archief’s IIIF service. The key was taken from the first cipher line as above. A subagent transcribed pages 1 to 4 left sign by sign, and the key was applied to that transcription by script. Pages 4 right to 11 were deciphered directly from line crops with the key; pages 8, 9, 10 left and 11 turned out to be clear. Measured on 23 October 2026: 454 cipher words on pages 1–4 left, 14 of them uncertain; 993 on pages 4 right–10, 32 of them uncertain. That is about 97% of the cipher words read as Spanish sense.

About 46 words marked [?] or (?) in the readings, scattered, mostly where the copyist’s hand is cramped: page 4 right lines 5–6, a superscript on page 7 left, the last lines of page 10. The key is complete; these are reading gaps. Pages 4 right to 11 have a reading but no sign-level transcription. The persons need identifying: Juan de la Peña, absent from Spain and patron of an Alcalá college; and the college of which Gara became rector.

Juan Gara de Senisteros to Juan de la Peña, Alcalá, 23 Dec 1605 (NA 3.01.14 inv. 2442) Gara, newly canon and college rector at Alcalá, tells his patron how he forged the patron's signature on a blank sheet to send letters to the Cardinal of Toledo and the abbot and win the electors; reports the provisions of Sigüenza and Pamplona with suspicion of money; asks about the regent's canonry, the Lerma collegiate church and a student's debts; and passes on that the Inquisitor Salcedo's grandmother was a cleric's daughter by the wife of a smith reputed a converso.
