Clear passages are summarised in [brackets]. `[?]` marks words not read. ## p01 [With great pleasure I received Your Lordship's letter of 22 October, glad you are well and that the visitation and journeys are over; God grant it ends soon, as I wish and hope.] The secretary Francisco Gonçalez has given me very good hopes of this. Since the Sigüenza business came out I have not been able to find the letter to send to Your Lordship with the very words, which are particular, and more for his character; for being [?] I tore it up. From which I have gathered that when the see of Sigüenza was filled, the Duke [of Lerma] would say something about this, discussing Your Lordship and the consultations. God guide it as may best serve Him and suit us. ## p02R [...] Her favour can be of importance, and I have told her that I wish to see Your Lordship here and she wishes it greatly, and she laments much to see the times that run, and she sent me [?] about Sigüenza, because she had given me very good hopes; and many times they cannot, and other times they dare not speak to the Duke about it, because all have their own claims and go about displeased, and his own [relatives] many times dare not say anything to him; and so there is nothing for it but patience, and to do what we can as the times allow. ## p04L [...] I owe the acknowledgement that is due. Afterwards I went to visit Agustín Mexía, the regent's brother-in-law, and gave him the letters and told him what had been done and how the Cardinal had shown me favour; and when he heard it he went to the devil, saying the canonry was to go to Doctor Cetina or to Doctor Sosa, his relative, and that he did not know how these powers had come into my hands, making great show of it. I softened him as best I could, and fearing that he would undo it or give me some trouble, I would not speak to him or give him the letters until my business was done, as it was; and if it had not been so well contrived, no doubt he would have [done] some harm. ## p04R And it is that the first time I went to Toledo, Doctor García asked me whether I brought a letter from Your Lordship for the Cardinal, and I answered that it had not arrived. On the other side Horacio Doria asked me the same and I gave the same answer, and he told me it would matter a great deal that it should arrive, because, speaking to me as a friend and in secret, he did not fear [?] — unless the Cardinal and Garai should hesitate whether it was right, having made the inquiry into his nephew, and so as to give nothing to talk about; and for the same reason, since Doctor Capata had been rector that year and some had begun to talk when he sought the curacy [...], nobody but a middling man [was chosen] to stop the talk; but that reason was secret and for me alone. So it mattered a great deal that Your Lordship's letter should arrive, so that it would be understood that it was done for Your Lordship and not for [?]. And I found myself so pressed that, thinking it would please Your Lordship, I made a signature of Your Lordship's on a sheet of paper as best I could, and had a trusted servant of mine write the substance of the letter, saying that Your Lordship had left me some signatures in blank ## p05 I took care that the letter should be in Your Lordship's style, and it only said, to remove every objection, that the regent, thinking he could not freely come to reside in his canonry, had decided to resign it into the hands of His Most Illustrious Lordship [...]; and that Your Lordship begged him that, as I was there to serve him in it, he would do me the favour, which Your Lordship would value as the greatest. [Then came my brief from Rome to hold the rectorship with the canonry ... the visitors of the college, the abbot and the vice-chancellor are the electors ... I asked Francisco Gonçalez for two letters to the abbot and one to the vice-chancellor, which he wrote at once and very pressingly.] And so, seeing myself so well placed at this time, it seemed to me that I should make another letter in Your Lordship's name for the abbot, saying that I had written to Your Lordship of the favour he did me, and that on his advice the brief had been sent so that I could hold the canonry with the rectorship without any disability, and that Your Lordship was most grateful ## p06 for it and kissed his hands. These things I have done because they were so fitting on this occasion, and I think Your Lordship will approve; and if not, forgive me, I beg Your Lordship to pardon me; whoever tells it to Your Lordship when he could keep silent — Your Lordship will see the truth with which I act and with what desire to serve Your Lordship and please you in everything. [The Cardinal said he would answer from the road ... the see of Sigüenza was given to Fr. Mateo de Burgos, and Pamplona, which he held, to don Antonio Venegas of the Supreme Council of the Inquisition.] And though I do not believe, nor is it to be believed, as Your Lordship says, that they used bad means such as people say, I much fear that some occasion must have been given for the rumour; and some, I think, hold that by [?] and good diligence of the minister one can be given whatever seems just, and this road has been made so wide by those who know little that they [?] suffer. ## p07L [I wrote to the secretary that ... he and I had in mind] to aim at the abbacy of Lerma, where the Duke is now founding a collegiate church; only that we should try to bring in the [?]. He answered that he thought it good, and that when the time came [?] — truly his favour to us is a particular thing, and what we owe him. ## p07R [On the students:] Chaves, his long gown being over there [and his travelling cloak], and one without it, so it has been necessary to make him a gown like the others, because he says he made [?] of the cloak, and the rest [?], and he made a little cassock of black woollen cloth, and he asked me not to write to Your Lordship that I was making him more than a cassock because it was summer, and that for the cloak I should put up the money until his mother had money. Then he told me, when it came to counting the money he brought, that he had taken from the bag forty reales for some boots and other things, and that he would send them to her; and that I should also tell his mother. These are trifles that have annoyed me a little, though I have not let him see it in any way, for it is enough that he is the nephew of whom he is, and the good turn the Regent has done us in this matter of the canonry, that we should do what we can for his affairs. So Your Lordship will see what you order to be done about recovering from [?] the cost of the cloak and the forty reales; given that he does not know that Your Lordship knows it, he even asked me not to write it, as he wanted to [do it himself]. ## p10R [...] the man from La Poveda would have arranged it if he had had an answer from Your Lordship on a particular point I wrote about, which I dare not decide myself: it is that this lady and the Inquisitor Salcedo have for grandmother a daughter of a cleric and of a woman married to a smith, who is reputed a converso; and since it has been proved so clearly that the smith was away when the cleric fathered her on the woman, and that the cleric kept her in his house and raised her as his daughter, they must have made the inquisitor a collegial at Oviedo and then inquisitor; and since then brothers of gentlemen who have been collegials have married into these people, and now I am told that don García de Medrano, collegial of Santiago and Salamanca, a native of Soria, of the habit of Santiago and of the Royal Council, has married an elder brother of his to a sister of this young lady; and an oidor of the Chancery has married, because she was a rich woman; and with all this, since the smith's wife was a married woman and so many things about it are said so plainly, I dare do nothing without Your Lordship's opinion. Where Archivio di Stato di Siena, Concistoro 2308, fasc. 2, a faint pencil “5”(?); DECODE R4794, catalogued “1500–1599” with no status. The cipher A pigpen-like grid: the alphabet in blocks of four letters, each block one family of frames, and a dot moves a frame to another block; a dozen free signs as extra homophones; the numbers 26, 44, 67, 74 as a small nomenclator. How it was deciphered Claude transcribed the slip and George Lasry refined it in CTTS; CTTS cryptanalysis gave 23 values, and Claude completed the key by crib guessing and dragging. What it says “Di alcuni pezzi [d’]i artigliaria 44 di 26”: Their Lordships should act with prudence, since 67 too has some suspicion, and not come to an understanding with the present 74 of 26. The writer trusts that Their Lordships, as he knows, will see that the matter is handled with prudence, since 67 too has some suspicion of it; and he adds that it is not intended that Their Lordships should come to an understanding with the present 74 of 26. Historical context and dating Little can be said: the slip carries no clear text, sender, address or date. Its Tuscan spellings (artigliaria, ancho, prudentia, governin), the numbered nomenclator and the geometric hand point to the 16th century, as does DECODE's dating (1500–1599); no key preserved in Concistoro 2308 reads it, though two Sienese pigpen-type keys of about 1530–55 (DECODE R4776, R4786) share its style. Sebastián Puig y Puig printed fourteen letters from the Schism papers of Francesc Climent, Benedict XIII’s agent in Barcelona, with their cipher passages deciphered. This letter, of 4 December 1398, is not one of them. He printed its clear text as appendix XIX and noted that a ciphered line follows, “de clave desconocida”, in a key he did not know, without printing it. Benedict XIII’s own cipher letters, whose key was rebuilt here from Puig’s one facsimile page, are on Benedict XIII to Climent, 1399–1403 (a different cipher, with its own page). The original is not digitised, and the archivist Josep Mas noted that Puig studied many of these papers at home in 1920–30 and did not return them all. The line may survive in the Arxiu Capitular de Barcelona, or not at all.
The cipher line : not read. Blocker: needs the original. Without its signs nothing can be tried, not even Benedict XIII’s key.

Aus Euer Excellenz wohl erhaltenen schreiben von 1. 9bris, vor welches gehorsamst danckh erstatte, habe unter anderen abzunehmen, dass der Eugen mir gar nicht [?gut] [?seyn], willen Kayser selbst widerrathen [?ihm] eine excusation zu machen. Willen er mir nemlich ganz ungereimbt, als ihme berichtet, dass wir einander besucht, solcher gestalten schreibt, und ich ihn aber [?abfertige], wie beyligende Copia ausweiset, welche allein in wahren brüderlich schuldigsten vertrauen überschickhe, willen er aber [205] sicherlich gegen niemand davon melden wird, bitte ganz gehorsamst ebenfalls niemand, auch selbst dem Althann nicht, etwas davon zu sagen, es wäre dan eveniente casu zu meiner rechtfertigung. Solcher gestalten mache mir feindschafften ohne mein verschulden, sed beati, qui propter justitiam patiuntur. Ich glaube es heisset bey [205] manus manum lavat, von diesem und übrigen wären wunderliche dinge zu sagen, ich will aber einen fiscal abgeben. In puncto der Compagnie ist fast nicht zu glauben, wie nicht allein die [151] sondern auch sonsten jederman die liebe vor Eugen, ia selbsten Kayser täglich [?mehr] verliehret, in ansehen, dass nach dem der curier endlich nach so langer zeit [?mit] des Prinz Plan zu [?Wien] angelanget, Eugen selben schon über 2 monathe [?nicht] [?eröffnen] lasse, hiermit die zeit vergehe, dass ganze werckh aus solchen ursachen in das stecken gerathe, Kayser aber ganz gelassen zusehe. Auf solche weise könte ich füglich die Leüthe nicht länger mehr bey der gedult erhalten. Die Engländer wie auch [?Franzosen] wollen nacher haus gehen, und dörfften als dan unseran [?Hof] und [204] wenig rühmliches durchgehends [?ausstrechen]. [102] belieben nochmahlen amore Patriae, et boni publici den letzten versuch zu thun. Gibt es nichts aus, so kan ich noch weniger das werckh länger souteniren, perditio tua ex te Israel. Ich wirdt succumbiren, der Prinz gloriren, Kayser aber will [168] verliehre Compagnie und die [181] [206] worden, welches der effect bald weisen solle. Meine Dienst aber, so Euer Excellenz auch allen falls an allerhöchsten orth nach dero erleuchten gutbefindten vorlegen könten, werden jederzeit verbleiben, als wahre kennzeichen meiner schuldigsten treüe, und eyfer, wird solche auch nicht erkent, ist doch virtus per semet ipsam laudanda. Der Congress solle anizo bald angehen, weillen der [?hisp.] von Madrit zurückh gekommene currier dem Possobueno zu Londen ordre mitgebracht bey auswechslung deren respectiven Renuntiationen ratione titulorum just einen solchen articulum reservatorium aufzurichten, wie es der Graf von Windischgräz, sunt clara verba, mit dem Marchese Beretti Landi im den Haag zu zeit der [?hisp.] Accession gemacht hätte, welches mich recht consoliert hat, und sehe anizo nichts mehr vor, was die Eröffnung des Congress hindern möchte. Gott gebe, dass das Miosch versprechen einen guten effect haben, sonsten will der Wertheimber nicht mehr zuhalten. Das dieselben mir nun selbst einrathen an eine [?Breunsche] Succession [?nicht] zu gedencken, ist mir umb so lieber, als ich mir ein principe d'honneur gemacht solches nebst villen anderen ursachen hauptsächlich derumb niehemahlen anzunehmen, damit [?nicht] seine, ich hat der Prinz [206] umb dessen dienste zu [?haben], welches schändlich wäre, und was beschehen, nur zu [?ihro] Kayser gethan [?haben]. Ich bitte aber Euer Excellenz seyen so gnädig mir die wahre gemüths neigung Ihrer Kayserlichen Majestät gegen meine wenigkeit zu berichten, damit ich getrost wissen möge, was zu hoffen, wie mich von meinen grossen depensen zu erhollen haben und wider die mir gemachte so ansehentliche feindschafften soutenirt sehen därffte. Dieses wirdt mich animiren umb desto eyfriger denen schweren geschäfften des Congress zu unterziehen. Spes sustinet, animat, et auget. Ich verharre in aller consideration h. C. ## Notes - Codes with a value (Mírka's list or a sibling gloss): 54 Althann, 78 Compagnie, 85 der/dem, 86 die, 99 Engländer, 103 Eugen, 135 hat, 145 ich, 152 Kayser, 167 Miosch, 197 Plan, 198 Prinz. Every letter-spelled passage decrypts with Mírka's table unchanged (`dec.txt`). - Tier B, sense only (holes): 101 [?eröffnen] (new: Engländer 99 < 101 < Eugen 103; "Eugen selben ... nicht [101] lasse"), 111 [?Franzosen], 130 [?gut], 131 [?haben], 139 [?Hof], 146 [?ihm], 149 [?ihro], 164 [?mehr], 168 open, 172 [?mit], 182 [?nicht], 209 [?seyn], 225 [?Wien] (new: after Starhemberg 213, the courier "zu [225] angelanget"). 102 would fit *Euer* (Engländer < 102 < Eugen; "[102] belieben ... den letzten versuch zu thun"), 205 a person (the earlier "Rialp" and "Sinzendorf" both fit the bracket), 151 a feminine or plural noun before *Kayser* (Mírka's "Kaiserin" is out of order); left open. - The full clear text settles the writer: he is the imperial plenipotentiary who must open the Congress (of Cambrai), quotes an order naming "der Graf von Windischgräz" for the Spanish accession made with Beretti Landi at The Hague (1720), and writes from Brussels to a brother at court ("von dort aus", "an allerhöchsten orth"): Ernst Friedrich to Leopold Viktorin, the reverse of DECODE's direction. - *willen* = weilen (because), as in the clear text throughout. *dörfften* = dürften. Translation R5029_en.md # R5029: Brussels, 18 November 1721, English translation Translation of `R5029_reading.md` (Claude Opus 5.5, 23 Oct 2026). The holes are the same: `[?word]` rests on the sense and the alphabetical order of the code list only, `[205]` is a code with no value, `[word]` is supplied. ## Translation Brussels, 18 November 1721. High-born Count. From Your Excellency's letter of 1 November, safely received, for which I most humbly give thanks, I gather among other things that Eugene is not at all [?well-disposed] towards me, because the Emperor himself advised [?him] against making an excuse. If I am supported from there even a little, the advice is very good, but otherwise not; [205] is probably also holding [?with] the Prince under hand. For he writes to me in that way, quite absurdly, when he was told that we had visited each other, and I [?answer] him, as the enclosed copy shows, which I send only in true, most dutiful brotherly confidence; but since [205] will surely mention it to no one, I most humbly ask you likewise to say nothing of it to anyone, not even to Althann, unless it should come to my justification. In this way I make enemies through no fault of mine, but blessed are they who suffer for justice's sake. I believe that with [205] it is "one hand washes the other"; of this and the rest there would be strange things to say, but I will not play the prosecutor. On the matter of the [Ostend] Company it is almost unbelievable how not only the [151] but everyone else loses the love for Eugene, even the Emperor, [?more] every day, seeing that after the courier at last, after so long, arrived [?with] the Prince's plan in [?Vienna], Eugene has [?not] let it [?be opened] for over two months now, so that the time passes and the whole business gets stuck for these reasons, while the Emperor looks on quite calmly. In this way I could hardly keep the people patient any longer. The English and also the [?French] want to go home, and might then [?spread] little to the credit of our [?court] and [204] everywhere. [102] please, once more, for love of the fatherland and the public good, to make the last attempt. If nothing comes of it, I can still less sustain the business: thy destruction is of thyself, O Israel. I shall succumb, the Prince triumph, but the Emperor will [168] lose the Company and the [181] [206] were, as the outcome will soon show. My services, however, which Your Excellency could in any case lay before the highest place as your enlightened judgement sees fit, will always remain true marks of my most dutiful loyalty and zeal; if they are not recognised, virtue is still to be praised for its own sake. The Congress should now open soon, because the [?Spanish] courier come back from Madrid has brought Pozobueno in London the order, at the exchange of the respective renunciations concerning the titles, to set up exactly such a reserving article as the Count of Windischgrätz (those are the very words) made with the Marquis Beretti Landi at The Hague at the time of the [?Spanish] accession; which has much consoled me, and I now see nothing more that could hinder the opening of the Congress. God grant that Miosch's promise has a good effect; otherwise Wertheimer will not hold on any longer. That you yourself now advise me [?not] to think of a [?Breuner] succession is all the more welcome to me, as I have made it a point of honour never to accept it, chiefly, among many other reasons, so that it should [?not] be said: the Prince has [206] me in order to [?have] his services, which would be shameful, and what was done, done only for [?Her] Emperor [?have]. But I beg Your Excellency to be so gracious as to tell me His Imperial Majesty's true disposition towards my humble self, so that I may know with confidence what to hope for, how I am to recover from my great expenses, and whether I might see myself supported against the very considerable enmities raised against me. This will spur me to undertake the heavy business of the Congress all the more zealously. Hope sustains, encourages and increases. I remain with all consideration, h. C.
